THE FIELD SCORPION-GRAS9.—Anyone who is fami- liar with the beainiful forgetene-neitef our streams will have little dtrictilty in detecting a family likeness be- tween it and our present plant; both are members Of the same genus, Mgosotis though the former is un- doubtedly the more attraciiveof the two. We have in Britain some six or seven species of scorpion-grass— some of them of considerable rarity, and others widely distributed.and commonly to beTaet with—and of these the field scorpion-grass, the subject of our present illus- tration, isthe most abundant of all. It -will be found on hedge-banks, the edges of -woods and 'copses, and perhaps more especially on 'cultivated ground, its bunches Of grayish green leaves soon making their ap- pearance on any part of the garden or field that has 0- caped the hoe, and its flowers being ,displayed during June, jut, and August. The stem is weak, often some- what Straggling, and a foot ors° in length, both stems land leaves being a good deal clothed with soft hairs. The calyx is acutely five-cleft, and shorter than the pedicekbearing it. The flowers, when weeompare them with those of the forget-me-net, are small and insigni- ficant-leeking, though they are of too bright and pure a blue to altogether escape our notice. The corolla is Widely displayed and all in ,me piece, but cut up into five bread, rounded lobes. ''The flowers are borne on long lettlftess racemes. Thesellowering stems often fork off into Pairs, and at their termination roll round lflize the tail•of a scorpion, a peculiarity that we may see in the comfrey and some few ether flowers, and which has Procured for our plant its most common popular name. It is sometimes also calledathe field forget-me-not.— " Familiar Wild Flowers," for 0.-toter. When those that look out of the windows be darkened."— Eccles. ill., 5. • Rapt in a world of long ago, Granny sits dreaming half the day; Life's eventide for her grows gray; Even the sunset's lingering glow
4 hoe Viite

Fades fast away. Dear Granny! sun, and moon, and stars For her have lost their wonted light; The eyes that once were sparkling bright Can see no more the golden bars, , And all is night! Yet God is good, and with the cross Ile sends such love her years to bless-- Such wealth of patient tenderness— That day by day de= Granny's loss Grows less and less. And children's children haunt the place - Where' Granny sits, and, full of glee, They clamber wildly on her knee, And love to kiss the dear old face That seems to see. And one Wee figure, quaintly wise, Will linger there when others play, . And never care to'run away; We always call her " Grammy's eyes," The children say. For hour by hour by Granny's side The little maid will sit and read; Or perhaps the tottering footsteps lead, So that.the blind, withench fond guide Caa see indeed. So Granny dear is glad and bright, Fully content on earth to Stay, Till, in the Father's Own good way, - . The sun shall shine, and all the night • Be turned to day. nole.olllevo York Evangslist. "IT'S ONLY A. BEGGAR !" There's a clamour in the city, And the tramp of busy feet; Men and woirfee pass each Other, - Friends and strangers in the street. What care they for ene more being? - Nothing think they, nothing say; Helpless, starving, just a beggar— So they pass him on the way. There's 4 dirty open doorway, Sickening odours up the lane; But a child's face looks and wonders Through a broken window pane— Wondering eyes that seem to question, - Are you hungry? Are you sick? - And tie beggar stops a moment, Leaning weakly on his stick. Church bells•ring, and noisy traffic Of the city's in his brain; Yet the child's face at the window Brings'back memories again. Be is weary,iall of sorrow; • But a little curly head Holds him with a strange, strong power Far the sake of some one dead. .Ah, the beggar's eyes are filling, .111nd his lips are strangely-white, ll'ar he sees in memory's pmcture Forms that long have left his sight— ' Chillish hands that him had fondled, 'Home and baby-laughter sweet; And he felt there was no music 7 'Like the sound oCchildren's feet! Venerlboxid mto all-endearing As the touch of baby-lips; .ol achain that holds a mother Like a baby's finger tips. ..And the beggar's home is empty; Wonder not his eyes are dim— Years ago God took his baby, 'And the mother followed him. There's. a. stillness in the city, •.And the shadows fall apace; •And beneath an arch the moonlight Shines upon an upturned face. But he is no longer lonely; an the country out of sight, 'ln the region we call dreamland, ;Fein s found hisZhome to-night! ••--,l3assell's.*Saturdayiroarnal.

So a go dd rider can tide a horse when he has got one, while a good horseman can makes good hunter out of a horse that knows nothing about it, and can improve, to a considerable degree, a horse that has already learned the andiments of hisstinde. As a rule, 'what ,is called a , hat& _.rider is not a very good horseman. A horse gene- ' rally comes out of his hands no better educated than he , was when he went into them. Again, being able to ride I anything, which some people think is a test of a, goo& rider, is,httle or no test of a good horseman. Many then, can 'ride almost any sort' of a horse in a certain way, who are utterly unable to teach a horse anything,lwhile some, men may be very geed horsemen who are neither bold nor forward riders. AS a rule'' men who are good riders when they are youeg, become better horsemen as they get older, but not better riders. If anyone ,wishes to' form en opiniones to how good a rider or horseman he is, let aim try the follow experiment :—Let him take the handiest horse in his stable, and ;take it alone to ,a moderately-sized hedge and ditch. Then;et him put a half-crown piece between each leg and the saddle, 'wher- ever he thinks best, and tie his reins with a bit of pack thread to the breastplate,l so that they will not fly over the horse's head when he jumps, and then let hien seelf he can take 'his horse up to the fence and jump him over it with his bands in his pockets without dropping the half- crowns. If he cannot do this, or if his horse will not allow him to do this, both he and his horse have bothl somethieg to learn. My readers must not think that if they cannot do this they are not good riders. Very many goodlriders 'could not do it. I only give this as s specimen of what a good horseman can teach himself and his horse' to do.-N. ' • ' THE AUTUMN Orrreose—A correspondent writes to a contemporary :—The weather has been of a very mixed- character dung the last weak, and has told upon the appearance of'the country very much, it has brfught farmers face tO face with the provision of winter quar- ters for their cattle, and put-Bauch of their work upon a winter basis. Generally speaking, cattle are looking well, as they have plenty,of good" food in' the fields to , put them in co6dition tfor wintering ii was upon ' Freckleton mid Newton Marshes on Monday morning, and noticed that a great number of the cattle that are summered there were locking thin, and many of them had their coats standing mpright, as:if the night's cold had been too severe for 'them. The situation is far from being a bleak one, and is well Stocked with food, so that those cattle which were in moretexposed Situations must have suffered keenly. The time for ending the term of the summer's agistment on, these marshes is7the end of the present month.. ffir-some places it is a little earlier Remnants of the harvest are happily very scarce as com- pared with whet we have seen for many years past, but m the Ribble Valley I noticed a field of beans and one of barley AEI unbowed. The latter was first sown, with oats, and having failed was sown with barley, which appears to have done fairly well. During the week much wheatbas been sown, with the ground in excellent condition. The course system Of cultivation operates somewhat ,atbitrarily in the matter of grain growing, else it is hard ,to believe that- men would venture to sownOlvaat with such prices before them. .A. South Lancashire farmer, who has invetted £3,000 in his stock, orb/elev. daysLago, said that he-was satisfied with his landlord, his lend, and his crops,- but the prices were simply ruinous. For interest on his capital be should netblaave a farthing deft after paying rent and other babilitiesthis year. The only crop which be had grown to profit :during the year Awes clover. I a.m afraid thatnhis is true picture asesgards many of our Lancashire and Cheshire cropping, farmers. With regard to the retail price of wheat in 'Mena-Lester, I find that fairly'goodbeead flour is selling at is. 4d. per dozen pounds; while wheat which is simply dressed for 'finteety 61111ftwourite food in this part of Eng- land—is sold-at Ad per pound, or 20. if the purchase amounts to half a damn pounds. It is. quite evident from these facts ,that neither , the grower nor the con- sumer is much considered. . The week has seen ,a vast quantity of potatoes lifMct out of the ground' in good condition. In the F'ylde district I was invariably told that the weight Of the crop was very 'satisfactory, but the tubers wereaindersized. The sharp frost of Sunday night I suspect would Put a check upon Aihe peranospera infestans. 'ffhe•frost penetrated through the dead tops and got freely about the drills, and I do mot expect to hear of much losS for some time to comeby the disease. The prices are ninth complained of by, growers. One mason -Which is urged for a great area of potatoes being planted is that more attention has been pepi to disease- resisting sorts, 'hence the greater security of the crop. In spite ,of the complaints about unprofitable farming, I find that -there is very little market in the, land to let, and I did not mediae pq, far so many "bsekernd " sales of stock where farms.ardehanging hands. This indicates that farmers have not entirely lost hope in the future."— A correspondent from the Garstang districts writes "The cold weather setting in so severely and suddenly has caused farmers to lay in their cattle -earlier than usual. Grass is very plentiful, and pasture fields are lookhigqiiite fresh; cattle are consequentlydobking very well Indeed. 'Potato digging is about ever. , They are not quite so heavy a crop as was anticipanedi and they realise very little money. In fact, the outlook for farmers with large, areas under the plough is very dis- couraging. Turnips and cabbages are very good; yet the prices of wheat, oatmeal, and potatoes are such that ; there is no profit, and in some cases positive loss in 1 growing them:"

NOTES ON. AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURU, &a. , DEN IN 04_,ovER.—A correspondent istrl lave tifeiaces at cici-,rer very full of spots uf d ataivluch ha ncreseod very mach since' harvest.. Could you, or any of our readers, suggest a remedy to stop it spread- ing further ?" Answer.—lt is not common to hear of dodder at this time of year. Probably the miltl autuma has caused it to grow. If cut off now (and it will be: best to mow a circle at least four feet wide round each patch!), and burned where it is, it will be dertroyed ; bra ever thew there may, be. seed in the ground that will . . spring up next year. ~ Fate 'GOOSEBERRY Gichatres.—A 'correspondent writes --. " I see in the 'Gooseberry Growers' Register,' which has jest beeir published, that the Fylde growers have been successful in takkig some 4of the first prizes at the National Show .held in the Botanical Gardens, Manchester, M. ,Roger :Parker; of Klswick, being the heaviest with-twin be Antagonist,' 37dwts.21grs. Mr. Parker also took one 'Of the ft,ur preminm prizes with 'Antagonist,' 23thots. 16grs. ; .Mr. Jas. Threlfall, of Esprick, with 4 Plunder," 24dwts. Mgrs., and .Mr. Parker with ‘Stockwell,',23ciwts. lOgrs. .It is quite musual for the Fykie growers to-claim such honours amcingst the great guns of Cheshire and Staffordshire. I hope that others from the Fylde. will take courage and not be left., behind." . , , A !fovea CAMMiti...NTAL DAIRY SHOW.—The Dairy Show,,l which has just been held at Munich was one of the most successful of the kind that has ever been. held in Ger- many. It was &old in a beautifully-constructed build- ing, the entranoehall of which is very spacious. the roof 1 being- upheld lby massive columns ornamented with statues and handsomely painted. At the end of-the hall is a beautiful fountain,. constructed of red sandstonei which divides the entrance hill front the other departa ments. 111 a-scientific part of the show is in a building which represents Alpine and Bavarian mountain scenery, huts, chalets, hospices, etc., with rocks, fir trees, heather on the bloom, cascades etc. In short, one is suddenly. transported from civilised German life to Alpine rus- ticity, ana one can draw milk from the living goats. The pleasure ofit all is not at all diminished by know- ing that the massive, columns and the rocks are made from cloth and linen. The imitation, however, is so perfect that it defies detection; the sound alone betrays the artifice, as the large halls have a hollow ring about them that is unmistakable. Swam' ENSILAGE.—One of the sweet ensilaav silos of Mr. Fry, of Chobham, near Woking, has just been opened. When the silo was made, rye from about five acres wag first put in whole, and trifolium, also whole, was put. on-the top-of the rye. After this a mixture of closer and rye grass was carted in, filling the silos. Mr. Fry, instead of ramming down the fodder, to make it solid, and to exclude the air as far as possible, puts it in loosely, a few tons at a time, in layers about 3ft. thick, with-the objact of inducing its heating too temperature of at least 122 degieel Far., so as to make sweet instead of lhe'ordiriary sour silage. The result of the opening of the silo showed that the clover and rye grass at the top of the silo had become sweet ensilage. The trifo- Burn, which came next, was mostly sour, though there were layers of it sweet in places. The rye at the bot- tom, as low as it was to be seen, was sour. The clover and rye grass in a second silo was excellent sweet silage. Itavill be seen that Mr. Fry has been entirely successful in. Making sweet silage from clover and rye grass, as he AMISS last year with the same mixture (or clover alone- -we are not sure which) and with meadow hay. No dry- ing in the field is required for these crops. THE MILKING TRIALS AT THE DAIRY SHOW..—The Te- 9111IS of the milking trials at the National Dairy Show have excited much interest. On the Wednesday the cows competing were milked morning and evening, and tthe testing of the milk was carried out by Dr. Voelcker, IMr. Roumieu, and Mr. Tisdall. The awards *ere made upon the "point" system. On Friday afternoon the fol- lowing results were made known :--Champion Prize of 'five guineas, given by Messrs. Tunks and Tisdall, Ken- sington, so many points being given for quantity and so many for quality of the milk, and so many for the time that has elapsed since the birth of the cow's last calf; 1100 points the maximum for the best milking cow in all the classes : Joseph Phillips, Peterborough, for short- horn'cross; Red Cherry, eight years old, birth of last calf May 3rd, total weight of the two milkings 511b5., num- ber of points 99-95. Pure-bred Shorthorns: 1 and 2, ,L N. Edwards', St. Albans, for Cordele, six years; birth of last calf May 25th, 24ilbs., Points 73-74. Shorthorns not • eligible fot nerd Book: 1, Joseph Phillips, for Red Cherry, winner 'Oft e champion prize; 2, A. Stansfield, Todmor- ! den, for Una 2nd, age five years, last calf September 19th, ' weight of milk 44albs. points 94-39. The champion milker, the cow, of Mr. Edwards, is a very fine type of a dairy cow—long, deep, straight, wide and square in the qharters, with thin chine and enormous udder, and excellent milk veins. She has a truly feminine head, a nice fed colour, and a shorthorn all over. , THE BUTTER AND CHEESE EXHIDITS AT +THE DAIRY Snow.—The butter and cheese contests at the National Dairy Show, which has just ended, were very close, and ' the prizes were widely distributed. There was given a champion prize of £3 by the Lord Mayor and Corpora- tion of London for the best sample of butter made in the United Kingdom. The first prize was given to Thomas Mercer, Smalley Fold, Balderstone, Blackburn. Silver 'medals were given for the sample in each of the fresh butter clagges which on the last day of the show is found" in the sweetest and best condition. The first prize for fresh butter, perfectly free from salt, made from fresh cream, also went to Mr. Mercer. Mr. Mercer's fresh ' cream butter showed very fine quality and colour, but amongst so many really good samples it would be in- vidious to particularise freely. In the fresh or slightly salted classes, Ireland scarcely took such a prominent position as it had done in some former years. It, how- 'ever, contributed a few very good samples, and Mr. M. ! 'Forrest, of Rathcoole, co. Cork, one of the most success- ' dul dairy farmers in the south of Ireland,won the second ' .prize in a very large class. The butter-making contest ; took place on Friday, when only four dairymaids com- peted: The first prize was won by Mrs. Holmes, of ‘Sundridge Park Farm, Bron-dey, Kent; the second by, daughter, Miss Fanny Holmes, who was not quite so . expert in salting the butter; and the third by Mrs. G. !Green, of Avon Dairy,. Ringwood, Hants. In the pre- mium "Any other variety" of cheese, in which there ' were 16 entries, an entry made by Mr. J. Cowpe, of ' ,Goosnargh, was highly commended. ' Nonni Laxessmax NOTES.—A fine spell, of weather has again set in. Potatoes are now being cleared off the land, and the latter is working up nicely for winter ' wheat. The potato yield shows a very large percentage •of small tubers, some of them not larger than ordinary ' marbles; but as there is very little disease prices get ' lower, and culinary potatoes are being sold retail in the market at 3d, per stone. Our hay stocks are light, as ' also straw; and, to add to the deficiency of winter food ; for live stocks, the swede crop—never very promising, ' but which was making fair autumn growth—has now 1 been attacked with mildew, and the white, washed-out ' leaves are sadly too numerous in many fields. Our win- ter-keep prospects are still worse, for when the mildew I once attacks the leaves of the swedes the roots make no ' further growth. to speak of. Potatoes are now being ' purchased for cattle and pig feeding, and the old prac- ' tioe of 'steaming potatdes for cattle and pig food, so ! common on our farms prior to 1845, is 'now being gone book to.. Champions can be bought at £1 13s. 4d. per ' ton. Three ' years , ago it was thought the Champion ' would work a revolution in the potato trade—that it : world prove disease-resisting, a good cropper, and a ' good culinary potato. This has not been borne out, for ; under cultivation it has grown coarse, and most of the ' tubent are hollow, so that it is now mainly used for aril- ' mal leod. The Magnum Bonum is one of the best pota- toes grown, and much resembles the old favourite fluke. ' Skerries are still considerably grown, although they are ' not liked in the kitchen, for the number of eyes Makes 5 them difficult aud wasteful top. It is more than pro- ' bable,awing to the use of potatoes for cattle food, that 5 prices will be Up considerably in the ipiing.—R., la, ~ ...., 43.... .HE 1, OF WKSTMINSTER AND 'DAIRY FARMING.— The Duelress of Westminster, on Wednesday, distributed ; the prizes awarded at the annual dairy show at Chester. ' Responding to a vote of thanks on behalf of the Duchess, , the Duke. of - Westminster, after stating that the associa- tion was in an increasingly prosperous condition, said it must be remembered that milk was the only article in ' agriculturaliproduce which ;lately had paid its way at ' all. This -year he found there were 2,350,000 cows in , milk, and dining the year there had been added 278,000 ' young stock, which was a very considerable increase. ' The value of 'the milk produced in Great Britain ; amounted to .the enormous sum of £40,000,000 a year, 5 and he might .say in passing that, the consumption ; of, he believed, the whole of the native produce ' and that of foreign. countries did not amount to • much more than one-third of the cost of drink. ' They could only-wish that that one-third might be ex- tended, and that AS liquqr went down milk would go up. (Applause.) iConnected with this production'af ' milk there was an army of 300,000 milkers employed, ; '.who, at an average of, 3s. 6d. a• week, derived irawages ' T 2,400,000 a year, 'besides the cost of dairymen and ' her, expenses connected. with • the production. This : reierred to Great Britain_ The foreign trade amounted in money value—that was, in milk:. production—to .Z 4500,000 a month. One. London firm alone cleared annually £30,000 by dealing with a French firm of milk-, men in butter alone, included in, the foreign prodaets' which were supposed to the derived 'from milk came ,a. very large quantity, he was sorry to say, of adulterated; matter, which was sold to.thc poorer classes under the; name of cheese or of butter. (Hear, hear.) His Gmca referred also to the question of ensilage, and causedl some laughter by stating that he had made in experk meat with thistles. He confidently believed that by), this time next year he would baable to report in favour' of ensilage made entirely of thistles. (Laughter and cheers.) RIDERS AND HGRSEMEN.—It is difficult to define or classify a good rider, but, in order to give an idea of what I mean, I will divide riding men who can aide, into two classes—good riders and good horsemen. A man may think, and-think with truth, that he is a good rider, but still he may only he an indifferent horseman. 'There is the same sort of ilistinction between a man who scan simply ride well and a finished horseman, that there is between a musician and a musical composer. One of them can play almost anything, but requires his music to be given him, while the other creates his own music,

The reading room at the Vatican Library is now open .to students. No document later than 1815 can be exam- ined. All notes or extracts must be shown to the librarian before leaving. The new Indian institute, situate at the end of Broad- street; Oxford, the foundation stone of which was laid by the Prince of Wales 18 months ago, was opened on Wednesday by the Vice-Chancellor, the Master of Bal- liol, Professor Jewett, in the ,presence of a large and dis- tinguished gathering. THE Nonni POLE.—The following, according to the G4rap4ical Magazine, are the deductions from the work of the Finland Polar Expedition to Sodankyla, in Fin- nish Lapland, during 1883-4, given in the reports of the expedition to the Finland Society of Sciences The North Pole is surrounded by a zone in which terrestrial electric currents are stronger and more variable than on -its northern or southern sides, and the position of which probably depends on a polar auroral zone. The polar aurora is produced,hy an atmospheric electric current, which is capable of being measured and generally of being studied by the, practical methods employed by the Finland expedition, whose instruments have very often produced a diffused light giving the -known spectro- scopic reaetien of the polar aurora." Tux Cnotwia.—The Lancet reports a." well-authenti- cated" case of a cholera patient having been given up as dead and prepared for interment while still capable 'of recovery, Which occurred a week ago in Genoa; and adds that a list of such cases, divided into two cate- gories—first, those who have been ultimately recog;nised as living and rescued in time, and, second, those who have indeed been recognised as such but too late for measures of recovery—is in preparation by an Italian physician. The discussion on cholera has been con- tinued at the Paris Academy of Sciences this week. The most interesting incident was the appearance of M. Ricord, the "father" of the Academy, to make what he called his "profession of faith." M. Ricord said his ex- periences dated a long wax back. He first took arms against the cholera in 1832 in the Paris Hospital, where he was left alone with 600 patients, his colleagues haying taken fright and fled. He then formed the opinion that .cholera is not contagious, and he has seen nothing since to induce him to change that opinion. He admits that, at least in France, the contagionists are pow in the ma- jority, but for his own part he is faithful to his early conviction,. His doctrine is that cholera originates spon- taneously in the place where an epidemic breaks out, but he was careful to explain that this does not mean that it has not "a special cause." But he is opposed to quarantine measures in general, which he considers to be *useless, vexatious, and dangerous." He would have "only one kind of quarantine,' that which would "pre- vent a healthy man from going to live in a milieu where cholera reigns." The room was crowded to excess to hear M. Ricord's declaration. GEOGRAPHICAL SOCIE'TY FOR MANCHESTER.—A meeting to constitute the Manchester Geographical Society, and to appoint a provisional committee, was held in the Mayor's Parlour of the Manchester Town Hall on Wed- nesday. .The Mayor (Mr. P. Goldschmidt) presided. Among those present were the Roman Catholic Bishop of Salford, Mr. B. Armitage, M.P., Mr. John Slagg, M.P., Mr. J. F. Hutton (chairman of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce), the Rev. W. R. Murray, Mr. Alderman Thompson, Mr. S. Ogden, Mr. J. Plant, Mr. H. J. Roby, and others.—The Mayor said it had often been a matter of surprise to him that while Continental nations, like France, Germany, and Austria, devoted so much atten- tion to Geographical research and placed that science so high, yet a maritime and colonising people like the Eng- lish treated it with comparative indifference. While there were so many geographical societies on the Con- tinent, so far as he knew there was in England only one. More was done by either of the nations he had men- tioned, especially by Germany, than by Englishmen in the way of making known to the world the vast un- known tracts of land which lay beyond the beaten track of the ordinary traveller. Though we could boast of having a Grant, Speke, Livingstone, and Johnson, yet this made it all the more wonderful that so little interest seemed to be taken in the matter by the great mass of Englishmen. The importance of such a society, espe- cially from a commercial point of view, was unnecessary for him to point out. For the requirements of trade it was important that they should find new markets for their produce.—Mr: Hutton said such a society would be of enormous value to the. eommunity, and it was a dis- krace to Manchester that there was no such society al- ready established. There were 21 such societies in France, four in Portugal, five in Africa. The one society in England numbered 3,400 members, and had an income of £7,200 per annum, aided by a Government grant of £5OO. They would require a room for the use of the society, where the Members could study maps and geo- graphical literature. They wanted 500 or 600 members, and unless the society included ten or a dozen of the leading, merchants of Manchester to give their energy and time to make it a success, he was afraid Mr. Sower- butts would have but poor success.—Mr. B. Armitage, M.P., the Bishop of Salford, Mr. J. Slag, M.P., and others having tho eatalalkshment of such a, society, a resolution to that effect was carried, and a provisional committee appointed.

div.head: ALLEGED CHILD MURDER AT
div.p: ALLEGED CHILD MURDER AT
RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, Mr. T. J. Ridg- way, the coroner for the honour and fee of Halton, held an inquest on the body of the male child of Ellen Lunt. domestic servant to Miss Boyers, grocer, Church-street, Run- corn.—Mr. W. Handley was the foreman of the jury, abd Mr. Superintendent Leah was present on behalf of the police.

Eliza Boyers said she was a single woman living at 57, Church-street, Runcorn, and kept a grocer's shop there. The only person living in the shop besides herself was Ellen Lunt. She was her general servant, and had been with her for 15 months. She was not aware until Friday, the 17th instant, that anything was the matter with Lunt. On that day, about soon, she saw Lunt in great pain, and she told her to go to bed and she would bring her a cup of tea in a while. Lunt afterwards went upstairs, and she was followed by Mrs. Yarwood, who came down in a few minutes. She (witness) then went into Lunt's bedroom. Lunt was then at the loot of the bed. Witness said to her "Get into bed ; you will be starved ;" and she replied "No, I'm not starved." She then went downstairs, and in a few minutes went up again, when Lunt was standing at the foot of the bed. She got into bed, and witness asked her if she would have some more clothes on, and she answered that she was warm enough. Witness lifted up the valance of the bed, and looking into the chamber utensil saw that something was wrong, She said to Lunt "What have yon done? You ' have brought disgrace on me and yourself. I did not know you had a sweetheart. I have never seen you speak to any- one except your brother-in-law, and surely you have not brought that shame ;" or some words to that effect. Lunt said "No," and she went for Mrs. Yarwood, who went back with her, and thev went upstairs together. Witness then said "Whose baby is it ?" and Lunt made no reply. She then sent for Dr. Bagnall. He came, and went upstairs, and afterwards went for the police. She had no idea that Lunt was enciente, and so far as she knew Lunt had made no pre- paration for her confinement. _

P.S. Walley said about two o'clock on Friday, Dr. Bag- nail came to the police station, and he accompanied him to Miss Boyer's house. Dr. Bagnall and Mrs. Yarwood went upstairs, and then Dr. Bagiaall returned with a chamber utensil, from which he took a child. The child was washed by Mrs. Yarwood and „placed In a small box, and he brought it to the police station. It had since been in his custody. Dr. Bagnall deposed to finding the child in le chamber utensil, head downwards. Life was extinct, but the body was not cold. He thought it was quite possible the child might have passed into the utensil in the position be found it without any external herd pressure being used on the part of the mother. He saw that Lunt had the appearance of being just confined. She said she had made no prepara- tions. He described at length a post-mortem examination he had made, and said in his opinion the child was born alive, and had an existence apart from the mother. In the utensil there was a.v.antity of fluid, and he thought the child had been suffocated in it. The Coroner said the point of real importance which the jury had to consider Was whether the child had come to a natural death or whether it bad been murdered, or whether the child had died in being born. It was a case which must rest entirely on the medical evidence, and to enable them to return a verdict of wilful murder against the mother, they most be satisfied in their own minds that the child was bern alive and had an existence , apart from the mother. They had the evidence of the doctor that the child bad breathed, and theftfore to that extent was born alive. The coroner then pointed out that the fact that Lunt bad not made any preparation for the birth of the child was enspi: dons. The doctor's opinion was that the child had died from suffocation, but 80 far as this particular case went he did not think that question arose. The first question the jury had to consider was 2,8 to the birth of the child. The jury then retired, and after an absence of about 20 • minutes returned. The foreman said the verdict of the jury was that the child was born alive and died from want of attention at birth through that negligence of the mother. —The Coroner : That is a verdict of wilful murder against the mother of the child.

At the Pont des Arts, in Paris, is a blind man, who carries •a board around his neck with this singular sign —"Blind by Birth' apd by Accident." "See here, my good man," said a passer-by, "your sign is positively distracting. Can you tell us how you happen to be blind ,by birth and by accident at the same time ? " "Easy enough," said the old man. "You see I'm blinq by birth myself, and I've bought out a blind man who dui business at- the other 'end of the bridge. He was blind by accident."

TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION. HICIPBY Wnernam. We hear it said on all sides that this is an "age of transition." Not only in the political world but in Ithe labour world this is true. The signs of the times point in a very marked fashion to the very great necessity that exists for working-men to take such steps as shall bring the control of coming events, much more than as at present, within their grasp. It needs no philosopher to point out that the political element which bears so much upon the welfare of the masses has since 1832 been silently, yet surely, enabling the people to work out their own redemp- tion. In whatever direction we look, efforts are be- ing made, by those who are gifted with a little foresight, to "educate our masters." Robert Lowe could see that when once the thin end of the wedge was inserted no one could tell where it would be driven to. Borough suffrage meant county suffrage, which in its turn means manhood suffrage. But while this is being worked out by the politicians we must not forget that it is only the means to an end. And who shall say what the end maybe? Education is being forced upon our children in the day school, and for our young men Technical Instruction of such a character is in existence that in the near future most undoubtedly that nation only will win that has taken advantage of its opportunities. I am fed to make these remarks in consequence of having studied the report issued by the Royal Com- missioners on Technical Instiuction. The report is in two large volumes, and the mass of information brought together is simply surprising, and I must say that I think every employer ought to spend a sum of money in the purchase of the report, and by this means spread it amongst the people. I have noticed copious reviews in the various daily papers, and I was pleased to see the Warrington Examiner some time ago gave lengthy extracts of portions, more especially referring to the agricultural interest. It is no secret that the agricultural like the trading interest of England will need strict attention, and that scientific methods must, where possible, be adopted if we in England are to hold our own. The English working-man is essentially of a conser- vative turn of mind. It is not without mush per- suasion that he leaves the old ruts. The same bears out with the English farmer. As a consequence of this reforms come about but slowly. But once convince the farmer that certain methods will of a certainty bring larger profits and, unless the land- owner stands in the way, he at once adopts them. The reaping machine has superseded the reaping hook and the scythe. The threshing machine hao taken the place of the flail, and in consequence new trades have sprung up in the towns. A great change has come over the face of the country side. Scientific farming shows itself wherever adopted. Schools are established for teaching agriculture. But in the report before me how little is done in Great Britain and how much has yet to be done may be seen at a glance. Of course the change is great as compared with the past. In Germany there are thirteen Institutes of the highest class, more or less sup- ported by Government, and at which practical and scientific farming forms a compulsory part of the young farmer's education. In Great Britain we have established a Chair of Agriculture at South Kensing- ton and made a grant of £l5O a year towards the endowment of a Chair of Agriculture at the Univer - sity of Edinburgh, and still we expect to hold our own. Other institutions exist, but they are either of a voluntary or self-supporting character. But it is in the mechanical trades that the greatest discrepancy is seen. I wonder how many workmen there are in Warrington who could turn to a technical school for information in their own particular craft; yet in Germany and throughout the Continent this is a possibility within reach of the workman. The fact is Trade Unionism works in a vicious circle ; where it starts it ends, and at home here it takes no notice of the workman so long as he pays his contribution. About the trade itself it bothers little BO long as the highest standard of wages can be maintained. The employer in this differs not one jot from the work- man ; together they squeeze the goose that lays the golden egg, forgetting that while they are doing the goose to death our neighbours on the Continent are doing their best to nurture it. I may give an example or two of what they are doing on the Continent. In Remscheid, 18 miles from Diisseldorf, a trade school has very recently been established for the instruction of apprentices in the construction of edge tools and other implements manufactured in the district, in which it competes with Sheffield and Birmingham. From this town, which a few years ago was a mere village, an important trade is carried on, including some with our own colonies. Now comes an impor- tant feature. The school established for the promo- tion of this industry has been erected at a cost of £lO,OOO. The pupils are taught drawing and design in its applieation to the different kinds of ironwork. Think of this, fellow-workingmen, and don't wonder any longer how it is that our trade is not so brisk as we could like it. In all trades it is alike—proficiency if possible, but profit under any circumstances. In France we have M. de Lnynes lecturing on the manufacture of glass. He exhibited the potters" wheel at work, and had glass blowers from various works to illustrate the mode of blowing glass. Another feature, not at all a desirable one, was wit- nessed at Lyons. A lecture, one of a course, was de- livered on Sunday morning on the art of weaving, and , about 150 persons were present. Classes for women are held with the view of fitting them to enter busi- ness houses. At Bonn, boys 14 years of age, were en- gaged drawing and painting rough designs on cheap earthenware. Those boys displaying the most artistic skill are, of conrse, promoted to work of a higher character. But it is in the machine shops, I think, where the greatest efforts are put forth. Side by side in the mills and factories may be seen English and foreign machines of the beat and newest kinds. A student of the highest class does not consider his education com- plete by serving at one factory or learning at one in- stitute. But strangest feature of all last year there were 6 English students at Mullhouse completing their trade education. There can be no doubt that if the Englishman cares to set himself to the work he need not fear anything on the Continent. Very few in- stances exist where foreigners, unaided, have beaten us out of the markets. I have noticed on the German railways locomotives from Manchester. In their factories are looms bearing the names of Bradford and Keighley makers, and the report gives numerous instances where men have been sent over to England to fit themselves to take manager's situations in their own native towns. Since the Great Exhibition, over 30 years ago, some strange things have come to pass. We sent there our best machinery. We invited the intelligent foreigner to come over and see it in full working order. Orders came to our machinists; but from that time competition became keener. Associa • tions were formed, and we have invited the keen- visioned foreigner to inspect our works; but the Iron and Steel Institute this year thought to put a stop to such things. The Sheffielders refused to open their works to the gaze of everyone, and in a pet the scien- tists took themselves off to Chester. We are now in for the race, not exactly for wealth, but for very ex- istence; and workmen will have to ask themselves the questions—ls it for my welfare? Is it for the national welfare that I should refuse to do what I am assured can be done? If they answer in the affirmative, well; but if not, why all will be lost. I have no wish to act or speak as the Cassandra on trade questions. I have pointed out how our neighbours across the channel are preparing themselves for the struggle. I hope the time is near when the Bismarkian grasp will be wrenched from the German workman's throat, and that he will rise to a higher level, but in the meantime—what? We have the word of Professor Leone Levi that "a brighter future is at hand, and that some years of success and prosperity:might before long reward the patient hand of labour and cheer the anxious endeavours of our merchants and manufac- turers." In the report to which I have so slightly referred, Germany, Switzerland, and Italy ' are dealt with very largely, and to these, as partaking more of the foreigner, has my attention been drawn. Little is said of the position these workmen occupy in the social scale. From my own observation and reading I am bound to state that it is one of degradation, and that all their efforts to raise themselves end in nearly all cases at the prison ; that while we have a Morris and a Tucicwell lecturing to the masses on art, and preparing the way for comfortable and happy homes, black bread and German sausage, wooded shoes and saur kraut, bound the horizon of these poor workmen.

THE REFORM AGITATION. LORD SALISBURY MOBBED IN SCOTLAND. On Tuesday evening the Marquis of Salisbury addressed a large meeting of Conservatives at Dumfries, it being the last speech it had been arranged he should make during his stay in Scotland. Tne noble Marquis, who had been the guest of the Earl of Galloway since Friday, arrived in the town shortly after five o'clock by special train, and was accompanied by Lord Cranborne. Lord Salisbury was met at the station by the leading members of the Conservative party in the district, and received a very enthusiastic wel- come, which was repeated when be arrived at the King's Arms Hotel, where dinner was served. The meeting after- wards took place in a large marquee, and was crowded, accommodation having been provided for about 5,000 per- sons. The Duke of Buccleuch and Queensbury took the chair, and was infinentially supported. Various addresses from local Conservative Associations having been presented, Lord Salisbury, in reply, passed a high eulogium upon the character otthe late Duke of Buccieuch,and then proceeded to say that he approached the task before him with satisfac- tion, because they now were upon the verge of the close of the autumn campaign. It appeared to him it had left the Conservative party more united than ever it was before, and it had given to the country an opportunity of discussing questions deeply affecting the constitutional working of our Government, an opportunity of hearing both sides of the question, and forming their judgment thereupon. From what he saw and heard, he did not think the judgment was very unfavourable to the existing constituencies of the country. (Cheers.) While he was being driven to the station the windows Of Lord SalisJury's carriage were smashed with stones. For- tunately the occupants were not injured. The crowd bad previously smashed the windows of some of the other car- riages used by the leading gentlemen who had attended the meeting. On Lord Salisbury arriving at the station a great crowd was found to have assembled there. He immediately passed inside to his saloon, the constables meanwhile keep- ing the people back. But no sooner had he got inside than a struggle arose between the different parties in the crowd about the booking office, and the police had to draw their staves and clear the station. The turbulence heard during the progress of the meeting manifested itself in more than mere groaning. A considerable number of the rougher CliiB bad gathered in the vicinity of the meeting place. After hooting and groaning for a while they began to make attempts to carry the barricades by assault. These attemPtel however, proved ineffectual until after Lord Salisbury bee' left the place. Then the barricades were broken down. Stone-throwing became pretty general, and the consequence was that many of the public lamps in the neighbourhood were completely shattered. A crowd gathered also in front of the King's Arms Hotel, and here more stoning was in- dulged in. Most of the lower and several of the higher windows in the hotel were wrecked. Whilst engaged in the performance of his duty one of the constables was severely cut about the face. The mob outside the hotel was composed almost entirely of young roughs, who were most demonstra- tive in their expressions of hostility towards the noble Mar- quis. Just before 11-30 the mailed steamed into the station, and Lord Salisbury's saloon having been attached in a cen- tral position, it departed for London amid loud cheering, ac- companied by considerable hooting.

Mr. J. Chamberlain, M.P., attended a meeting held at Newtown, on Saturday, by the Liberals of Montgomerl- shire, and delivered two vigorous, incisive speeches on the question of Reform, and on the line of conduct that is at present being pursued by the Conservative leader'. In Ilia first speech, he remarked that there was only one word which could characterise the charge which Lord Randolph Churchill had made against the Birmingham Corporation. The statement was a falsehood, and it was a wanton false- hood, for the slightest inquiry wculd have convinced Lord R. Churchill bow groundless was his attack. In the right hon. gentleman's second speech, he said he was a good deal puzzled when he read that Lord Salisbury, in acknowledg- ing the receipt of a resolution sent to him from a town in Wales, said he "rejoiced to know that the voice of Wales was entirely on the side of the House of Peers." It had since been whispered to him, however, that "the voice a Wales" which gave Lord Salisbury so much satisfaction proceeded from the back parlour of a public-house, and wee concocted by a committee of three, of whom one was a paid secretary, and the other a very little boy. Lord Salisbury had challenged him to march up to London at the head of his constituents, and had expressed a hope that he woald get his head broken for his pains. He accepted Lord Salisbury's challege on condition that Lord Salisbury headed the column that he had to withstand him (Mr. Chamberlain). The Government, Mr. Chamberlain added, would continue to resist the pretension of the Peers, as in doing so they believed they were defending the liberties of the people. Speaking at a great Liberal demonstration at Denbigh, on Monday, Mr. Chamberlain directed attention mainly to the position occupied by the House of Lords, not only in refer- ence ui the extension of the franchise, but also to le,gisla- Hon generally. The chronicles at that House he said, were one long record of confessions, delayed until they had lost their grace, of rights denied until they had been ex.' torted from their fears. He instanced the conduct of the Lords towards Ireland and Welsh Nonconformity in the past in support of these assertions. "We have been too long a Peer-ridden nation," the right hon. gentleman added, " but I hope you will see to it that if they will not bow to the mandate of the people they ehelllose for ever the author- ity which they have so long abused." Sir Charles Dilke, addressing his constituents at Kensing- ton Town on Monday night, dwelt on the importance to the constituencies of obtaining a redistribution of electoral power, but pointed out that the first step towards a large and complete redistribution was the franchise. He admit- ted that some regard should be paid to historical considera- tions, and that a census population was somewhat falla- cious as a test of electoral requirements but it was that of the Conservatives. He severely criticised the statements of Lord Randolph Churchill about the scheme of redistri- bution recently published, showing that the noble lerd'e figure were ridiculously erroneous,and that they displayed an extraordinary recklessness in misstatements of figures even for the noble lord. It was not by misstatement of figures or blocking of bills that the country would be baulked Of reform. The people were now thoroughly aroused, and if they were met again by the rejection of the Fran- chise Bill their triumph would only be more crushing and complete. The Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Childers, on Mon- day evening addressed a crowded and enthusiastic meeting of his constituents in the Town Hall at Pontefract. He could perceive of no greater misfortune for the Lords or for their influence in the country than that they should again reject the Franchise Bill, and thus bring about the calamity which would certainly follow. The Conservatives should remember that in following Lord Salisbury on this question - they were rejecting advice given by the late Lord Beacons- field, and were reversing his policy. At present it looked as if the contest must be fought out to the bitter end. In the end., however, the popular will must prevail. Speaking on Monday night at Newport (Mon.), Mr. Her- bert Gladstone said the Government had nailed their colours to the mast, and would not surrender to Conservatives. They might concede more than the Opposition had a right to expect, but they would maintain the absolute right of managing their own business, and would not submit to the House of Lords dictating the time of a dissolution. At all the above and at many other meetings resolutione strongly supporting the Government have been passed. A very successful demonstration of the Conservatives of West Cheshire, in support of the action of the House of Lords on the question of reform and of the general policy of the Conservative party, took place on Saturday at Chester. Nearly 2,000 persons attended the meeting held in the Music Hall in that city, at which Sir Philip de Malrale Grey Egerton presided. The principal speakers were the Marquis of Waterford and Sir Richard A. Cross, M.P., and among the other gentlemen on the platform were the meaw bers of Parliament for West Cheshire (the Hon. W. F. Tollemache and Mr, H. J. Tollemache) and a large number of the prominent 'Conservatives of that division of the county.—Sir Richard Cross said in the first place they had met, to use Lord Hartington's own phrase, to demonstrate and to show that they did not believe the outcry which was made now against the House of Lords was an honest outcry —(cheers)--and that with them at all events this outcry should fail in the results which it was wished to produce. (Cheers.) And in the second place they were anxious to know bow to destroy the fallacies which their enemies had placed before them on the questions of enfranchisement and redistribution for the purpose of misrepresenting the true state of things and of misleading public opinion on those points. (Applause.) The one thing which the present Government and all the members of it seemed most terribly afraid of was facing the constituencies. (Applause.) This showed that they must be ashamed of their conduct. (An- plause.) It used to be the boast of the Liberal party that they were never afraid to go to the country, that they kneW the people were on their aide, and that whatever happened in the House of Commons they might at all events fearlesslF appeal to the people; but that was what now they dared not do, and they were prepared by any possible means to pre- vent it. The majority which the Government might obtain on the Franchise Bill in the autumn session would not ex- press the private and individual feeling of the members Of the House of Commons, it would be secured by the power of the Caucus; and it was in such cases as that that we felt the full value of the House of Lords, who in their past action and that which they would undoubtedly again take were doing no more than their duty to the people. (Applause.) The Dublin Constitutional Club held a meeting on Tues- day in support of the action of the House of Lords i.E7 reference to the Franchise Bill. Mr. Gibson, M.P., presi- ded.

Mr. Childers, Chancellor of the Exchequer, addressed his constituents on Tuesday night, at Knottingley Town Hall. He said the Liberals were in the middle of a severe struggle with their opponents, whose citadel was a majority in the House of Lords; and in the course of that struggle the Go- vernment would be compelled, as a matter of duty, when they-met again to introduce the Franchise Bill, and try to prove to their opponents the simple truth that if two men had to ride one horse one must sit behind. The Conser- vatives did not believe it, and the liberals were bound to prove it.

- Speaking at a great Conservative meeting at Hereford, on Tuesday, Sir N. Hicks• Beach said he had a strong objec- tion to increasing the members of the House of Commons. He was against abolishing the three•cornered constituen- cies., The publication of such a scheme ought to make the Conservatives more determined than ever that the Prime Minister should not be enabled by a lever to force an unfair scheme through Parliament —A vote of censure on the Go- vernment policy was passed.

FRUIT TuxEs.—Fruit growers from variouacauses are frequently compelled to move trees of several' years' growth, and in most instances the trees are much bone- fitted by it. Those acquainted with the walk find no difficulty, with kpreper appliances, in moving trees with hundredweights or tons of soil attached to them. -. 'Here life shall just •explain how a cottager, in a very short time, could move a tree of a dozen years' growth if he desired it, with the assistance of one or two of the 'neighbours. Assuming that the tree has been-cut round, as we have already explained for other purposes, as well as being tuaderzinuedk so that if pushed on one side it will give way, showing that all root communication is cut off. One sidekof the hole must be cut to slope; then if the plank is 'leaned to one side and a strong plank thrust under, or, if necessary, two, and in this case they should be braced together by nailing a piece ortwo of wood across. Tliet tree may now be drawn in an up- right position, arid,the: base brought to rest on the planks, which are to serve the purpose of a sledge to convey it to where it is required. An easy method to get it on the sledge is to place a few uprightstaves round the ball tif , earth, and a rope or a chainrround that; and, whilst oue steadies the tree, a few lads would be :delighted with 'the job of pulling it to its place, when the rope may be detached and secured-to the sledge to draw the ,plant to its new ' home. Previous to depositing it in the hole, it 'is of importance to ascertain ' that it is of the "right depth as it may involve much unnecessary labour if, after it is put in, it is either too deep or too shallow. The only way to make sure ia by actual measurement of the depth of soil attached•to the tree and the depth of the hole. To prevent the plant dropping with a sudden jerk the•sides should be sloped as in the one it came from. What militates against the wellbeing of moved trees is the great reduction of roots that must unavad- ably take place, sometimes to the extent of two-thirds. This demands that great care must be taken of those left. • When we have laden able 'to foresee that a • tree must be moved, we have thought best to cut a harrow trench half way round and about two or three feet mom the stem of the tree End fill it with soil and half decayed leaves or manure, in which abundance of young' roots will be formed in a year, and most of the added com- post will depart from them when required. The follow- ing year the other side may be done, and the plant will the year following be so , well furnished with feeding roots that nothing can happen to it if moved. We would advise novices in tree planting to practice the above on all trees they intend moving, and we must also remind them that in taking up trees so operated upon the ex- i coveting must commence outside the boundary of thej ring of fresh compost or all the roots will be lacerated. In moving such a tree it isquite safe to remove all loose: soil or such as may be moved by the prongs of the fork., There is frequently more sail left on the surface round, the stem than there need be, as it , only increases thek weight to be conveyed, and so long as it is not well penetrated by roots by all means move it. THE FRONT GARDEN.—We may write.' Ichabod " over the front garden for 1884, for its glory has.suddenly and speedily departed. Dahlias, ageratums, heliotropes (cherry pie), geraniums, and lobelias bowed their heads with forced submission on the morning of the 10th, in the presence of "Jack Frost." Everything ic destroyed that the destructive energy of 11 degrees of frost could accomplish. We were almost stunned when on the morning of the 10th we viewed the garden and wit- nessed so many prostrate friends. There had not been any previous warning beyond the immense 'flakes of snow that fell the day before. It is true, there had been one or two slight frosts, but not snough to hurt the most tender plant exposed to its influence. There had not been the usual nipping for a night or two, and then the final blow, but the blow first. Some owners of gardens have got excited, and have rushed at the throats of the poor dahlia's,' and cut their heads 'off. Apprehen- sive that the roots would suffer like the tops, they have dug them up, forgetting that the frost must be of suffi- cient severity to penetrate through tWo or three inches of soil before it reaches them. So far only the leaves and the very young shoots have been damaged, and so long as there is any green in the stem and main shonts they have a duty to perform to the roots, and, however disagreeable their appearance may be, it must be endured for two or three weeks longer, though there can be no harm done by moving the dead portions. ' ' THE WINDOW.—No time should be lost in securing the requisite number of bulbs, such as hyacinths and tulip ' /31 as well as a suitable soil and the-required number o ' clean pots. The soil usually employed is composed o turfy loam, in which the grass is decayed. Coarse said, such as may be procured from a river, or that which has:been washed by water currents, also leaf mould, to the extent of a sixth or an eighth, with sufficient sand to give it a sandy appearance. Two or three-year-old cow dung, passed through a quarter-inch sieve, is much thought of by some growers, and is added in the same proportion as the leaf soil, which depends on the tena. city of the soil or turf. GREAT LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT WARRINGTON SPEECHES BY MR. WILLIAM CROSFIELD, J.P., MR. SLAGG, M.P., MR. McMINNIES, M.P., AND MR. P. RYLANDS, M.P. TORCHLIGHT PROCESSION. On Monday night another great demonstration in favour of the Franchise Bill and in condemnation of the action of the House of Lords was held in the Public Hall, Warring- ton. Although it was not found necessary to provide means for holding an overflow meeting as on the previous occasion when Lord Dalhoasie,,a member of Her Majesty's Govern- ment, waspresent, yet the present demonstration was in some respects an even more striking display of the Liberal feeliug of the borough. Not only was the Public Hall filled to overflowing by an enthusiastic audience, but after the meet- ing the political ardour of the gathering was exhibited in a still more unique and striking manner by a torchlight pro- cession, an account of which we give below. The meeting was timed to cemmence at a quarter to eight o'clock, but the deors were thrown open two hours before that time and the hall was rapidly filled in every part. The hall, as usual on such occasions, had bean enlivened with banners and political mottoes. In front of the organ a large banner was placed, on which were inscribed in bold letters " Gladstone, the people's Will ;" along the front of the gallery were the words "The will of the nation shall not be set aside by the whisper of a faction,"" The House of Lords must be mended or ended" and the names of prominent Liberals—" Bright, Hartington, Granville, Chamberlain, Harcourt, Dilke." At the end of the hall opposite the platform a banner with the words "Crosfield forever" upon it was placed in a position to be seen of all observers. The figures-529—0f the majority by which Mr. McMinnies was returned te the present Parliament were again placed in front of the platform and their being affixed was the signal for a round of cheer- ing. The long period of waiting before the meeting com- menced was enlivened by polical songs, which were sung by a Mr. Ratcliffe, from Bedford Leigh, and inspiriting re- citations by another gentleman from Tyldesley. On the arrival on the platform of the party of speakers and promi- nent local Liberals there was a great outburst of cheering, Mr. W. Crosfieli and Mr. Mcninnies coming in for specially warm receptions. The chair was occupied by Mr. Geo. Crosfield. J.P., and there were also on the platform— Mr. J.G. memianics, M.P., Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., Mr. John Slagg, aI.P., Revs. R Filcher, Edward Moore, Wm. Pilling, A. Keaworthy, and G. E. Cutting; Mr. William DdcMinnies, J.P., Councillor Charles Broadbent, J.P., Coun- cillor John Crosfield, J.P., Councillor Fred. Monks, J.P , Alderman John Burgess, J P., Mr. Ziba Armitage, J.P., Alderman C. J. Holmes, J.P., Mr. Nicholson (barrister), London, Councillors George Dakin, William Pierpoint, John Brown, F. Dixon, James Barker, and Peter Caldwell ; Messrs. James Parkinson, J. Bonnell, T. Morris, T. Birchall, C. S. Burgess, Frank A. Roberts, Richard Dutton (Lymm), J. H. Gornall (Penketh), J. Swanwick (Lymm), 1.1. Cameron (Lymm), E. J. Guest, J. Winser, A. H. Crosfield, John Crosfield, jun., T. H. Poole, F. Wright, C. Sudlow, J. Mona. field, sen., L. Ellison, J. Titehett, T. Flood, F. W. Monks, H. Thornton, J. Bouehier, S. Barlow, H. Whitham, W. Longshaw, T. Davies, J. W. Hall, E. Twiss, J. Summers- gill, A. Bamford, B Farrar, H. Roberts (Liberal agent), and W. Roberts. Mr. H. ROBERTS said he had had a letter from their worthy president. Mr. Samuel Rigby. tCheers.) He should not take up the time of the meeting by reading it but would hand it to the reporters to publish. He had an an- nouncement to make with reference to the procession. That matter, he explained, had been forced upon them in a great measure as the spontaneous wish of the patty. (Hear, hear.) He had informed the Chief Constable of their pro- cedure on Saturday morning last, and he acknowledged the information by saying he would do everything he possibly could to assist in carrying it out; but he had had an inti- mation from him that night that he could not be responsible for the peace of the town. (Cries of "Shame" and " We will.") He thought the only observation he would make in reference to that matter was that the Chief Constable might have told him earlier than last last thing that night. (Hear, hear.) He thought the Liberal party might be safely responsible for the peace of the town—Cloud cheers) —and therefore he had only to ask them for the credit of the party and for the credit of ehe town to which they be- longed to see that the procession was carried out in a satis- factory, in a gentlemanly, and in a perfectly peaceable way. (Hear, hear.) He did not think they should have any pro- vocation from the other side, and they were not going to give them any provocation. (Cheers;) He then explained the route the procession would take, saying that they would end by going along Wilderspool Causeway—(A voice: To the brewery," and loud laughter)—they should stop about half a mile from Wilderspool brewery—(laughter)—and the procession would file around Mr. Crostield's carriage and return back to the Liberal club. He did not think any of them would have any regrets after the whole thing was over—certainly not if the Conservatives did not offer any opposition. (Hear, hear and cheers.) The following is a copy of the letter from Mr. Rigby: —" Fern Bank, Liverpool-road, Chester, 18th October, 1884. My dear am very sorry not to be at your meeting on Monday, but at present my doctor forbids me attending exciting public meetings from home. I hope you will have a good strong meeting, and some good homely expressions of opinion as to the desirability that the Franchise Bill should pass soon—and no compromise—of our confidence in the present Government, also in condemnation of the persistent obstruction in the House of Commons to all useful legisla- tion. It becomes most manifest that the time has arrived when the House of Lords should undergo some re-modelling. Mr. Morley says ended or mended—e would rather mend than end. Let the House be purged of all those members who never attend except at the beck of the wire-pullers of the Tory party, and those only retained who have shown their fitness to aid and counsel rather than hinder good laws when fatly debated in the other House. Wishing you every success,—Believe me, yours truly, SAMUEL RIGET.—TO Mr. Henry Roberts." The CHAIRMAN, who was received with load applause, said that although he was not a resident in the borough their friend Mr. Roberts did not like to let him go into the background, and permit him to take his part in London in the political affairs of this nation. He (Mr. Roberts) sell he belonged to Warrington and that he must continue to perform his duties, to which he could not give an unwilling consent. (Hear, hear.) He was sorry he could not be down at the last meeting when Lord Dalhousie was here, owing to engagements, but he made up his mind that nothing would prevent him coming that night. (Cheers.) They had held that meeting to ex- press their opinion as to the moral right of the House of Lords to refuse their assent to the Franchise Bill which the House of Commons, the representatives of the people, had by large majorities three or four times over, passed. (Hear, hear.) He was a constituent of South-West Lan- cashire, though not of the borough of Warrington, and they had there got a representative who had the title of G.C.B. (Laughter.) Well, Sir R. Cross had made use of some of the most—he did not want to use an offensive word but he would say extreme expressions of al- most any of the members who occupied the front bench of the opposition side of the House of Commons.
