What is the use of the 700 or 800 meetings that have been held throughout the country to protest against the action of the House of Lords, if they had not rejected the Bill ? " He wondered what Sir R. Cross would say if the Franchise Bill were passed, and if when he CAIRO to look at the figures of the poll of South-West Lancashire he found himself third or fourth upon the poll. Would he say that a man told a wil- ful and deliberate lie if he said that South-West Lancashire had rejected hies ? (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He (the chairman) thought it was a parallel case. If the House of Lords had not positively rejected the Bill they had refu- sed to pass it, and the distinction was without a differ- ence. (Hear, hear.) And what did these men say? They had made considerable progress during the last twelve months. This time last year they never found the Conser- vatives—he called them 'Tories—say that they were in fa. your of the county franchise being assimilated to the bor- ough franchise, but as the session went on they found that public opinion was so strong that they dare not venture to go against it. These Conservative members—or Tory mem- bers—he would not go wandering over the country but would take the speeches of those in their own vicinity. There was Mr. Wm. John Leigh, the member for East Cheshire, who said Why my constituents will be 30,000." They were at the present only 6,000, but Were the other 24,000 to remain without votes that Mr. Wm. John Leigh should continue to be member for East Cheshire ? ("No") Those 24,000 men were equally entitled to vo'e with those men whom they called the agricultural interest, but who, he said, were not the agricultural interest but the ,landed interest. (Hear, hear.) The landed interest and the agri- cultural interest were not identical. (Heae, hear.) the interest of the farmer who ploughed and cultivated the soil ought to be to please hie customers more than those from whom he bought. Those people who were engaged in bus- iness always found it to their interest to please their custo- mers. Well, Sir R. Cross went on to speak in the same line as Mr. W. J. Leigh. He did not speak of South-West Lan- cashire, but spoke of Lord Hartington's constituency of North-East Lancashire, and said if this Franchise Bill pas- sed in North-East Lancashire there would be 238,000 liv- ing outside the Parliamentary boroughs, of which 147,000 were in towns of 10,000 to 25,000, and that left only 90,000 agricultural people who would be swamped. Swamped was the word they used throughout the country, as if the agri- cultural interest was paramount. Now the agricultural in- terest was not paramount. (Hear, hear.) There was only one in twenty of the millions of population of this country engaged in agriculture, the other nineteen were en- mad in other occupations. Why, therefore, should the agricultural or landed interest have such a predominant in- fluence. (Hear, hear.) No wonder they resisted, because the Tories had a majority of 70 in the English counties. The English counties returned 173 members, of which 120

were Tories and 53 Liberals. If this Bill passed—though he was obliged to put the" if," for there was a very power- ful influence at work that would make it very hard work for them to get that accomplished—he feared it was not to be done yet awhile. The landed interest would fight to the last moment. They had parted with their influence by slow degrees., Before the union of Ireland with England there were three members of the House of Lords, the Mar- quis of Downshire, the Beresfords, now represented by the Marquis of Waterford, and the Ponsonbys, returned 60 mem- bers to the House of Commons--(" Shame ;') —besidee having themselves in the House of Lords. There was not mach benefit in the shaelO of laws given to the people of England daring that time. Soon after that the Corn LAWS were put on. The Reform Bill of 1832 diminished their power, but it still exists, and it will not be broken down until this Franchise Bill is passed. (Loud cheers.) He believed there had been about 700 meetings held to protest against the action of the House of Lords, and atiout 200 meetings in their favour. They could go no further at present. They had to wait and see the result. The Tories did not seem willing to listen to any concession or any com- promise, and they should have to speak louder if the Tories did not yield during the next week. (Cheers.) He must, however, not occupy their time any further, as there were three or fonr members of Parliament to follow besides his relative, who, he hoped, would be member for Warrington —(loud cheers)—although Sir R. Cross told them in San- key-street the other day that they (the Tories) knew they had the majority on the register. (Laughter.) Possibly Sir Richard was not always right. He did not remember a case when he was right. (Loud laughter and cheers.) Mr. Wm. CROSFLELD, who was received with loud and continued cheering, and the singing of " He's a jolly good fellow," said : Mr. Chairman, ladies, and gentlemen, the re- solution which I have the honour to propose is as follows : —" This meeting desires to thank her Majesty's Ministers for having redeemed the pledge given at the last election by introducing the Franchise Bill, and for secating its pas- sage through the House of Commons, and promises to sup- port them in their efforts to make it the law of the land ; this meeting also strongly condemns the tyrannical conduct of the majority of the House of Lords—(loud cheers)—in rejecting the measure, whereby two millions of capable citi- zens are excluded from their just electoral rights— (" shame ")—and at the same time demands such an altera- tion in the constitution of the Upper House as will make it impossible in the future for an irresponsible oligarchy to im- pede the progress of the national will." (Continued cheering.) Your reception of the sentiments of this resolution proves a statement which was made by an important Liberal organ on Saturday last, that no eloquent speeches are needed to show the people of Eagland on which side the right rests in the question now before us. (Hear, hear.) You and I are all agreed that Her Majesty's Ministers have redeemed the pledge which they gave by the numerous efforts which they made in the face of some opposition, but which ultimately culminated in the unchallenged vote of the 26th day of June, when the Franchise Bill passed, as I sail before, un- challenged through all the stages of the House of Commons. (Hear, hear.) By that action Her Majesty's Government have shown that they at any rate had a disposition to give us a national Franchise Bill alike in borough and in county, alike in every branch of the nation—(cheers); and we are satisfied—as the large majerity of the people of England have expressed themselves satisfied—with the measure which has passed so far. We do not need to disease the question of the Franchise. It would be as fruitless for us to expect the farmers who have been rejoicing in the bounti- ful harvest which they have threshed to turn again to the empty stacks of corn which are lying in their straw yards, and to beat them over again in the hope that they might get some further fruit from them. The discussion of the question of franchise will give us no new light. Columns upon columns of our newspapers have been read and read again. Hours npon hours have been spent in speaking to the people, a people who have listened with willing ears, and have accepted the statements which have been made in support of the Government action on this question; and we are all satisfied without further pureeing that branch of the question. (Hear, hear.) Those of us who have watched the migration of population have seen that there is an irre- sistible movement from country to town. Those who have looked into the figures have noticed that in the year 1861 there were 165 individuals in the towns for every 100 indi- viduals residing in the country. We find that to-day there are more than 200 individuals in the towns for every hun- dred living in the country. We find again that the House of Commons as at present constituted contains 348 members for boroughs and cities, against 292 for rural constituencies. That proportion should be altered. If it stood on a basis similar to the proportions of populations it should be altered to 434 town representatives to 217 county representatives. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) That, we expect, is the broad principle upon which redistribution must take place. I don't know whether any of you have been occupied as I was a few evenings ago in considering in a friendly assembly the various phases of redistribution. I found that even among ardent Liberals there are many suggestions made by individuals differing somewhat, differing, net in prin- ciple, but differing in slight 2niaatice, and you will find that the possibilities of discussion are enormous even among those who agree to the broad principle which I have just suggested by these figures. (Hear, hear.) We are satisfied that the question of redistribution is in safe hands in Her Majesty's Ministers. (Cheers.) When they from the emi- nent position they occupy have regarded this question in all its details, with the immense knowledge which they possess, knowledge which is not accessible to you and to me, when they are prepared to formulate a scheme, we can trust that the loyalty of the Liberal party will accept the scheme which is placed before them. (Hear, hear.) We are satisfied then that redistribution is safe in the hands of Her Majesty's present advisers. But since I had the pleasure of meeting you in this room in the middle of June we are all aware that there has been a halt cried in the on- ward march in which se have been engaged, and that halt has been caused by the Lords' rejection of the Bill. (Hisses, and a voice "No.") You and I call it rejection. (Hear, hear.) Perhaps you, like me, may prefer rather a smooth word, bat there is one who knows more perhaps about this rejection than you and I, who has used another expression. He has told us that the Lords did not reject it, but they "chucked it out." (Loud laughter.) I do not know what you think, but the word " chuck " struck me as rather a vulgar word. (A. voice: "We will chuck them oat.") Had it not been that this phrase was evidently a choice phrase, and was selected by one in whose veins runs the blue blood of the Lowthers—(loud laughter)—we might have put it aside as too vulgar for our use. But it occurred to me that it was worthy of some respect, and I took the trouble to re- fer to a dictionary to know what it really did mean. I read that "to chuck" is "to throw anything by a quick and dexterous motion so that it shall fall nicely in a given place." (Laughter.) Now, see the appropriateness of this word which the Right Hon. James Lowther selected to ex- plain the position. (Loud cries of "Jemmy:") Quick it certainly was. You remember that the Lords only gave themselves the trouble to discuss this question for two nights. A Monday and Tuesday night Was enough, and they " chucked " it out." (Laughter.) Dexterous is a meaning of" chuck." We may well leave the consideration of the dexterity until we see the issue. (Hear, hear.) And now, while the motion is lying " nicely " in the place which their Lordships designed that it should occupy—outside their Lordships' House—we may without irreverence survey the position. Their Lordships have been anxious to save the people from their representatives, (laughter)—. those representatives whom they chose ic 1880 —chose so mneh to the astonishment of the Lords and the friends of the Lords—(A voice: "Chuck the Lords out ")—the representatives whom they chose to pass the Franchise Bill. They wished to save the people from those representatives in order that the thing might be done more quietly, more demurely, and with more consideration; that again the people may have the opportunity of considering whether they will or no that this question should pass. These Lords desire to be looked upon as the exponents of the people's opinion. Why, a very large majority of their lordships' House, a very large majority of those who were engaged in chucking out this Bill have had little or no healthy political intercourse with the people, whose cham- pions tie?), desire to make themselves. (Cheers.) An examinatlon. of the list shows us that the creations of many of the majority took place at a time when the political life of England was saturated with corruption. (Hear, hear.) Many of their Lordships' ancestors were elevated for deeds which would certainly in this day, at the hands of our gracious and noble Queen, receive anything but honour. (Hear, hear.) And these are the gentlemen who wish to protect the people Their Lordships need to be told that Dower without control is disastrous to a nation. The influence which their Lordships did wield has for many years been gradeally waning. The passing of the Reform Bill of 1832, though it did not entirely withdraw from borough-mongers and those who had previously held authority over the representatives in the House of Commons, gave at any rate a hint that their time was coining and that they must prepare for a change; and then, for the first time, the people of England began to look forward to a fair and honest representation of their opinions. They then began to take a fair share in the government of themselves and of the nation at large; and from that time the influence of the Lords has become gradu- ally more and more intolerable. (Cheers.) Whilst we say these, which may seem rather hard things, let us not be misunderstood. We must all acknowledge there are in the House of Lords men of undoubted talent; men whose i ex- perience n the public service, whose education, and whose devotion to duty, render them most valuable public servants; and such men we would not venture—we would not with—to shut out from a share in the honour of serving the public and the Crown. It is against this assembly as an assembly of eldest sons—(hear, hear)—and you and I, Mr. Chairman, have no reason to cast any disparagement upon eldest sons—(laughter)—but we have a right to object that amen because he is an eldest son should assume to put himself in front and prevent us from obtaining that which we regard to be our due. One of their own number, speak- ing of the House of Lords the other day, told his audience I that they were the vacuum brake of politics. Now, Mr. Chairman, it does not need your experience of railway man- agement to know that the essence of a vacuum brake is its emptiness. (Laughter.) We learnt when we were at school that nature abhors a vacuum, and we only follow the natural law when we protest av,ainst such hindrances being applied to the general weal. We object to that House be- cause those who have ability to govern in it are too often satisfied to leave legislation to a minute quorum. A very shrewd observer, who gives us a weekly description of Par- liamentary life under the well-known signature of "Toby," told us a few weeks ago in describing the House of Lords, that they never come till after four and rarely stay till five. (Loud laughter.) It is against a House which leaves public work to be so neglected, but which assembles in its hundreds simply to cry "Non-content" to political

j questions to the consideration of which they will not de- ' vote their time or the thoughts that they have. We are told that it is very unsatisfactory to be asking the country to express its opinion in this informal way. Well, if we were on the other side, and if there were 700 huge meetings heing held to show that oar course was wrong, and if we could only produce 200 small meetings to show that we were right, perhaps we might agree with those sentiments and say it was an unsatisfactory way of looking at it. But our memories are long enough to remember that a great states- man who had the confidence of the country, used to appeal In times between general elections to the notion and the men in the street. We remember another great statesman whe had the fullest confidence of our oppenente, who, at a time of great crisis, when he was doing what we believed to be an exceedingly unpalatable thing, used to appeal to his letter bag, and he used to say that because the number of his letters had vastly increased that, therefore, the people of England were in favour of the coarse which he was adopt- ing. This, oar system of agitation, is to go down to history with the label of "agitation by picnic." We on our aide don't see much of the picnic; but we have the satisfaction of knowing that our numbers are vast, and that the opinion of those numbers is hearty and unanimous. (Cheers.) There is one phase of this movement which I think is exceedingly striking, and that is, that we, who are assenlbled here, and the large number of those who have met for a similar purpose, are not here to ask anything for ourselves. (Hear, hear.) It has been said that the political world is divided between the " haves" and the" have note ;" and I claim that we to might are assemeiled to represent the "haves," ana that we are demanding justice for the " have note." (Loud Cheers.) The national pulse beats quick. Withio a week Parliament will again be considering this great ques- tion, and it will be for us to stand by and quietly to wait. Te the Ministers who will meet Parliament on Thursday next we say, "Stand to your guns." (Cheers.) To the House of Lords we sey, You have thought once, and the result of your thinking has been unwisdorn. You are now about to think twice. If the time comes for thought a third time it will be the people, the nation that will think—(hear, hear,)—and the nation will think of the paper duties which were passed in the manner described by Mr Gladstone— (loud cheers)—abolished in direct opposition to the will of the House of Lords. They will think that ten years after- wards, in 1871, army purchase was abolished in direct and expressed opposition to the House of Lords, and they were ! "left lamenting." They will remember, as we have been told within the last few days, that the resources of the Con- stitution are not exhausted. (Hear, hear.) The people will say. and the Lords must one day also join in the same cry, "Victory is with the people." (Prolonged cheers.) The CHAIRMAN, who was again cheered on rising, said that when one was not accustomed to public speaking and came to face two or three thousand people—though before- hand be thought he would make a very good speech and could remember this thing and the other—somehow in the ex- citement of the thing one forgot to say what he intended to, and sometimes said things that he ought not to say. , (Laughter.) But he would tell them an anecdote about Sir ' Richard Cross. He knew they were fond of anecdotes, because had seen the effects of them upon their counten- anees. When he read Sir Richard Cross's statement that when it was said that the House of Lords had rejected the Franchise Bill it was a wilful and deliberate lie, he was re- minded of the story of a bishop in the Midland Counties— he believed it was a former bishop of Lichfield—who was in his diocese about noon one day when he heard some men sitting outside their place of work making a great noise. He went to them and said "What are you men making so much noise about ?" They said Mister, we are trying to tell which can tell t' biggest lie. (Laughter,) We have got a new kettle here, and we have agreed among ourselves that him that can tell t' biggest lie shall have le kettle." The , Bishop said "It is very wrong. Don't you know it is very I wicked to tell a lie ;" and one of them Interposed " Well, 1 Mister, and did you never tell a lie? ' The Bishop replied , "No," and the men acid instantly "Give him th' kettle." (Laughter and cheers.) MrAJOHN CHALMERS rose to second the resolution pro- posed by Mr. Crosfield. He could not but think that it was surprising that in these enlightened times they should-have to call such a large meeting to protest against the action of the Hoarse of Lords—a House that had always posed jbefore 1 the people as being the light and the guide of the nation, I and that had tried to destroy all the useful measures that that had been brought before it, of which the present Fran- chise Bill was only another illustration. The Peers had always opposed reform and the popular will. Having enu- merated in detail the various bills opposed by the House of Lords since 1831-2, Mr. Chalmers claimed that for fifty years the Peers had opposed all useful measures in regard to land laws, religious equality, Irish reforms, social and commercial affairs, and every demand for reform. He could not help thinking that there were more reasons than one why they rejected the present Franchise Bill. One, he thought, was because it would act as a source of education to the people which it proposed to enfranchise, who would take advantage of the facilities offered to get political educa- tion when they were placed in a position to make use of it. They could take part in the discussion of the affairs that from time to time came before the nation, and might form an opinion as to who were the best men to represent them in Parliament, hat they could go no further. The right way denied to them by those who lapsed before the public as the patriotic party, the party of light and leading, and the de- fenders of the crown and constitution. He Would not give much for the constitution if Lord Salisbury was to have the guidance of the destinies of the nation. Since working-men received votes education had made great progress, and now the working-man was better prepared to discuss the great questions of the day than at any other period in the history of the country. (Cheers.) He appealed to his fellow. townsmen not to let the meter drop, but to work for the bill, the whole bill, and nothing but the bill. (Applause.) Mr. J. SLAGG, M.P. for Manchester, was received with loud cheers. He said that he could not sufficiently thank ; his audience for the very hearty welcome they had given I him to Warrington. (Cheers.) Sach kindness made him wish that he ever had done, or was ever likely to do, any- thing to deserve such a warm reception. (Hear, hear.) But he recognised in their cheers and enthusiasm not a tribute to any services he had rendered, not even, perhaps, altogether a compliment to the great constituency he had , the honour to represent, but an acknowledgment of the fact that they were fellow-workers in the same cause—(cheers) —that they were soldiers standing shoulder to shoulder in the great army of the people—(renewed cheers)—determined to fight and to conquer in the Canes of freedom. He wished especially that night to say a few words in relation to , speeches that were made in Warrington by Sir Stafford ! Northcote and Sir Richard Cross, because he thought it a very useful thing to answer men who put forward proposi- tions which appeared to him—and which he thought had appeared to them—monstrous and untenable, and to make , an answer upon the grounds on which those sentiments had I been uttered. Sir Stafford Northcote said at Warrington that the Conservatives were determined that the franchise question should be settled On the old lines of the constitu- tion. That remark was interesting from many points of view, bat it was particularly interesting when compared with a great number of preceding declarations from the Tory Dirty in relation to their determination about the franchise question. They began by declaring that no one in this country wanted an extension of the franchise at all, and then they proceeded to affirm that it should be accom- panied, at any rate, by redistribution. Then they declared that the Government had lost entirely the confidence of the people and that the measure should not be undertaken until a fresh appeal was made to the congituencies. Finally they declared that there wee in reality no great agitation whatever, and all that the Liberals wanted to do was to compass the destructioe of the House of Lords. Therefore, Sir Stafford Northcote's declaration about the old lines of the Coostitution was especially interesting. Sir Stafford was good enough to explain what he meant by this remark , —that this subject was not to be settled by Parliament in the streets. Well, he was not aware that the Liberal party in the House of Commons had departed from the old lines of the Constitution—(applause)—in their promotion of this question. They were sent up at the general election of 1880 with the express demand of the people to pass that measure. It was presented by Mr. Gladstone—(applause) —and was passed by overwhelming majorities hr the Home of Commons. (Cheers.) If anyone had appealed to the streets he should think it was the Tory party—(cheers)— who by their action had caused an agitation which would never otherwise have been brought about. (Renewed cheers.) In his opinion they had been the unconstitutioual party, for they had deliberately resisted the popular will. He considered that the Constitution was the popular will, for the general election determined the composition of the House of Commons, the Minister of that House advised the Queen, who, they were proud to know, took that advice. (Cheers.) • Therefore it appeared to him that the only dis- cordant and unnecessary element in their constitutional system at the present moment was the House of Lords. (Applause.) He knew that it was alleged by their Tory friends that the House Of Lords was co-equal with the other estates of government, but how could that be when the House of Commons had the purse strings of the nation, and when without their consent the government of the country could not be carried on for a single day. Sir Stafford. in his remarkable speech at Warrington, went on to say that this agitation was a theatrical display of fireworks, and that he had been in various parts of the country to test the feeling of the people. He thought that was an allusion which showed considerable courage on Sir Stafford Northcote's part, and he should like to know what Sir Stafford thought was the general opinion of the country now that he had tested it. He did not think that the Tory party could be said to have tested the feelingof the country. He believed most of their meetings had been of a packed nature —ticket meetings—or so held as to exclude dissentient voices. If such meetings had been free and open he did not think they could have passed one resolution in favour of their policy or of the House of Lords. (Cheers.) Now they came to Sir Richard Cross. (Laughter and hisses.) Sir Richard Cross told them at Warrington that the opinion of the country was against them (the Liberals), and that the Honed of Lords was stronger new than ever before" be- cause it was speaking in the cause of freedom." Well, that of course was a matter of opinion, but if it was speaking in that cause to deny the just privileges of citizenship to 2,000,000, people whom the Tories now declared were entitled to it, Sir Richard Cross's opinion of freedom and his (the speaker's) were very strangely at variance. (Applause.) Sir Richard, speaking for himself and the Tory party gener- ally, said, "We do not object to the extension of the fran- chise, and no one has ever heard me utter a syllable against it." (Laughter.) What, never, Sir Richard? Now, there were were one or two ways of objecting to a thing. They could object to a thing strongly and openly as James Lowther did—(laughter)—or as Sir Richard Cross did, by offering secretly and openly every possible obstruction and opposi- tion that he could offer to it. He would rot them to cone

eider in what degree Sir Richard had been a friend of the franchise when they had listened to a few quotations. Sir Richard said at St. Helens that "nobody had asked for the corning Reform Bill except some of the extreme Radicals" —(laughter)--and at 800 Is he said that the "present was not the time for an extension of the franchise." That was a strange way of defending that great measure. He would give just one or two extracts to show the intense yearning and longing which their Tory frieads had for reform. He would take one or two of the smaller fry first. Lord Arthur Cecil said that he looked with apprehension on a proposal which would put the greatest part of political power in the hands of the working claases leaving the middle and upper classes entirely unrepresented. Again, there was a very extraordinary extract from a speech of Mr. W. H. Smith, who was also now a warm friend of the measure. That gentleman, speakiag to the Irish people in Dublin, said, Do von meaa to say, you electors ef Dublin and Ireland, you electors of Great Britain and Ireland, that it is a wise thidg, a prudent thing, a statesmanlike thing, to put into the hinds of the inhabitants of the mud cabins of Ireland a power of saying who shall be the representatives of Ireland in the Imperial Parliament." (Hisses.) Now, it seemed to him (Mr. Stagg) that the Tory party had swallowed the Irish—mud cabins and all—and that even the Peers did not object to the Irish or their places of residence. Again, Mr. Gibson, speaking at Wolverhampton, said "Once ad- mit fitness as a right and it lands you in universal suf- frage, because, given household suffrage, it can still be pointed out with great force Meet there are thousands of men just as fit, free from the expensive and aanoying en- cumbrance of a house ; once admit that fitness is a right, and there is no finality about the proposed bill." He (the speaker) claimed that by their stumping about the country the Tories had admitted it, and it seemed to him that having admitted it. by the dictum of Mr. Gibson, they were irrevocably committed to universal suffrage. He had no objection to that. (Hear, hear.) It was an extension that was sure to come in the end. (Cheers.) But it was an ex- traordinary thing to find the cautious, constitutional party becoming its warm and logical advocates. (Applause.) He wanted to call their attention for a minute or two to one or two remarks from Lord Salisbury (groans) upon this sub- ject. Well, he thought they should be careful about their antagonistic expiossions with regard to Lord Salisbury, be- cause they would before long hall him as one of the greatest reformers of the day; a man who would have done much not only to pass for them the Franchise and Redistribution bill, but also to get rid of that assembly of which he was so proud an ornament. Speaking at Chelsea, Lord Salisbury, in pointing out that there was no great and violent public pressure, gave, in his opinion, a direct invitation to a row, but when they got the row, as they did the other day at Birmingham, they did not seem to like it as much as they might have been expected to do. He wished to refer to one of the most important members of the Opposition party—Lord Randolph Churchill. (Hisses and laugh- ter.) There was something that excited reasonable laughter and amusement in the uttering of the name of Lord Randolph Churchill, but they must I remember that they had not to deal with him and to ' regard him simply as a reckless and blatant Tory agitator, but as one of the coming members, if it be so, of a Tory Administeation. (Cries of "Never.") And that man whom at that moment they derided might, if they did not bold fast to their colours, stick firmly to their principles, and vigorously support their leaders, be in a position to rule over and influence the destinies ot this country, which might be no laughing matter for them. This great states- man said at Edinburgh:—" If I saw the agricultural labourers of Great Britain in a great state of excitement over this question; if I saw them holding mass meetings, I collecting together from all parts, neglecting their work, contributing from their scanty funds, marching on London,l palling down the railings in Hyde Park, engaging the police and even the military, I should say to myself those men have a great and a bitter grievance. It has not been raised in Parliament or has been neglected by Parliament, they know that if they had the franchise this grievance would no longer be neglected, that they would be represented and I remedied, and they have made up their minds to have the vote. The fact that they have made up their minds shows pretty well that they will know how to use the vote, and if we wish for peace, order, and stability in the realm of Britain we had better give them the vote. On these r grounds, and these only, would I consent to equalise the, political position of the agricultural labourer and the town artisan' and to destroy the wise inequality which has been ' created by nature and reiterated from time to time in our history by precedent, custom, and law." Having quoted 1 further from Lord R. Churchill, Mr. Stagg said he knew that at Pomona the noble lord recanted. He knew it not only because he had seen it in the papers, but because vast I groups of his Liberal friends went to that remarkable meet- ing. They did not go there for the pork pies or the fire- works, but for amusement, and he was perfectly sure that they got it. (Laughter and applause.) What was really the nature of this great crisis which the whole country was at present agitated about? The Tories said that they ab- solutely yearned for reform, and heahought gave some very curious specimens of that, yearning. The Lords said they would pass the Franchise Bill if the Goverament would give them a Redistribution Bill to play with at the same time, and they professed to fear that if they did not get the Redistribution Bill a general election upon the extended franchise would be forced upon them. He thought the Liberals had nothing whatever to fear in regard to redis- tribution. (Cheers.) He was perfectly sure that no scheme that was not absolutely unfair and unjust could possibly result to their disadvantage. --(Prolonged applause.) Whether they took a population, or rating basis, equal elec- toral districts as proposed by Lord R. Churchill, or the I jerrymandering scheme proposed by Lord Salisbury. the Liberal party was bound to win. (Applause.) For his Dart he should not hesitate one moment about passing a Redistribution Bill at the earliest possible moment. He wished to point out that there had never been a Tory majority of the people in any general election since 1841. In the Tory constituencies at the present time there were 12,000,000 population and only 1,000,000 electors, while in the Liberal constituencies there was a population of 22,000,000 with 2,000.000 electors. How could it therefore be supposed tqat the Tories even now in any wety represented the people of the country. There was talk about compro- mise. He thought many of them would be glad to find that there was less talk of it now than some time ago, but the members of the advanced Liberal party seemed to spend their lives in compromising. They compromised on the Franchise Bill and accepted something very like a Tory measure of enfranchisement. They bad more compromise before them in the Redistribution Bill, but the compromise that they were asked to submit to by the Tory party and their aristocratic caucus in the gilded chamber was one that would give them neither one bill or the other, and it was a com- promise that they certainly could never submit to. They could not surrender their dearest interests into the hands of those who had always proved cruel to their liberties; in- deed, a compromise like that could never be possible for them so long as there existed in them any sense of duty to themselves and to their country. (Prolonged applause.) Mr. Mclteetties, M.P., was received with loud and pro- longed cheering. He said : The contest in which we are engaged at the present time has been very properly des- cribed as being a contest to settle the question whether this country is to be governed by the House of Commons or by the House of Lords. (Hear, hear.) There can he no doubt, I think, that the pretensions of the House of Lords at the present time are both arrogint and insolent. What are the facts? The House of Commons, after considerable trouble and consideration, passed a measure which affected their own Rouse only. They proposed to extend the franchise which is sixteen years old, to a considerable section of the community to whom it had not been extended, because they happened to reside outside Parliamentary boraughs. There is no question now ot the fitness of the prooose4 new con. etituencles. Everybody admits that they should have the franchise.* It is quite true, as some of the speakers have stid to-night, that some time ago the Tories said that they did -Rot want the Franchise and that they were not fit to exer- cise it. Bat you see that is all a mistake. It does seem very mach like kicking it down stairs—but it was only dis- semblel love. (Laughter.) They were always in favour of this franchise. "They loved and never told their love, but let concealment like a worm i' the bud feed on their damask cheeks," so that we really are obliged to confess that there never was a•time when they did not desire this franchise, and I for one will do them the credit of taking them at their word. One fault of a Tory and irresponsible chamber is that all good measures have to be considered in reference to what that chamber is likely to do with them. The framers of all such measures have to frame them in the "fear of the Lords" and so to lighten them of all good that they may float over, as Lord John Russell once said, the bar of the House of Lords. (Laughter.) Now this is a great evil under the sun.. There is nothing in the House of Lords as at present constituted that gives it any claim what- soever to the pretensions it makes. Neither by antiquity, nor by public services, nor by intel- ligence, is the House of Lords fitted and capable of exercising that influence upon the country that it professes and wants to do. It is already an unsettled and doubted principle whether a second chamber is required at all. I remember a quotation from Sir James Mackintosh in a pamphlet which he wrote about the beginning of the pre- sent century, in which he says "an organ to collect the public will and a hand to execute it are all the machinery required for the government of the nation." Generally speaking, second chambers in the freest ceuntries exist, and I am not going to say now or at any future time whether a second chamber is necessary or not—but a great writer and philosopher, so you see, said that it is not. I am not a prophet or the son of a prophet, and I cannot foretell what will be the fate of this franchise bill in the House of Commons or in the House of Lords. I think it probable that in the House of Commons there will be great obstructions, that the Tory opposition will obstruct as long as they can and that they will probably have the assistance of certain allies who last session voted for the bill. We shall be very fortunate indeed if we get the bill into the House of Lords by the end of next month. What its fate may be in the House of Lords I t ink we may, perhaps, foretell if we remember the history of the great Reform Bill of 1832. That bill was thrown out in the House of Lords. It was destroyed, at any rate, in the House of Lords, for they did not act in a frank and manly way, and reject it. They sneaked to their object in a mean and cowardly way, just as the Lords are doing now, and they destroyed the bill, but they did not positively reject it. A curioas coincidence between the two periods exists. There was in those days a Lord Carnarvon who said that the House of Lords had not rejected the bill, although they had destroyed it, and we have a Lord Carnarvon in these days who says exactly the same. (Laughter and cheers.) Allusion has been made to-night to the agitation in the country, and it has been said that the Lords and the Tories do not believe that the people are In earnest in desiring tine franchise bill.

Notwithstanding what has been said over and over again about the number of meetings in favour of the franchise bill, and about the importance and influence of these meet- ings, the Tories still profess to believe that the people are indifferent. I wonder what the House of Lords want? What vould they have? Would they have the Bristol riots, and the burning of Nottingham Castle, and the rest of the riotous conduct of 1832? Do they want the people to empty the House of Lords into the Thames—(laughter and applause)—before they believe that the people are in earnest? There is no doubt at all that in these days the riotous conduct of 1832 will not take place, hut if the Peers and the Tory party do require that the people should do something to prove that they are in earaest, you may depend upon it that the people will do it. (Cheers.) I re- member hearing an account of a controversy that took place in this very room between a reformed drankard and a companion of his who was not a reformed drunkard. They were both Lancashire working-men, and the controversy took oleos in the Lancashire dialect. One of them said "I reckon nowt o' thi teetotalism; there's nowt in it." The other said " Nowt in it ? Why, before I wor teetotal mi furniter could ha bin bowt for 55., and it wasn't worth it; and now I have A good eight days' clock, and I have a chest of drawers in every room, and I have a house as weel furnished as tha would wish ta see. Dust ta co that nowt? " "Yea," said the other, "aw co that nowt." "Well, afore I wer a teetotaller, our Ailse, poor wench, had nowt but th' clothes she had on, and they were all rags, and now she's a good silk gown on Sundays, is weel dressed at week days, and is as well dressed a woman as any working man need hey. Dot ta co that newt ? " "Yea," said the other, "aw co that nowt." Well, afore I wer teetotal, th' childer, poor things, were o' in rags, they couldn't go to school for they were not fit to be seen ; and now they're weel dressed and go to both Sunday and day school. Post be co that nowt?" "Yea," said the other, "aw co that nowt." "Well, then," said the narrator of this story, "aw wer gradely mad at 'im, he wer such a too, and aw lifted up my fist, aw doubled my nieve, aw hit ins a clout on't side o't yad, and aw knocked him to't floor, and aw said—Post taco that nowt? (Roars of laughter.) Now, gentlemen, as Captain Bunsen said, "The bearings of these observations are in their application." (Renewed laughter.) You may depend upon it that if the Peers and the Tory party will not believe that the English people are in earnest upon this matter unless they get a "clout at t' side o't yed," they'll get it. (Laughter and cheers.) • The thulium; then put the resolution,which was carried unanimously, and it was also decided that a copy of it be sent to the Prime Minister.

Mr. F. A. Rosman proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Slagg for his address. In so doing be bad peculiar plea- sure, for in 1880 he had the pleasure of not only votieg but also of doing his best in the work of returning Mr. Slagg as member for Manchester. They could not have listened to the speech of Mr. Slagg that evening without feeling that he was one of the coming men ot the future. (Applause.) Mr. Stagg, and a number of members of Parliament, Mr. Rylands amongst the number—(applause)—had devoted tbe recess that should have been a time of rest and recreation to informing the masses of the people of the action of the Lords on the Franchise Bill. If the bill had been passed the members might have had a quiet recess and have gone back to the House of Commons refreshed and invigorated for work. The House of Lords desired the opinion of the people. He thought Warrington had that night shown its opinion. Warrington said plainly "We want the bill." They said that they would have the franchise and then a redistribution bill, and then they would have a reform of the House of Lords. (Applause.) Mr. C. S. BURGESS seconded the motion, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Slagg. Mr. SLAG°, in responding, said that they bad nothing really to thank him for, but it would have been impossible to withstand the invitation given to him with so much kind- ness, and decline to come in support of his friend Mr. Mc- liiinnies—(applause)—and his friend Mr. Rylands. (Ap- plause.) They bad heard a great deal that would be use- ful and would occupy their minds for some time to come. Not only, as one of the speakers had said, in regard to the franchise bill, it would surely pass, but in regard to the gil- ded chamber and Tory caucus that had done so much mis- chief to the Liberal cause in the past, and as to which, he thought, they should take care that it should not continue on the same they again. (Applause.) They were a Conser- vative people in a certain sense, for they accepted changes very slowly, looking for a very good reason for them ; they respected vested interests, and some of them bad a very great admiration for the aristocracy, and relying upon these instincts and feelings of the English people the House of Lords, had they been wise, might have retained their posi- tion for a long while, and a number of noble and otherwise Insignificant personages who were only required to get themselves safely born might for a long time have occupied a position of very great importance and advantage to them- selves. But they bad not been so wise. They could have retained their position by exercising the commonest of common sense and discerning that the people were truly and absolutely in earnest, and that they would not allow class privileges te stand in the way of their great and legi- timate wants. It had been a pleasure to him to speak under the presidency of their venerable and worthy chairman. (Cheers.) He bad gone to meetings presided over by poli- ticians who had done much service in the past, and, when reflecting upon the difficulties and injustices in their path —to which in comparison those they now Suffered from were as nothing—he thought they must have been grand and noble-hearted men, and he hailed the chairman that night as one of the best and finest politicians of those days. (Cheers.) He proposed that the best thanks of the meeting be tendered to Mr. Crosfield for presiding. (Cheers). Mr. P. &memos, M.P., who was received with cheers, seconded the motion. He said that during the last few weeks, in common with other members of Parliament, he had been engaged in attending a number of public meetings , in different parts of the country, and he had seen, and had I also known from the intelligence in the newspapers of what had occurred elsewhere, the evidence of an amount of an enthusiastic determination on the part of the people such as he never before witnessed in the whole of his political ex- perience. (Cheers.) No doubt that enthusiasm had arisen from that high feeling of justice that made men already in the enjoyment of the franchise in our great towns feel that they ought to give to their rural brethren the same rights' that they themselves enjoyed. (Cheers.) The great towns and centres of political intelligence took a right and a just view of this great question, and when the representatives of the people, respecting as they did that intelligent feeling of justice on the part of the great majority of the nation, had passed a bill to give the boon of justice to their unenfran- chised brethren, and when that bill had been suspended, "chocked out," or destroyed, whatever they chose to call it, by the House of Lords, then another questior arose, ay, a question which, whenever it agitated the minds and con- sciences of the people of England had always stirred those consciences and those minds to their very depth. It was the question of privilege. Whenever in the church or state privileges had existed with their baneful influence it had been the part of the Liberal party or the Radical party to strike down those privileges, in order that men might in the commonwealth be equal, and might in the face of God be ready to fulfil their duties without let or hindrance. It had been an agreeable experience to find that the people of the country had risen in the way that they had done. TIP) Tories, with their picnics, fireworks, bands of music, and their refreshments at fixed charges —(laughter)—had not been able to muster any evidence of public opinion like those evidences that the Liberals had seen throughout the country. They had a right to see that the great body of the people supported those of them in Parliament who bad voted for the bill. Who were against them ? Who were stepping forward in order to prevent this bill ? Their opponents claimed a constitutional right to stop that great act of justice, and they appealed to their rights, privileges, and powers as being part of the constitution of the king- dom. Where did those rights, privileges, and powers come from ? They were the spawn of the dark ages of feudalism. (Cheers.) That they existed now was simply because the people had been gradually removing one privilege and interest after another. They had no doubt been engaged for the last generation or two on great reforms ; the turn of the House of Lords were coming. They were prepared to fight the struggle to the bitter end, and the Lords would have the bitter end. (Loud applause.) He had great confidence in Mr. Gladstone, and he believed that he would, whatever might be said about compromise, be determined upon two things, one was that the Franchise Bill must be passed— (cheers)—and the other was that the people should not be appealed to by a dissolution until the two mil- lions of unenfranchised had a right to vote. When the Tories seemed to say that the Peers could pre- vent the franchise and could control entirely the represen- tatives of the people, let them remember that the resources of the constitution were not ended, and that their very exis- tence depended upon the favour of the Crown. While the Crown could not make a single representative of the people it could make two or three hundred peers to-morrow. He hoped that rather than submit to the House of Lords Mr. Gladstone would be prepared to recommend to the Queen, if the Lords refused to pass the bill, that a suffi- cient number of Liberal peers should be appointed to make them pass it. It was their first duty to get that great measure of justice passed, then there would be redistribu- tion, which he trusted world be carried on broad lines. When they got five million instead of three million compe- tent voters, representing fairly distributed political power, then, he trusted, the people would not forget that they would have te deal with that branch of the legislature that had given them so much trouble, and that they should sweep away further those privileges which stood in the way of public progress. (Applause.) He was delighted to have had an opportunity of attending that meeting. It was the first he had attended in Warrington since his friend near him had been selected to be their candidate. (Cheers.) He had no doubt that Mr. Crosfield would become the represen- tative of the borough of Warrington. (Renewed cheers.) Ile much regretted that Mr. McMinnies was withdrawing from the House of Commas, but the state of his health made it a necessity. They had selected a good successor, who bore a very honoured name in that locality. They knew his family, and it was one that had always borne the highest reputation for every good work, and he was sure that Mr. William Crosfield would make an excellent member for Warrington. He had known Mr. George Crosfleld—who was not quite so venerable as Mr. Slagg seemed to think— since they were boys together. They worked together forty years ago in political matters, and had been working to- gether ever since. Their chairman was always ready as far as he was able to take his part in promoting great measures or progress and reform. He had been a great benefactor of the locality, and they all esteemed and res- pected him. They were glad to see him there and hoped that he might preside on many future and similar occa- sions. Their chairman had, with a number of others on the platform, engaged in struggles with privelege over and over

again, and although sometimes they had won and some- times been beaten, in the end they had coma out victori.ms. So in the cause in which they were now engaged they would have the satisfaction of again being victorious. (Cheere.) . The CHAIRMAN briefly replied and the meeting termin- ated.

div.head: TORCHLIGHT PROCESSION.
div.p: THE TORCHLIGHT PROCESSION.

lmost before the speaking had concluded inside a com- mencement was made to organise the torchlight procession in front of the Public Hall. A large number of torches had been provided, and these were all quickly lighted and held aloft by willing hands, and in addition hundreds of other Liberals fell into the procession, which, by the time a 1 movement was made, had attained a great length. The first place in the procession was taken up by about half a dozen torch bearers and a number of others who did not carry torches, immediately behind whom came the combined bands of Wycliffe and Legh-street, following whom was the. great body of the procession. In the meantime the streets which it bad been announced would be paraded had been densely filled by people, the turn-out of spectators being so great as to surprise even those who had been most sanguine in this respect. In Sankey-street, Bridge-street, and from the bridge in the direction of Wilderspool the thoroughfares were so crowded as to make it seem impossible for the proces- sion.to pass, and every passage and street opening into the line of procession was crowded with those eager to see the spec- tacle. As might have been expected under these circum- stancee very quick progress was not made, and it needed all I the energy and discipline of the large body of police, under the efficient command of the Chief Constable, and Inspec- tors Spinks and Berry, to keep a clear passage. The efforts of the police were, however, very largely facilitated by the marked prevalence of good humour in the crowd, the absence of anything in the shape of disorder or violence' and, in a large degree, by the evident sympathy felt for the ob- ject of the demonstration. The line of march which- had been previously arranged for the procession comprised Rylands-street, Bold-street, Bridge-street and along Wilders- pool Causeway to the borough boundary, where the proces- sion was to file around Mr. Crostield's carriage and return to the Liberal Club by way of Bridge-street. Horsernarket- street, and Bewsey-street, but it was found necessary to I make some slight alteration in this arrangement. On arriving at the level crossing on Wilderspool Causeway, it was found that the gates were closed across the road to allow of the passage of a train, and it was thought advisable not to block up the railway by the passsage of such a large number of people. The band and procession consequently filed around Mr. Crosfield's carriage at the near side of the crossing, and the return journey commenced. In its pas- sage through the streets some very striking displays were made by the procession. When passing down Bridge-street I the scene as viewed from the bridge was in particular ex- tremely attractive and beautiful. The flame of the torches, which were in reality a considerable distance apart from each other, seemed then to unite into one continuous stream of light, which flashed ,into innumerable fantastic shapes by the motions of the torch-bearers, and the effect was made all the more striking by the dark dense masses of people who filled the lower reaches of Bridge-street. Again a some- what similar effect was witnessed from Market-gate as the procession wended its way down Horsemarket-street and turned into Bewsey-street. On arriving at the Liberal Club the processionists formed into a circle till the band had played a tune, after which the torches were put out. The j assembled mass of people (at the suggestion of Mr. H. 1 Roberts) gave vent to its feelings by ringing cheers for leading Liberal statesmen, and for Mr. W. Crosfield, and subsequently quietly dispersed.

_ WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION (IST) V. EVERTON.—On Saturday the first team of the Warrington Association Club met Everton " A " team at Everton, the game resulting in a win for Everton by six goals to none. This result was due to the very strong team which Everton put into the field, comprising, it is said, eight first team men. On the part of the Warringtontans, however, there was some good defence. They also displayed an improvement in skill and discipline, through the want of which all new clubs are bound to suffer. The Warrington team was composed as follows :—Goal, Webster; backs, Davies, W. Dilloa ; half-backs, Walton, Royston, Parker; forwards, Yonge, Pearson, Matthews, Warren, and E. Dillon. WARRINGTON V. WIGAN (2ND TEAal).—Played at War- rington. The juniors did not play their usual combination, Appleton and Hewitt being absent. The state of the match was very even, a good game resulting with a victory for the home team by 2 tries and one minor point, to I try and 7 minor points. Littlewood, Dembell, and Baldwin got the tries for their respective teams. Teams :—Warrington : W. Speakman, back; 11. Boardman, W. Gregory, and H. Thoma- son, three-quarter backs ; J. Whittle and T. Bashford (captain), half backs; T. Balshaw, J. Savage, J. Ashurst, J. Jones, V. Potter, T. Forster, W. Dumbell, It. Littlewood, and W Brimelow, forwards. Umpire, T. Barnes. Wigan: 3. Dewier, back; W. Baldwin, E. Wardle, G. Schofield, three-quarter backs; F. Aspinall and J. W. Worsley, half backs ; F. Yates, F. Francis, C. Simms, W. Etarris, H. Green, S. Swift, W. Anderton, J. Anderton, and R. Richards, forwards. Umpire, R. Dawler. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB.—On Satur- day afternoon a match WAS played in the Field, Knutsford- road, Warrington, between the second team of the above club, and the second team of the Earlestown Wanderers. The kick-off took place shortly after three o'clock, and from that time up to the close of the game there was a good and evenly-contested struggle between the two teams. There was a clearly noticeable improvement in the style of the Warrington players, and there appears to be every promise that before long this new club will be able to win an hon- ourable position amongst association footballers. The game resulted in a victory for Earlestown by two goals to one, the latter of the two goals being scored just a few minutes before the blow of the whistle. The following were the Warrington players :—Goal, Gray ; backs, A. Dillon and Allen; half-backs, Hoolon, Shaw, Ford; forwards, West- brook, Cannon, Hough, Roach, and Savage. Easy CHEsumn V. WEST CHESEURE.—The meeting of the two Cheshire divisions at Runcorn on Saturday was looked forward to with much interest, as the game, in view of the forth-coming county engagement, was intended to furnish the Cheshire Committee with a clue to the best resources at their command. The weather being remarkably mild, there was a good muster, exceeding 2,000 spectators, while the general arrangements of the Runcorn Club were such as to leave nothing to be desired. At the last moment it tran- spired that Sale had drawn the whole of their men from the Eastern team, a proceeding which was severely comtnented upon. Great credit, however, is due to the Bowden and Runcorn clubs for having so promptly filled the vacancies, but although several of the substituted players, especially Latham (the captain) and Broady, played remarkably well, the team was so completely overmatched that eventually the game degenerated into a continued scramble on the Eastern goal-line, so feeble was the resistance offered. The most re- markable feature of the game was the extraordinary goal. kicking of J. Herron, of the New Brighton Club, who was entrusted with the " places" arising from the last nine tries obtained in this singularly one-sided game, which ter- minated in a victory for the West by ten goals, five tries, and two minor points to a touchdown; hostilities mutually terminating several minutes before the expiration et time. WLERINGTON Y. Wmaw.—The representatives of the above clubs met for the first time this season at Wigan on Saturday. Of the selection made by the committee no less than Six playerswere unable to make the journey. Notwith- standing their weak team the visitors from the moment of the kick-off were for some time dangerously near their op- ponents' line. Forward, the Wiganers were beaten, but their backs Stevin, Samuels, and Clegg, made amends, and by their efforts removed play to the opposite end. Scrim- mages in quick succession then occurred, and France got

over the line: Shortly afterwards Samuels repeated, and when half time was announced ends were changed with the score as above. Turner re-started, and operations were chiefly confined in the Wigan 25. At the call of no-side the score stood, Wigan 3 tries and 6 mmor points, to 2" minor points. The Wigan backs won the match, as Stevins and Samuels were very speedy. Clegg, Morris, Ingham, and France also were prominent. For Warrington, Massey ran I and kicked well, Walsh, Hough, Turner, l'ovey, and Davies also taking a leading part. Teams :—Warrington : T. lA'alsb, back; J. T. Massey, W. Warburton. and S. Hough, three- quarter backs; J. Russell and T. Lightfoot, half backs ; H. Ashton (captain), F. Tamer, W. Povey, L. Huuaphreys, T. Davies, J. Robinson, W. Hayes, W. Royce, and J. R. Cal- vert, forwards. Umpire, J. Bramhall. Wigan : J. Ander- ton, back; J. Stavin' T. Clegg, and J. C. Samuels, three- quarterbacks; T. Morris and J. Banks, half backs; France (captain), Ingham, Brayqhay, Pennington, Cronsbaw' T. Holland, P. T. Holland, Prestt, and Astley, forwards. Um- pine, G. Naylor.

. . LARLESTOWN V. LIVERPOOL AND LISTRICT.-0130 Of the most important matches eyer played at Earlestown took place on Saturday afternoon, when the representatives of the Earlestown club met a strong eleven, selected from the principal clubs of Liverpool and district. The proceeds of the match were for the benefit of Joseph Cameron (a former player with the Earlestown team, who had his leg broken in a recent match). Notwithstanding the threatening state of the weather a large number of spectators assembled to wit- ness the game, which was hard fought and very fast from the commencement. The teams made their appearance about three o'clock, there being but two alterations—and these in the Liverpool team—from the announced list of players. The Earlesto ten representatives were :—James Appleton, goal; R. Green and J. Green, backs; J. Whalley, R. Bowker, and F. Emmett, half-backs ; J. Dux- bury and J. Ogden, left wing; A. W. Dagnall, centre; J. Ellison and W. Rich, right wing. Their opponents were as follows :—C. Jolliffe (St. Benedict's), goal; G. Dover (Liverpool Stanley) and R. Righet (Birkenhead), backs; J. Griffiths (Bootle Wanderers) and J. Resketh (Birkenhea(l), half-hacks; J. A. Tebay (Bootle Wanderers) and W. Crellin (Birkenhead), right wing; J. A. Grayson (Bootle F.C.) and C. M. Kettley (captain, Cambrian F.C.), centre; R. Rehr (St. Benedict's) and R. Poole (St. Benedict's), left wing. Having won the toss, the home team captain chose to play up hill in the first half, with a moderately strong breeze in his favour. When the whistle blew for the change of ends, the home eleven led by two goals to one. The game was re- started by Dagnall for Earbstown, and after ten minutes' play Dagnall scored a third goal for the Earlestonians with a clever "screw" shot. The Liverpool players next showed to advantage, and the leather was taken into the harlestown quarters by Tebay and Crellin. It was ultimately passed to the centre, and after a short scrimmage the visitors scored their second point. Sten tly afterwards a clever centre by Duxbury enabled Ellison to score a foul th goal. The home team afterwards had the advantage up to the call of time, and ultimately retired the winners of a splendid game by foer goals to two. The umpires were Mr. P. Hastie (Earlee. tewn) and Mr. H. Crowther (Liverpool), and Mr. R. E. Lytteigoe, secretary of the Liverpool and District Football Association, officiated as referee. After the match the players and a few friends adjourned to the Sunbeam Inn, where they sat down to tea. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Liverpool players and the clubs they repre- sented for the kindness they had shown in consenting to play the match.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

On Saturday, in the Birmingham and District Cap Com- petition, St. George's beat Coxeley by 15 to none; The Excelsiors beat Arcadians by eight to one ; West Bromwich Albion beat Darlaeton All Saints by eight to none; Walsall beat Stonebridge Standard by 11 to none; Wolverhampton Wanderers beat St. Thomas's (Birmingham) by 11 to one; Smallheath Alliance beat Stafford Rangers by one to none; Wednesbury Old Athletic beat Sutton Coldfield by 16 to none; Nottingham atangers beat Derby Midland by two to one. In the Lancashire Cup Competi- tion, Bolton Wanderers 2nd beat Lowethouse by six to one; Sheffield Heeley beat Middlesbrough by three to two; Ox- ford University beat Old Foresters by six to one; Charter- house beat Clapham Rovers by one to none; Royal Engineers and Royal Military College played a drawn game without scoring ; Upton Park beat Somerset by four to one; Bradfield Wet the Swifts by four to two; at the opening of the new ground of the Queen's Park, Dumbarton and Queen's Park played a drawn game, neither side scoring; Notts Club and Sheffield Wednesday played a drawn game, no scoring, at Nottingham ; at Alexandria, the Vale of Leven beat Glasgow Rangers by three to one Pollokshields Athletic beat Cartvale by five to two; the 3;cl Lanark beat Camhuslang by four to three; Ayrshire beat Edinburgh by eight to none St. Bernard's, at Edinburzh, beat Harp (Dun- dee) by two to one; in the Edinburgh Shield Competition. the Hibernians beat Rose by 10 ta none, while Heart of Midlothian beat Easter by five to bone. For the twentieth time the Blackburn Rovers and Darwert were pitted against each other on Saturday, and, as the holders of the East Lancashire Charity Cup are emerging from the cloud which has to some extent dimmed the lustre of the club's achievements in the earlier days of Association football in Lancashire, the meeting on the Leamington Ground, Blackburn, was anticipated with great interest, particularly in Darwen. After a good game the match ended in favour of the Rovers by four goals to one. The victory of the Earlestown team on Saturday over Liverpool and District was a creditable one. To-day (Satur- day) a team journeys to Blackburn to play Vi'itton in the second round of the Lancashire Challenge Cap competition. The Earlestown second team beat Preston Olympic at Preston, and the Newton Rugby Club sustained a double defeat at the hands of St. Helens Recreation, the first teams playing at St. Helens and the second teams at Newton. Fully two years have elaped since the project of a West , Lancashire and Border Towns Rugby Union began to be urged alike in the interests of the pastime and of charity. By a bold and chivalrous stroke from an unexpected source. the work of organisation has been set in motion. A few days ago Mr. T. Egan, of Nevrton-le-Willows, issued a busi- nesslike circular calling upon the clubs in his district to aid , him in an effort to give effect to the long-cherished scheme. That they will cheerfully respond is a matter of certainty, and great good will result. A gathering of Rugby players took place at the Goat, Peter's-lane. Liverpool, on Saturday evening, with the ob- ject of forming a union in West Lancashire and border towns. The meeting was quite unanimous as to the de- sirability of banding together, and to give the project shape it was resolved to call a general meeting of all clubs within the district.

THE BOLTON MURDER.—During the present week another interview has been held in Strangeways Gaol with Kay Howarth, charged with the murder of Mr. Dugdale, commer- cial traveller, at Bolton. At his request he was visited by his brother. He seemed depressed by his position and was somewhat reserved, though he again asserted his innocence of the crime imputed to him, and said he did net fear the result if only justice were done him. In Bolton a meeting has been held and a subscription opened on behalf of the widow and children of Mr. Dugdale. A TERRIBLE POLITICAL TRAGEDY is reported from La Crosse, Wisconsin, U.S. Francis Burton, president of a Republican Club, while arranging a torchlight procession on Thursday week, was suddenly shot and killed by a dissolute character named Mitchell, who was arrested and placed in the gaol. The crime caused much excitement, and the procession moved en masse to the gaol demanding Mitchell's body. The Sheriff stoutly defended the place, but the mob battered down the doors, effected an entrance, captured Mitchell, and hanged him to a tree in the Court- house yard. Przarnirts' CONGRESS.—This Congress met on Monday at the Technical Institute, South Kensington, Mr. George Shaw, Master of the Plumbers' Company, presiding. There was a large attendance. Mr. Ernest Hart read a paper, en- titled " The Regulation and Registration of Plumbers." He supported the extension of the existing statute law as to house drainage, in order to provide for the mere efficient regulation and registration of plumbers. Mr. Eassie read a paper on the " Technical Instruction of Plumbers," Mr. Mills one on "Technical Education for Sanitary Plumb- ing," and several other gentlemen contributed papers, after which a discussion took place. TELEGRAPH CLERKS AND SUNDAY LABOUR.—A meeting of the Manchester postal telegraph clerks was held on Saturday evening at the Crown and Thistle Hotel, to con- eider the reply of the Postmaster-General .to the petition forwarded to him from them a short time since, asking for Overtime and payment for Sunday labour, which is already given to the London and Metropolitan district clerks. The reply stated that such payment could not be conceded to the provincial clerks, inasmuch as it was "exceptional " in London, whilst in the provinces t was not se. The fol- lowing resolution was passed : "That this meeting strongly aangaimettrtohpeoelxitcaeptional advantages enjoyed by the n district telegraph clerks in regard London protests d M to payment for Sunday duty, and pledges itself to use all means In its power to obtain payment as overtime for Sun- day dut:ein the provinces." ficatniaLF, DESTITUTION IN WIGAN. -- The Wigan bor- ough coroner held inquests on Saturday on the bodies of three children. The first case was as to the deaths of The- resa Holland, one year and eight months old, and Christo- pher Holland, seven years of age, the children of Margaret Holland, hying apart from her husband. She gained a wretched subsistence by begging and doing a little work. On Sunday the boy Christopher, who was blind and a crip- ple, was seized with a fit, and died in the evening. The coroner's officer went to the house, and on enquiring whe- ther there was a child dead there, the woman replied," Yes there are two." The room exhibited sigras of the greatest destitution and misery. A verdict of "Death from natural causes" was returned, the jury recommending that the re- maining children should be taken away from the mcther at onee and placed in the workhouse. On visiting the house after the inquest three surviving children were found locked up in the house and playing round the coffins, which had been supplied by the parish. The other Inquest was on the body of a child ten days old, daughter of a tinplate worker named Connor, living in a lodging-house in the Same por- tion of Scholes. The medical evidence showed that the cause of death was suffocation by carbonic acid gas poison- ing from the want of ventilation. The room contained three beds, and these were occupied on the Friday night by five adults and three children. The jury returned a ver- dict of "Death from natural causes," and said they consid- ered the house unfit to be registered.
