div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.

'intolerable. Mr. JOHN SLAGG, member fcr Manchester, received a hearty welcome on rising to address the assembly. His speech proved to be a merciless exposure of the in- sincerity of the present cry of the Tory party for reform. By quotation after quotation, he piled Ossa upon Pelion in the way of proof that, true to their traditions, the Tories had no love for an extended suffrage, and that they had all along done their level best" to strangle the Franchise Bill. 11. e held up to scorn the absurd pretension of Sir RICHARD CROSS that the House of Lords is stronger now than ever it was because it had stepped forward in the cause of freedom. What mockery! Here is a measure to en- franchise Two Millions of citizens which would to-day have been upen the statute book if it had not been for the obstinacy and wrong-headedness of the Peers. They are seeking to keep back the people—to grind the faces of the poor as has ever been their wont, and here is an upstart politican who that he may himself creep a bit nearer the gilded chamber dares to speak of freedom in connection with such an act of tyranny- If the electors of South-West Lancashire are wise, they will give Sir RICHARD CROSS the benefit of an "appeal to the people" at the next election; they will confer upon him the free- dom of the streets rather than of St. Stephen's—" the streets " at which the Tories so persistently sneer as something wholly beneath them, except when they want votes. But a reckoning day is at hand ; the streets are not to be trifled with, and Mr. McMni- rims, M.P., hit the nail on the head, as he usually does, when he said the pretensions of the House of Lords were regarded by the people as arrogant and insulting. He warned his hearers against the further obstruction which would in all probability be again offered to the Franchise Bill. They must wait and watch, and we venture to say that signs will not be wanted of that dissembled love which means, as heretofore, a vigorous effort to kick the bill downstairs. Nor on the other hand is there likely to be any sign want- ing of the determination of the people to carry the Reform Bill. If the Lords wish to see some show of violence they will doubtless be accommodated before the struggle is at an end—not, perhaps, exactly in the way Mr. McMiNmEs suggested by the inimitable illus- tration he gave, but certainly in a way which will leave not a shadow of a doubt as to the fact that in the struggle upon which the nation has entered the Peers are no match for the People. Whatever the Tories may have in view, the Liberals in this agitation are not picnicing. For one thing, they are not so distressed at their meetings with "dry" speeches as to be driven to call out for "a barrel of Wilderspool ale." Their claims are not to be liquidated in this pecu- liar fashion. The people demand their birth- right—the heritage which has so long been denied them; they have raised their voices, and they will next put forth their strength ; and if the House of Lords still stands in the way the House of Lords will most assuredly be driven to the wall.

div.head: SATURDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1884.
div.p: SATURDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1884.

TILE Liberal Demonstration in Warrington on Monday night to support the Govern- ment and to condemn the House of Lords was in every way worthy of the occasion. The Public Hall was filled to overflowing at an early hour; the speeches were earnest and eloquent; and the audience showed itself throughout to be united and enthusias- tic. There were no ex-Cabinet Ministers, to stimulate drooping spirits, such as were brought on the scene last week at the open- ing of the Conservative Club, and there was need of none. The people are with the Liberal party in demanding the speedy enfranchisement of Two Millions of their fellow country-men, a fact which the Tory party would °ascertain to their cost if they could bring about that dissolution of Parlia- ment which they are so blindly trying to enforce. But the people are not disposed to yield to clamour of this kind; they have a lquick eye for the situation, for it is note- worthy that, at every Liberal meeting, the intimation that Parliament must not be dis- solved at the bidding of the Peers is invari- ably greeted with a ringing cheer. Their motto is "no surrender ; " they evidently feel, as Mr. PETER RYLANDS put it in his short but spirited speech, that they are on the eve of victory, and are not disposed to throw away the results of a cam- paign which has been wantonly forced upon them. Several of the speakers at the meet- ing on Monday dealt with the statements made in the Conservative speeches of Wed- nesday week; but it was like fighting shadows—they were so unsubstantial. Mr. GEORGE CROSFIELD aptly characterised the statement that the Lords had refused , to pass but had not rejected thef Franchise Bill as a distinction with- out a difference. He dealt good hu-1 mouredly with Sir RICHARD CROSS'S blatant talk about "a wilful and deliberate lie "—tying a "kettle " to his tail in a way, which will make the member for South Lan- cashire a spectacle for some time to come. Very pertinent, too, was his reference to the agricultural and landed interest as one which, engaging one in twenty only of the male population, was not entitled to be regarded qs paramount. Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD, who as the Liberal candidate for Warrington was enthusiastically received, appropriately fol- lowed this up by showing that, whilst in z 86z there were 165 individuals in the towns to to every zoo in the country, the proportion was now 200 in the towns to roo in the 1 country. The inference to be drawn was that when they came to the question of the redis- tribution of seats they would have to take members from the country and give them to the towns—a process which, if carried , out with any approach to fairness, must in- evitably result in a gain to the Liberal party., The Tories perceive this, and hence the hol- lowness of their cry for a " complete " bill, which is exactly what they do not want. Mr. W. CROSFIELD made merry over Mr. Low- THEWS assertion that the Lords had "chucked out" the Franchise Bill—the phrase in- stantly eliciting the response from the audi- ence that it was time to " chuck " the Lords out. He uttered no uncertain sound on the question of the Reform of the Upper House. They did not wish, he said, to shut out able members of the aristocracy from a share in the honour of serving the public and the Crown; but they were against the House of Lords as an assembly of eldest sons, and it was as such that it was becoming more and more

IT is somewhat startling to learn that the PRIME MINISTER, at the present critical juncture in the affairs of the nation, has been writing a long letter to a Church Conference on the duty of the Church with regard to Disestablishment. But the reader who turns to it will find nothing to alarm him, if he be a Churchman clinging to the connection between Church and State, or to give hint hope of any immediate action if he be amongst those who are toiling for Disestab- lishment. Mr. GLADSTONE, as he states at the conclusion of his letter, has endeavoured to place himself at "a point of view which is impersonal, impartial, and historical," and, while describing what he sees from this stand- point it has been his object to avoid wound- ing the susceptibilities or assailing the opinions of anyone, and in this task—one of exceeding difficulty and delicacy—it must be said that he has succeeded wonderfully well. He asks as to Disestablishment, but does not attempt to answer the questions—Will it come ? ought it to come? must it come ? IS it near, or is it somewhat distant, or indefi- nitely remote? What, however, he empha- sises is that there are two ways in which Dis- establishment might come to be disgraceful —first, "if it were due to the neglect, in- difference, or deadness of the Church ;" and second, "if it were to arrive as a conse- quence of dissensions among the members of the Church." He gives his reasons for thinking the Church will not disgrace itself through neglect or deadness, and makes a noble appeal for the exercise of charity and forbearance in discussing the points of difference within the Church itself. It is evident that, if the PRIIIE MINISTER has been a silent spectator of what what he de- scribes as almost the savagery of their inward contentions, it is not that he has not been deeply interested, and at times strongly moved. Indeed, it may be gathered that if he has a fear of Dis- establishment it is in its being reached through dissensions within the Church; that is a disgrace which as a Churchman he would keenly feel. Mr. GLADSTONE indi- rectly, but not the less certainly, pays a high tribute to Nonconformity when he points to the fact that the "Puritanical element re- jected at the Restoration" has, on reasserting itself, "brought about a great religious revival in the English Church." It is this revival within the Church which, as it see ms to us, will be likely to work its overthrow as a State institution. Men of deep piety and oarnestnbss of purpose begin to feel more and more the evils of scandals. and anomalies to which they are tied, and by which they are tainted, but which they are power- less to reform. They may stay their hands for a time, as Mr. GLADSTONE would seem to suggest; but there are forces now at work which will inevitably—perhaps at no distant date—bring about Disestablishment from within, if not from without, the Church.

WE had occasion last week to direct atten- tion to the fact that several of the St. Helens provision dealers had been fined for selling " butterine "as butter. This week there has been a case of adulteration of another kind— that of selling rum with too great an admix- ture with water. The offender was one THO hIAS WOODS, the landlord of the "Bottle and Glass," and he seems to have given a reading of his own to the celebrated song equivalent to—" Let the bottle pass, and we'll add another glass "—of water for the men of " Merrie England." He fell very simply, if not very innocently, into the trap which two constables were laying for him when they or- dered and obtained a quart of rum. They then asked for a quart of whisky, the order follow- ing so closely on the heels of the first de- mand as to be staggering to those who were accustomed to the quiet business of Hill-top. THE Freeholders of Runcorn have taken the right course in putting themselves in the hands of the Improvement Commissioners with a view to enclosing and regulating the common lands within the township. Single- handed they can do little, but combined with the ratepayers everything may be done that is required to be done to preserve the Heath and Common to the present and future inhabitants. The acreage of Runcorn Hill is given at 57 acres, and the Heath at 21 acres, and this broad land over which the wind as yet blows freshly and freely is surely worth preserving to the people. It may bel that there is not much occasion at present for fear that the land-grabber will lay his hand on any portion of it; but "safe bind, safe find," is a good rule to act upon in a matter of this kind. There are from fifteen to twenty acres of common land at Salesbury, just beyond Blackburn, that are being walled in by neighbouring landowners, although the land has been held in common so long that "the memory of man runneth not back to the contrary." These "pickers and stealers" are not, as it happens, likely to have their way in the matter without a fight for it. Por- tions of the wall have been pulled down, and the feeling of resistance is strong throughout the township. But the Freeholders are for the most part exceedingly poor, and at the same time dependent upon the men who are endeavouring to do them this wrong. So far as they are concerned, the landlords, it is to be feared, would have had their own way; but the Corporation of Black- burn are stepping in under the Commons Act of 1876 (under which it is proposed to take proceedings at Runcorn), and there is reason to believe that a stop will be put to this attempted robbery of a portion of mother- earth. There is happily no great difficulty in the way of taking steps to preserve the com- mon lands of Runcorn. There is a certain amount of indifference to be overcome, and it may be that there will be a few ratepayers who will object to any expenditure in this di- xection. Now, however' that they have begun, " t'were best it were done quickly." They must strike while the iron is hot; they have let it cool once, and have had to re-heat it. With the Riyer Mersey on one side and a Ship Canal on the other' who can say what Runcorn will become Once enclosed, the common lands may ere long undergo such change as to warrant their being spoken of as Runcorn Park.

POOR-RATES.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the magistrates signed poor-rates as follows :—Of 9d in the pound for the township of Clifton, to realise £155 2s lid ; of 7d in the pound for Aston-by-Sutton, to realise £lBO Sc 3d; of 8d in the pound for Aston Grange, to realise £49 8s Bd. SUDDEN DEATH AT WlDNES.—Margaret ROWSOI3, a mar- ried woman, 35 years of age, who lived at 45, Davis-street, Widnes, died suddenly ou Tuesday morning. She was in good health on Monday, and ate a hearty supper before re- tiring to rest, but shortly after midnight she was seized with a sudden illness. Three hours later, notwithstenoing the efforts of Drs. McDonnell, Pattison, and Richards, she died. It is not thought necessary to hold an inquest. MISSIONARY MEETING AT WIDNES.—A meeting in con- nection with the Wesleyan Home and Foreign Missions was beld in Hartland chapel on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. R. Fogg. Addrele On missionary labours were delivered by the chairman the Rev. J. Codd, R. ee Harper, and J. Hothersall. At the conclusion a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Codd and the chairman for their services, on the motion of Mr. W. Hartland. HALTON COURT LEET.—This ancient court beet was held at Halton Castle on Saturday, before Mr. Robert Davies, the steward. There was a good attendance of jurymen. Mr. Thomas Bennett, of Keckwick, was appointed foreman. The steward delivered an address on the antiquity of the court. Mr. Rutter was appointed butleyman, and Messrs. William Fryer and John Newport were re-appointed con- stables. Subsequently the company sat down to a dinner prepared by Mr. Phillips. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WO—Before Mr. E. Gib- bon and Mr. W. L. Danby, on behalf of the Widnes School Board, prosecuted the following persons for neglect- ing to send their children regularly to school :—David finehes, Thomas Reynolds, Wm. Percival, Peter Riley, Anthony Armstrong, James Cunliffe, Matthew O'Connor, John McDermott, John Nicholson, Thomas McAnley, Martin Dunne, and Michael McPartlan. The usual fine of 5s was imposed in each case. A DANGEROUS DOG AT WESTON.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Phcebe Barrow, landlady of the Royal Oak Inn, Weston, was summoned for having a dangerous dog which she did not keep under proper control.—lt was stated that on the sth inst. the defendant's dog, a terrier, jumped at the son, aged six, of Michael Moran, tore his trousers, and left the marks of its teeth upon his body.—A girl named Maggie Farrel said on one occasion the dog hed torn her clothes.—The defen4ant denied that the dog was dangerous; it was playful.—The Bench ordered the de- fendant to keep the dog under proper control, and pay costs, 15s. MARRIAGE PRESENT FROII RUNCORN.— On Wednesday last week Mr. Edward Mount of Liverpool, secretary to the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, was married to Miss Elizibeth Sumner, second daughter of Mr. Thomas Sumner, , Stone Barn, Magleull, at St. Andrew's Church, Maghull. The officials of the works at Runcorn presented the bride- groom with a handsome dining-room black marble clock, and ornaments to match, and also with an aneroid barometer in dark oak elaborately carved. Accompanying these gifts was an ad- dress of an enloeistic character, signed by Messrs F. G. Claudet, G. Bell, W. Armstrong, J. Poole, J. Brookfield, and A. McMillan. THE Row AT THE APPLETON RECREATION GROUNDS.— At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Samuel Morris and Patrick Cannon, young men, and members of the Widnes Football Club, were charged under a warrant with assaulting G. Holden, landlord of the Millfield Inn. It will be remembered that a week ago defendants were sentenced to a month's bard labour in their absence, but subsequently ' on the application of Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, the Bench erased the conviction, and consented that the case should be heard. On Wednesday Mr. Knowles offered a I complete apology to the prosecutor on behalf of the de- ' fendants, and Mr. Holden thereupon withdrew the charges ! with the permission of the Bench. A DOUBTFUL CASE AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Ann Jane Gibson, a girl about 12 years of age, very scantily clothed, and without shoes or stockings, was charged with stealing three herrings worth 31, the property of Charles Clifton, (fish and fruit dealer, Waterloo-road, Widnes. On Saturday night P.C. Holbrook saw the prisoner walk up to the window of the prosecutor's shop and take the herrings from a box. He took her into custody and she said "It is not my fault. My father sent ' me to steal them." The prisoner denied that she took the I fish, and the father in a very noisy manner said be never sent the children out to steal.—Mr. E. Gibbon said the I Bench thought that he did send the children out in the man- ner stated, and a greater offence they could not imagine. The child would be dismissed on this occaston. If he had sent out the child they advised him not to do it again. ROBBERY AT linercome.—At the Runcorn Police Court ' on Wednesday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. James Handley, Alice Ransom and Mary Ann Steadman were brought up, charged with stealing 11 pairs of knitted stock. lugs, value £1 7s 61, the property of Messrs. Unsworth ' Brothers, High-street, Runcorn. The stockings were missed from the shop on Tuesday morning, and at noon the same day P.C. Bason had occasion to go to Die Half-way Besrhonse, Halton-road. The prisoners were there under the influence of drink, and they offered to sell the officer a pair of stockings. They had four pairs in their posses- sion' having sold the rest of the stolen goods. The officer took the prisoners into custody and charged them with the robbery. Steadinan replied that she took the stockings, and Ransom denied that she had anything to do with the matter.—The Bench sentenced each prisoner to a menth's hard labour. CLAIM FOR WAGES AT RUNCORN.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Hughes, able-bodied seaman, claimed from Robert Lloyd, captain of the schooner Emma and Esther, the sum of £7 2s 6d, wages due for services rendered.—Mr. Barton appeared for the complainant, and stated that on the sth September, 1883, the complainant shipped with the de- fendant for wages at the rate of £3 per month. The total amount that would have been due to the complainant at the present time was £4O 6s, but he had received on account £33 38 61, leaving the balance claimed. The complainant had kept an account of the money he had received, and there was an entry of £4 received at Newcastle.—The de- fendant contended that he paid the complainant £5 at that place, and acknowledged that he owed him now £6 2s 6d.— After hearing the evidence. the Bench made an order for the payment of the amount claimed, and costs, £133. RUFFIANLY CONDUCT AT FARISWORTII.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Robert Powell, a youth, was charged with having on the 17th October assaulted a girl named Emma Davies, who lived at Farnworth.—Several witnesses were called to prove that on the evening of the day in question the defendant arid his father threatened to ill-use Davies in consequence of jealousy which existed about some matter. Later as Davies and several companions were returning home from work they SAW defendant and his father leaning against the rails along the lane side. Im- mediately they had passed the defendant went up to Davies and struck her about the head and breast in a violent man- ner. She had in consequence of his violence to put herself under the care of the doctor.—The defendant had nothing to say in extenuation of his offence, but the father stated that his son never struck the girl, but only pushed her. He did this because Davies had "knocked his sister " about the night previous.—The Bench bound the defendant over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO and one surety in £5, and pay the costs 14e. He was informed that he would be committed to gaol without the option of a fine if he repeated the offence, and Mr. Gibbon told the father he had not behaved much better than his son. A YOreso Tnenv AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. W. L. Evans, 'at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, William Henry Butler, 16 years of age, was charged with stealing, on the 17th inst., a number of negatives and photographs belong- ing to William Henry Hadfield, photographer, Victoria. road, Widnes.—The prosecutor deposed that the articles were worth 'IL—P.C. Cummings said he apprehended the prisoner, who took him to the yard of Mr. Stringer, hair dresser, Victoria-road, where the negatives and photographs were concealed. The prisoner acknowledged stealing the articles whilst the owner was away.—The prisoner was then charged with stealing a case containing 12 bottles of whisky, value £2 2s, from the Railway Hotel, Victoria-road.—John Anderson, landlord of the hotel, said on the evening of the 16th inst. there was a case containing 12 bottles of whisky lin the lobby of his house. The following morning he missed them, and he gave information to the police. At noon he found ten bottles of the whisky at the back of his house.—P.C. Cummings stated that the prisoner told him he had stolen the whisky and had broken a bottle in open- ing the case with an axe.—The prisoner, who had served several years in an industrial school, was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment, and afterwards five years in a reforma- tory school. WIDNES SUNDAY SCHOOL UNION.—ANNUAL MEETING. A tea party in connection with Widnes Sunday School Union was held in Lacey-street school-room on Monday evening. Subsequently the annual meeting and distribu- tion of prizes took place, the room being well filled. Mr. B. Brown, the president, occupied the chair, and amongst those present were the Revs R. Harper, J. Hothersall. R. Yeat- man, Messrs, R. Shaw (Runcorn), J. Robinson, J. Hargreaves, F. Lawricson, R.Fogg, G. Rev, and T. J. Peters (hon. sec.) A choir of children from the various schools, numbering 150 voices, rendered several selections of music in a very efficient manner under the leadership of Mr. S. Lamb. They were accompanied by a band of instrumentalists from the Primitive Methodist and Wesleyan Methodist String Band. Mr. C. Taylor was at the harmonium. In opening the pro- ceedings the Chairman delivered an address. He said it gave him great pleasure to meet them attain at this their second meeting for the distribution of prizes in connection with the Union. The first examination did not realise their expec- tations by a great deal, neither in the number of scholars who presented themselves or the quality of the work they performed. This year there had been a marked Improve- ment both in the number of candidates and the quality of the papers. (Hear, hear.) About 18 females and 15 males offered themselves for examination, and had answered the questions in a very creditable manner. He had been con- nected with Sunday schools for a great many years, and it was his opinion that never were they so hardly pressed in meeting the demands of the young people as they were at the present time. All connected with Sunday school labour would have it forced upon them that the teaching required 10 or 12 years ago would not suit the requirements of the present time. (Hear, hear.) If he would keep a class to- gether and engage their attention he must prepare and work for it, and endeavour in every possible way to meet the growing intellectual requirements of the scholars. In this matter no difficulty need be experienced, because teachers could easily and cheaply fit themselves for their work, and there were many more facilities for acquiring knowledge of the proper kind than there were in former days.— The ttev. R. Harper explained the mode in which the ex- amination was conducted by the examiners—the Rev. D. Davies, J. Hothersall, and himself, In the senior section , the number of marks attainable was 40, and amongst the girls the highest obtained was 28, and the boys 17.—Mr. T. J. Peters then briefly addressed the meeting, and read the paper written by Miss Sasannah Glover, who obtained the first prize.—Mr. R. Shaw before distributing the prizes and certificates delivered a short speech, in which he eaid that the Widnes Sunday School Union was doing a grand and noble work in these examinations, and the results spoke , well for the ability of the teachers. He pointed out that 1 children were now taught to think in the excellent day schools in the town, and the Sunday school teacher must be prepared to turn these thoughts into a proper channel. He then distributed the prizes. Appended is a list of the sac. 1 cessful scholars :—Senior division Ist, S. Glover ; 2nd, Jane Sadler; 3rd, Edith Hurst. Certificates : Harry Row- lands, John Shaw, Emily Stringer. Middle division: Ist, Ethel M. Taylor ; 2nd, Henry Wright; eqoal, 3rd, Eliza- beth Glover and Herbert Clarkson. Extra prizes, Fanny Brown, Sarah Stringer, and Thomas H. Jones. Certificates: John Reid, Edward Parsons, and Wm. Teesdale. Junior division: Equal first,. Lettie Harper and Mora Drought ; 2nd. Mary J. Davies. Extra prize: Annie Bennett. Cer- tificates : Alice Swindell, Hannah Tunnercliffe, Reginald Blakemore, Peter Ice, Richard Jenkins, J. H. Dickson, and Ann Reid.—The Rev. J. Hothersall moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Shaw for his kindness that evening, and he mentioned that that gentleman had also promised the Union pecuniary assistance.—Mr. Lawrinsoa seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation.—A. similar compliment was also paid to the examiners, and to the president.—The meeting concluded with the choir singing the anthem •' Praise ye the Lord,"

THE HOURS OF PUPIL TEACHERs : ALLEGED OVER- PRESSURE —Mr. R. H. Davies moved the following resolu- tion, of which he had given notice:—" In order to comply with the requirements of the Education Department, which provide that pupil teachers shall not be employed more than 25 hours per week, it is resolved that the pupil teachers under this Board be liberated from teaching two half-days per week, and that the School Management Committee be instructed to engage at once a competent mistress at a salary not exceeding £l2O per annum, to give instruction to the female pupil teachers, and to superintend their studies when not employed in actual teaching ; and that the central classes as at present constituted for the teaching of female pupil teachers be discontinued from December 31st, 1884. Mr. Davies said he did not move the resolution in opposi- tion to the School Management Cummittee but so that the question could be fully discussed and decided by the Board. He reminded the Board that the law that teachers should only work 25 hours per week had been in existence for al- most two years' and during that time the Board had been acting in contravention of the law and also in spite of their agreements with the pupil teachers as expressed io their in- dentures. He pointed out that the future of the schools de- pended in a great measure upon their treatment and training of the pupil teachers. (Hear, hear.) Their present system of training was very good, and the central classes were a great improvement over the old state of affairs, but still those classes had not done all that was expected of them. He contended that overpressure existed amongst the pupil teachers in the schools. (The Chairman: Hear, hear.)— Mr. Deacon seconded the motion, and observed that a re- commendation similar to that proposed by the School Man- agement Committee that day was passed in July last, and it thus seemed pretty clear that the committee had found that the teachers had not been able to carry out the instruc- tions. Speaking of the central classes Mr. Deacon pointed out that already £l2O was paid to the head teacher for teach- ing the girls in the central school, so that the amount men- tioned in the resolution was not an addition to the expenses of the Board. If, however, all the pupil teachers were liberated two half-days each week they would require about a fifth more staff, and he thought they would be more than repaid for the expenditure lacurred.—The Rev. Father Finegan rose to a point of order. Some of the teachers had indentures under the new law,and some had indentures which required them to work 30 hours per week, and he contended that only so far as the motion affected the new indentures could it be discussed.—Mr. Deacon said the Board was not prevented fram applying the new law to the teachers who were engaged before it was passed.—The Rev. Father Finegan said the rule must be met.—The Chairman ruled that the resolution could only affect the teachers engaged under the new indentures.—Mr. Davis: I think we had better have the motion adjourned if that is the case.—Mr. Shaw said there were only two ways of dealing with the question, either the teachers must close the schools earlier than they did now or the Board must provide some means by which the teachers could be employed according to law and the school kept open as now.—Mr. Glover supported the motion, remarking that the Board ought to honourably NMI its engagements.—The Rev. Father Clarke protested against the motion passing. He had always been in favour of an efficient teaching staff, bat if this was passed he thought they would altogether upset their system of teaching.—Mr. Davis amended his motion so that it would read that the school management consider and report upon the scheme.— The Chairman thought the committee ought to be allowed to consider the question wholly unfettered. He agreed that over-pressure existed amongst the pupil teachers, and if the relaxation allowed by law was to be given then it followed that some re-arrangement of the staff was necessary. (Hear, hear.)—The Rey. Father Finegan said there had been many references to over-pressure of pupil teachers, but they most remember that they had passed a medical examination and had obtained doctors' certificates.—Mr. Shaw hoped the committee would formulate some scheme by which the over- pressure of the teachers would be relieved and the require- ments of the law carried out.—The Chairman asked the Rev. Father Finegan whether, as Chairman of the Scheel Management Committee, he would accept the following re- solution : "That in order to comply with the requirements of the Education Department, which provides that pupil teachers shall not be employed more than 25 hours per week, the School Management Committee be anthorieed to make such re-arrangement of the teaching staff as may be necessary, and report to the Board?'—The Rev. Father Finegan : Yes.—Mr. Brock seconded the amendment, which was carried, and the meeting terminated.

Tba directors cannot refrain from expressing the gratifica- tion they feel in noticing how large is the number of chil- dren who have gained p-izes and certificates. The number in the Board schools is larger than that in the voluntary schools, but it must be remembered that in the Board echools a somewhat similar system of prizes had been in force for two 'ears. It is satisfactory to note that, in the Board schools, although the money value of the Ist prize had decreased from about Ms last year to 14s this year, yet that the number of children who have gained Ist prizes has slightly increased. From this circumstance the directors hope that the prizes and rewards offered by the Council, though of no great monetary value, will act as an induce- ment to regular attendance. It is also a most satisfactory feature that the majority of children still hold in the sav- ings' bank the deposal gained as prizes during the 2 years before the Council of Education was formed. The Gover- nors of the Farnworth Graminar School having offered two free scholarships, tenable for three years, for competition manually amongst the boys attending elementary schools within the parish of Farnwortb, it was decided that, when the successful boys had attended a public eiemen- tary school in Widnes, the Council should make , a grant of not exceeding £1 per anuum for books necessary for each of the successful boys' and, where the circumstances of the parent rendered it advisable, should grant a sum of 15s per month to asAst in clothing and maintaining the bay. The two hip) who were successful in gaining the free scholarships at the Farnworth Grammar hchool were both educated in pub- lic elementary schools in Widne., and the directors have Promised, on the application of the father cf one of the boys, to pay the grant for maintenance. In accordance with I rule 3 of the constitution, the directors have decided, by ballot, that the following named gentlemen—Revs. J. Clarke, T. Finegan, and J. Wright Williams; Messrs, J. Brock end H. Wade Deacon, shall retire at the general meeting. Below is an estimate of receipts and expenditure for the first year. The directors are glad to have a balance to begin the second year with, as they expect and hope that the expenditure of next year will be greater then that of this. Anticipating increased expenditure, tha directors keg to ask the sub- scribers to urge their friends to join the Council.—Estimated receipts :—Subscriptions promised. £206 19s. Estimated expenditurs:-Printine, &e ,S', prizes, £lO3 10s; cerrdicatPs, £O5; scholarship grant,. sell ; balance, £22 9s; total £206 193. The Chairman moved the adoption of the report with much pleasure. He observed that although the inducement to attend the Board schools on every oceasion they were opened had been reduced, the number of scholars who had made every possible attendance had increased. He thought this was extremely satisfactory, and showed that good haoits when once formed were permanent, and also proved that the view of some of the subscribers was right—that the money prieees were not the only inducement, but even an ornamen- tal card was an inducement for the scholars to attend regu- larly. They would remember before the scheme of the Council of Education was formed, part of the money prize was paid to the child's parent and part into the post office sayings bank fo- the child. They had not got the exact figures before them, but they had enough to warrant them I in saying that the majority of the bank books were still in possession of the children.—This fact was very gratifying, and showed that thrifty habits were being formed, and that these little depoeite were guarded and valued. The Chair- ' man referred to the Farnworth scholarships, which he be- lieved had worked satisfactorily, and he hoped that the I prizes the Council were giving to the scholars would be valued. They were giving extremely pretty cards. As a rule the cottages of the working-men were not ornamental, and these cards would tend to ornament them, as if a child brought home four or five during its educational career, they would be pleasing to look upon and quite ornament the dwelling. Mr. Brock seconded the adoption of the report. Mt. Deacon drew attention to the rule of the Council which stated that the prizes and certificates should be dis- tributed in as mac a manner as possible. The Rev. Father Finegan said he had to raise an objec- tion to the clause relating to the scholarships, inasmuch as it was too exclusive. He thought that giving the grant to Farnworth, and Farnworth alone, was to a certain extent , going against the constitntion of the Council, because in the case of his own schools scholar who bad won a scholar- ' ship might not wish to go to Farnworth, and it would be a great disadvantage to him if the grant Only allowed him to finish his education at Farnworth. The Chairman said be believed the desire of the sub- scribers when they formed the Council was that there should be no preference or privileges to any one party, but that equal justice should be done, and if their Roman Catholic friends did not see their way to send their children to Farn- worth, he did not see why they should not send them where they liked if they got the grant. But Father Fine- gan could bring the subject again before the committee. , Rev. Father Finegan : I don't press it. I think it is sufficient to take notice of it. I fully agree with the re- port. The report was then adopted. The retiring directors were the Revs. J. Wright-Wil- liams, Father Finegan, Father Clarke, Mr. Deacon' and Mr. Brock.—Mr. Brock expressed a desire to retire from the Board of directors, and on the motion of the Chairman. Dr. McLennan was appointed in his place, and the other direc- tors were re-appointed. Mr. F. IL Gouge was re-appointed hon. treasurer, on the motion of the Rev. Father Clarke, seconded by Mr. Danby.—The Rev. Father Finegan pro- posed the re-appointment of Mr. Deacon to the hon. secre- taryship.—Mr. S. K. Muspratt seconded the motion and the Chairman supported it , all speaking in complimentary terms of Mr. Deacon's labonrs.—Tbe motion was carried.— Mr. Deacon said the school teachers had been asking whether the Council intended to continue the same system of prizes for the present year.—The Council approved of tbe system adopted by the Executive Committee, which will be continued.—Votes of thanks to the chairman and secretary concluded the meeting.

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The mcnthly meeting of this Board was held yesterday morning. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were present the Rev. Father Fennelly, Messrs. Pritchard, Nor- man, Elazlehurst, and and F. Rigby (clerk). Fmances.—The Clerk presented a statement of the receipts and expenditure for the year ended the 29th Sep- tember. It stated that at the commencement of the year there was a balance in hand of £159 9s 9d, and the receipts, including the balance, amoanted to £685 6s 106. The grants from the Council on Education amounted to £9l Ti, school fees to £73 5s 56, and there had been received from the rating authorities £350 at 155 per pound. The total expenditure amounted to £531 5s 61, and there was a balance in hand of £154 Is 56. The election had coat £8 18s 6d, and there had been paid salaries of officers of the Board £195 us 86, legal and other expenses of administra- tion £79 3s sd. salaries of teachers £l4O 4e, repayment of loans £24 113 4d, interest £2435 Bd. The outstanding loans amounted to £628 9s.—The Clerk observed that for 1881 the rate was 2id in the pound, and for 1882 and 1883 26 in the pound.—The accounts were passed. THE VICAR'S ANNUAL LETTER: A CORRECTION.— Mr. Pritchard drew attention to a paragraph in Canon Barclay's annual letter, which stated that the education of each child in the Board school cost 255, so that by maintaining the national day schools, the ratepayers were saved at least £9OO per year. In consequence of various inquiries, he had been led to examine into the statement and found that for the year ending the 30th June last they received from the rates for Mill Brow school £l3 178 10d, which for 128 children would make 2. 2d for each child for the year. But suppose they added to this sum £4B 103 4d, a capital charge for purchasing school premises—and that was really a permanent investment for the present and future genera. tions of children he could only then make the cost 9s 9d for each child. Be was glad to see Canon Barclay present, and he was quite sure he would not be willing to give currency to any misleading statement. If he (the vicar) had been inadvertently led into an error of figures, he would be glad that publicity should be given to that which was correct and true. The Clerk remarked that for the year ending June, 1883, the rates amounted to £l5 8s 26, and if they added to that the capital charge of £4B the cost per child would be 10s.—Af ter examining the balance- sheets for 1883 and 1884, the Chairman said he must have based his figures on wrong statistics. He was mistaken in some manner, but it was so long since the letter was writ- ten that he could not remember. He was very glad Mr. Pritchard had called his attention to it. AN ArPomnauarr.—There were nine applications for the position of assistant mistress at Mill Brow Board Schools. —After some discussion Miss Mary Ann Simkin, of Bedford Leigh, a native of Runcorn, was unanimously appointed. Ina PROPOSED NEW .SCHOOL.—Mr. Holme, of the firm of Messrs. F. and G. llolme, architects. Liverpool, attended and discussed the plans of the proposed new Board School. There was no ether business of public interest.

WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIIII SOCIRTY.—A quarterly meeting of the members of this society was held in the Co- operative Hall, on Monday evening, the chair being occu- pied by Mr. Thomas Birchall, president. It was stated that the sales for the past quarter had amounted to ..t3,479 4e Bi, and it was resolved that a dividend of 2s 8d in the pound on members' purchases be paid. literviss"r FESTIVAL AT STRATTON —Thanksgiving Ser- vices were held in Stretton Church, on Sunday last. Holy Communion was celebrated at 8.30, and at the subsequent morning service there was a large attendance. The preacher was the Vicar, the Rev. Canon Dodd, who chose as his text Proverbs x, 5, "He that gethereth in summer is a wise eon; but he that sleepeth in harvest is a son that causeth shame." In the afternoon the Rev. W. Williams, vicar of Padgate, preached to a very large gathering. The church had been decorated in a very tasteful style by Mrs Whitley, Mrs. Dodd. Mrs. Kerr, Miss Atherton, Mrs. Grange, Mr. de Prez, Mr. mo. Bennett, and Mr. Isaac Hewitt. The offer- tory amounted to over £l4. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending Saturday, October 11th, 1884. The mean tfsaweratare was 411 Fahrenheit, and therefore 7.1 degrees colder than preceding week. The maximum temperature 59 Fahrenheit was recorded on the 6th inst., and the minimum temperature 22 Fahrenheit on the 11th inst. The rainfaii measured an inch. The general direction of the wind was north-west. During the week, which was the 41st of the current year, 27 births and 19 deaths were registered. The ddath rate from all causes was equal to 22 1 per 1,000, against 211 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 165 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 4 from diarrhrea, 5 from measles, 1 from whooping cough, 1 from dropsy, 1 from old age, 2 from liver disease, and 4 from brain dtsease.—JOHN H. GoRNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

Parliament met to-day in circumstances which indicated the importance of the crisis. At the commencement of oldinary sessions there is always something of a crowd at the entrance to Parliament-yard. People who have nothing else to do and happen to be in the neighbourhood stroll down to see the nimbus pass, hoping above all things to catch a glimpse of Mr. Gladstone. But there is an idle purposeless aspect with the crowd that indicates the nature of their errand. To-day the ordinary crowd was more than doubled, and there was about it an almost fierce, restless, movement very useful to contemplate by the men who are responsible for the present crisis. 'f hey were evidently al- most without exception. Liberals and their views were ex- pressed with a freedom and loudness of tone that showed they felt they were discussing a public question and need , not speak with bated breath. The outbreaks at Birming- -1 ham and Dumfries are, of course, regrettable, and have been publicly bewailed in all respectable newspapers. But I have to-day heard more than one sober-minded member ex- press the opinion that there are compensatory aspects. Lord Randolph Churchill in his frank way has openly declared that nothing but physical force would convince the Tories of the earnestness of the people in the matter of Reform. Lord Salisbury in more guarded language has also taunt- ingly referred to the absence of those outbreaks which shook the resolve of the peers in 1832, and, later, during the Corn Law crisis. At Birmingham and Dumfries there was the slightest possible foretaste of what may come and what certainly will come if there be no other way. There was something of this attitude about the crowd at Palace-yard j to-day which might have been studied with advantage by Lord Salisbury. Inside, matters did not look so exciting. The attendance of members was below the average on an Opening day. Many are still hurrying home from shortened holiday. Others like to fiuish up the week and know it will be time enough if they put in an appearance en Monday. Beyond this, members have had the edge taken off their appetite for excitement round the Franchise Bill. Most of them during the weeks that have passed since the prorogation have been engaged in speech-making, and to come back on the edge of winter to the very head and fount of speech-making is rather depressing than otherwise. Besides it is known that what took place to-night with the exception of Mr. Glad- stone's speech, and what will follow for some days to come, Is not business. There will be much dreary speech-making unnaturally prolonged. Members have come to town in October to pass the Franchise Bill. When that is reached they will waken up. In the ineantim., tilling to-night as an example—always excepting the pe sonal reception of Mr. Gladstone—matters were a trifle dull.

The most eager talk went to the heat and soul of the matter. What will the L,..,rds do ? And then ? are the two questions which passed about the beetling thtong that gathered in the lobby and on the floor of the House be- tween half-past three and half-past four. In anawer to the first I find a general impression that the Lords will again throw out the Bill, not perhaps in the same rude peremptory manner that recommended itself to Lord Salisbury last see- sin, but with equal effect by hanging it up, ty making it a condition that it shall not become law till the Redistri- bution Bill has been passed. As to what will follow upon the second flouting of the popular will there are of course many possibilities. Mr. Gladstone may make sufficient peers to cirry the Bill through. He may immediately dis- solve and appeal to the country, or he may give the Lords a third chance by bringing the Bill up again next session. On the first suggestion there is a difficulty which, though not unsurinountable, must be taken account et. The Con- servative majority in the Loras is so great that it would be necessary, in order to overcome it, to create peers by whole- sale. At least fly new peers must be made, an accession fearful to contemplate, except with the assurance that shortly after they have been created the whole institution will he abolished. With respect to dissolution that is en- tirely out of the question. To dissolve now would be to play into the hands of Lord Salisbury and give him the very thing he has peremptorily demanded. I hear upon high authority of another and better consi- dered course which Mr. Gladstone is prepared to adopt. Should the Lords again throw out the Franchise Bill the Premier will introduce in the House of Commons a reso- lution to the effect that the House of Lords as at present constituted is a danger to the State, and urgently demands reform. This will pass by an overwhelming majority in the House of Commons, and will be received with acclaim throughout the country. It will be left to work its effect for a few weeks, and early in January of next year Parlia- ment will be summoned, and once more and for the last time the Franchise Bill will go up to the Lords. Upon its third rejection an appeal will be made to the country, but not solely upon the Franchise Bill. The existence of the House of Lords in its present form, and illustrated by its recent action, will be alsa submitted to the country, and its solemn verdict asked. What that verdict will be Lord Salisbury can scarcely doubt, and may think it wise to do in 1885, what he has twice declined to concede in 1884. But it will then be too late as far as the sanctity of the House of Lords is concerned. The resolution referred to will stand upon record; the question will have been irrevo- cably raised and the burning question • that will be sub- mitted to the new constituencies, enlarged by the addition of two million voters, will be: Shall the House of Lords continue to exist as a co-eval part of the legislature of the country?

The death of A. M. Sullivan has elicited a wider and ap- parently more genuine manifestation of personal regret than has in recent years graced the memory of any public man. No one would have been more surprised than Mr. Sullivan himself to learn how strong a hold he had upon the affection and esteem of widely diverse people. He was, among other tare qualities, one of the most modest of men, and was con- tinually surprised by evidences of good will received during his lifetime. This was particularly the case when he retired from Parliamentary life and took to the bar. It was by. special favour that certain difficulties in the way of his join- ing the English bat were overcome. In the task of putting them aside men so diverse in character and so widely separated in politics as Sir Henry James and the late Sir John Holker heartily joined. It was the same in the House of Commons, in London society, and even in Ireland. I once had the great pleasure of travelling through Ireland with Mr. Sullivan. This was years ago, at the close of his first Parliamentary session where, again to his unfeigned sur- prise, he had been crowned with laurel as the most success- ful private member of the year. At every town we stopped at in Ireland there was a popular rush to get at Sullivan, shake his hand, and hear his voice. At Bantry in particu- lar, his native town, there was a concert given which he with the party of his travelling campanions attended. Sul- livan secreted himself in a remote corner of the hall. But be bad been discovered, and all through the evening there was a chorus of " Ah 'lm Soollivan," and at lastthe blushing orator was obliged to come forward and say a few words te his fellow townsmen. That was one of the few holidays he ever took. It was in truth overwork that killed him. Rest was a rare visitant to his eager impressionable nature. A bonester, more chivalrously honourable, kinder hearted, more lovable man than A. M. Sullivan never lived.

The great loss to the public service occasioned by the withdrawal of Mr. Trevelyan front the Chief Secretaryship of Ireland is only partly compensated for by the elevation of Mr. Dodson to the House of Lords. Mr. Trevelyan has I proved one of tke principal personal successes of the present administration, and it is well known there are several. He undertook the office at a time not only of profound political crisin, but even of some personal danger. His predecessor bad just been audaciously murdered, and no one could say that the successor was not foredoomed to a similar fate. Mr. Trevelyan undertook the work with a due sense of its responsibilities and dangers, and has accomplished it in a , manner that extorts the admiration even of the kind of men with whom he has been in conflict in the House of Commons. That he should retire is no wonder. Two years of the Irish Secretaryship is long enough for any man, too long for on of the sensitive nature of Mr. Trevelyan. How deeply be felt the toi:s of his position is proved by striking testimony. When net quite two years ago he accepted the poet, he had an abundant crop of black hair with a coal black beard and moustache. Now his hair is thickly strewn , with grey, whilst his beard is positively white.

Mr. Dodson has for many years been a political sphinx. Amongst Ministers, and above all as a Cabinet Minister, he has in political circles created the same kind of marvel which the discovery of an apple in the dumpling filled the mind of King George. " How he got there" no one could say, or even imagine. He was a very fair Chairman of Committees, though between 1865 and 1872 that was an office very different from what it is at present. Mr. Dodson , had the good fortune to retire just before the birth of the arnellite party. That was the high-water mark of his

CADISHEAD. HARVEST SERV/CES.—Cadishead and Irlam CongreL;a- tional Church held their harvest thanksgiving services en Sunday. A children's service was held in the morning t 10-30, conducted by the Rev. G. Brimacombe. In the afternoon, at 2-30, the Rev. J. Yonge, of Warrington, preached a most impressive and excellent sermon. In th e evening, at 6 o'clock, the Rev. G. Brimacombe delivered an earnest discourse. The chapel was tastefully decorated for the occasion with corn, fruit, flowers, and vegetables. Ap- propriate hymns and anthems were sung by the choir. The chapel was filled at all the services. The collections amounted bo £l4 ss.

SERMONS, ,AT IRLAM.—The annual missionary ser- mons were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday by the Rev. A. Wood, of Manchester, both morning and even- ing, to excellent congregations. The public meeting was held on Monday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr: Walker, of Manchester, who made a suggestive sp.?ech. This was followed by a stirring address by the Rev. H. Bone, of Manchester (Oxford-road). The report was read by the Rev. R. Dillon, of the Cadishead Circuit. The col- lections realised £l3.

ALARtriNo COLLISION. TWO HORSES KILLED.—There was a collision between two traps on Wednesday evening oa the road from Warrington, a little beyond Hollins Green. A baker's conveyance, on its way back to Warrington, ran into Mr. Fairhurst's trap, of Cadishead, with great force. Damage to a considerable extent waS done to the traps, and both horses have died through the injuries they received. There is likely to be a law snit before the affair is settled.

Sarn—aher----Before Mr. Jtabn Faircleugk and Alderman Chandler: A SUSPICIOUS Caaaecnta.—David Barker, a tramp, was charged with breaking into an empty house in Lovely-lane on Friday, doing damage to the amount of 2s 6d, and with stealing therefrom a bell-handle and a door-key.—Prisoner, who gave no account of himself and did not appear te under- stand the charge against him, was found asleep in the house by a constable.—The Bench dealt with the case as one of being found on the premises for an unlawful purpose, and sent him to prison for a.month. div.head: TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN SALFORD. MURDER OF A WIFE AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OF TEE MURDERER.
div.p: TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN SALFORD. MURDER OF A WIFE AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OF TEE MURDERER.

Much consternation has been caused on Thursday after- noon in the neighbourhood of Ordsal-lane, Salford, by tho commission of a terrible domestic tragedy, which has jeopardised the lives of three persons. In Tatton-place, a small side street in the middle of a large population, lived a young couple named M'Laren, and it is their house which has been brought into terrible notoriety by the murderous deed. M'Laren's father, who was by trade a dyer, has for some time been out of employment, and with his wife had been living at the house of their son. The father, Patrick M'Laren, has. during the last six months, given frequent in- dications that his mind was affected, and during the last three weeks he hoe made three separate attempts on the life of his wife Amelia. At last she was compelled to leave him and went to live with her son, and as she refused to return to live with him her husband broke up his house and the furniture was sold. Since then he has visited his wife at Tattoo-piece and has stayed partly there and partly with a sister at Pendleton. On Wednesday, however, he mode another attempt on the life of his wife, and an application was made to the authorities for protection On Thursday morning, however, the man went again to Tatton Place, but he seemed quiet and more like himself, and though a certain amount of terror was inspired by his presence there was no apprehension of the terrible deed which in a few minutes startled the whole neighbourhood. Shortly after twelve o'clock Mrs. M'Laren, the mother, went downstalis to fetch some coal. No sooner had she got upon the cellar steps than her husband rushed to the front door and fastened it, and then dashed down the cellar after her. Seizing a coal hammer he struck the unfortunate woman a fearful blow with it, and knocked her down in the far corner of the cellar. She screamed for help, and appealed to her husband for mercy, and her daughter-in-law, who was up- stairs, rushed down the cellar to her assistance. She found M'Laren standing over his wife nith an open razor in his hand, with which he had already made an incision in her throat. She endeavoured to pull the man away and made a desperate attempt to secure the razor, but the man was too strong for her, and, pulling her towards him' he contrived whilst holding his wife on the floor to push his daughter- in-law against the wall. He told her that he would do for her, but she implored him to save her for the sake of her child. He paid no heed, however, to her entreaties, and a desperate effort to cut her throat also, but she struggled successfully with him, and after receiving several severe cuts about the hands she escaped from him and rushed into the street and gave the alarm. In the meantime M'Laren had continued the savage work. He made cut after cut at the throat of the prostrate woman and did not cease until the head was nearly severed from the body. By this time a large crowd had assembled outside the house, but no one dared to venture into the cellar where the murderer was heard walking about. He still had the razor in his hand, and after an interval of about five min- utes he was heard to fall. Some of the neighbours then went into the cellar and found Ml,aren and his wife lying on the ground literally bathed in blood. They were remo- ved to the house place upstairs, and Dr. Leonard and Dr. Cran were soon in attendance. They, however, pronounced life to la! extinct in the case of the woman, and the man had inflicted suck fearful injuries on his own throat that his death is only a question of a short time. . .

McLaren met with an accident about eighteen years ago, when the eight of the eye was destroyed by a piece of steel. ' Some months ago he commenced to show signs of mental aberration, and a medical man who was consulted stated that the piece of steel was still in his head and was affect- ing his brain. For the last six months he has been pecu- liar, but it is only during the last few weeks that a homici- dal tendency bas manifested itself. He is 43 years of age, and his wife was 42. They leave two children, one the son in whose house the terrible accident was caused, and the other a girl of seven. The injuries sustained by the daugh- ter-in-law are severe, but not of a serious nature.

div.head: ENGLAND AND CANADA.
div.p: ENGLAND AND CANADA.

'England and Canada, a Summer Tour between Old and New Westminster, with historical Notes," by Sand- ford Fleming, E.G., C.M.G., ; London: Sampson Low, Marston Searle, and Rivington. The title of 'this volume hardly does justice to this important work, bat the author shown himself throughout to be unpretentious. It is so much the rule to find taking titles which are too fre- quently a "take in," that it is especially agreeable to come across a work which promises little and performs so much. The book is a substantial well-printed volume of over 400 pages, and presents Canada, for it is almost solely with Canada that it deals, in such a way as to excite a deep in- terest in the mind of the untravelled reader. Mr. Fleming presents a carefully prepared map so that his journevings to and fro can be followed with ease; and what his travelling involved will be in some degree realized when it is stated that altogether, by sea and land, he covered about 14,000 miles. "These notes," he says, " give a sketch of the first continuous journey ever made, indeed the only one yet at- tempted, through the whole longitudinal extent of the Dominion by the route taken." The following passage from the introductory chapter is suggestive of the scope of the work, and it in at the same time a fair specimen of the author's style : Continuing our glance westward, a thousand miles from Bonavista, beyond the ancient fortress of Quebec, we be- hold Montreal, the commercial metropolis of the Dominion. Here are seen ocean steamers of the largest class discharging cargoes loaded twelve days back in Liverpool, Glasgow and other parts of Europe. Advancing our view another thousand miles, over cultivated fields and flourishing cities and lakes of unrivalled magnitude, our vision carries us through deep forests beyond the Province of Ontario to the confines of Manitoba, in the middle of the continent. Still another thousand miles to the west, across prairies abounding with a tabulous fertility of soil, we reach the foot-hills of a snow- capped mountain range, concealing the country which lies beyond it To penetrate this barrier we must advance by the known passes, and for hundreds of miles follow deep defiles, traversing further mountain ranges, until we reach the wide grassy plateau, interspersed with picturesque lakes, in the heart of British Columbia. We may still pierce another serrated wall of mountains by a deep and rugged valley, and, by following a tortuous and foaming river to its mouth, we meet the flow of tide of another ocean far greater in extent than that which lies behind us. Carrying our vision beyond the shore of the western mainland, across a strait similar to that separating England from Europe, we see the Island of Vancouver, washed by currents warmed in the seas of Asia. Vancouver Island is not quite so large as England, bat it enjoys the same climatic conditions, and possesses in profusion many of the same mineral treasures. - _

British Columbia is the youngest colony of the Empire, and until recently was practically the most distant from the Imperial centre. Its chief city bears the name of Her Majesty. The son does not rise on Victoria, the capital of British Columbia, until eight hours after it gilds the towers of Westminster. One-third of the complete circle of the globe separates the Imperial capital from the capital of the Pacific Province, but no land intervenes which is not British, and the whole distance is under the shadow of the one national flag. In imagination we first glanced across the ocean at its narrowest limit. Turning our glance landward, we have looked across a continent at its greatest width. All we have scanned, from sea to sea, is Canada. The vast proportions of the Dominion, its varied features, its lakes and rivers, mountains and plains, its sources of wealth and magnificent scenery, are but little known to Englishmen. A country to be known must be seen. It is not enough to examine a terrestrial globe or ponder over maps and geographies in order to form an estimate of the character of half a con- tinent. They suggest but a faint idea of territorial extent. You must traverse its different sections, and bestow time in examining its fields and forests, its natural landscape, its cities and civilization. _

There are few, indeed, who possess anything like an adequate conception ef the immense extent and resources of the Dominion. It is scarcely possible even for Canadians themselves to conceive the wealth of territory and the varied magnificence of scenery and the productive capacity of the land, the destinies of which it is their privilege to control.

The work is fittingly dedicated to the Marquis of Lorne. It is to be hoped it will find a wide circle of readers, calcula- ted as it is to bring England and Canada into closer and better relationship.

Mr. W. F. Wallett, the " Queen's Jester," is confined to his bed at Beeston, Notts. On Saturday last he was seized with a paralytic stroke, which has slightly affected his right , side. He had to be taken home from an engagement he was fulfilling at a chcus in Dudley. UNFENCED MACHINERY.—The Staveley Coal and Iron Company, Limited, were fined £5O by the Chesterfield magi- strates on Saturday for a breach of the Factory Act, in neg- lecting to have properly fenced some brick-making machin- ery, in which a girl employed by them became entangled and lost her life.

div.head: EXAMINER. SA TtIRDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SA TtIRDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1884.

EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. THE NILE EXPEDITION. CAIRO, MONDAY.—The 19th Hussars and the First Bat- tery of the Ist Brigade of Garrison Artillery, 13th division, will go up the Nile at the earliest opportunity. In defer- ence to the objections raised by the Egyptian Government, the proposal made by Lord Northbrook for the complete abolition of the Egytian army has been abandoned, and a reduction to 3000 men has been decided upow. This mea- sure will reduce the army estimates to £150,0001 The police estimates have been reduced to £900,000, notwithstanding an intended increase of the force by 1,200 men. The hear- ing of the law suit brought by the Csisse of Public Debt against the Egyptian Government has been postponed until the 17th prox.--Standard. WADY HA,LFA, SATURDAY.—Lord Wolseley returned here this evening. Captain Brocklehurst has arrived here on special service. The steamer which brought him had 33 whale boats in tow. WADY HALFA, MONDAY.—COI. Butler, C.ll, has arrived here in charge of a barge, bringing portions of a Yarrow steamer. Three officers, with drafts and details for the Sus- sex Regiment, have left here for Hannek. Twe.more deaths from enteric fever have occurred, the victims being a sapper and a hospital orderly. ALEXANDRIA, SATIIRDAY.—The rest of the Nile boats from England have arrived here. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—Lord Northbrook had an audience of the Khedive this morning, and took leave of His High- ness previous to his return to England. COL. STEWART'S RUMOUEED DEATH. DONGOLA, TOESDAY.—The latest report received here con- cerning the steamer alleged to have been run aground at Wady Game, states that two nuggars and not a steamer was captured by the rebels. Their occupants, Berberecn merchants and families from Khartoum, were released un- harmed after the rebels had appropriated their possessions. DEATH OF TEIR DUKE OF BRUNSWICK. Baensu, SATURDAY.—The Duke of Brunswick expired at a quarter past one o'clock this morning. BRUNSWICK, SAYDRDAI.—The Council of Regency has assembled, and declared that, in consequence of the Duke deinise.the Council convened in virtue of the Re- gency Law of 1879 will provisionally conduct the govern- ment of the country in accordance with the provisions of the law in question. General Hilgers, Prussian General of Bri- gade here, has issued a proclamation to the inhabitants of Brunswick, statiag that, in virtue of the Federal treaty of 18137, and the Imperial Constitution, the right of examin- ing the question of the appointment of a successer to the late Duke belongs to the Imperial Government. General lingers adds that the Emperor has conferred upon him the chief command of the troops stationed in the Duchy, and he therefore, in the Emperor's name, calls upon the inhabit- ants to await with confidence the decision of the Imperial Government. BREsLAII, SuNDAy.—Yesterday at noon the Chief Presi- dent arrived at the Castle of Oels, and informed the offi- cials of the Ducal household that, by order of the Prussian Minister of the Interior, he took possession of the whole of the landed estate of Oels in the name of the King and Crown Prince of Prussia. The Chief President has now assumed the administration of the property, which will, as a Crown estate, be immediately incorporated with Prussia. FRANCE AND CHINA. Pears, MONDAY.—Vice-Admiral Peyren has received the following from General Briere de l'lsle, dated Haiphong, Sunday:—" Large masses of the enemy, who had appeared in the Red River region, attacked Triguen (titan on the 13th instant. They were repulsed with heavy loss. There was no less on the French side. All the wounded are doing well and oat of danger." Admiral Kourbet, Kelung, Sunday:— "The troops are engaged in constructing block-houses round our positions. The work has been impeded by bad weather." BERLIN SUNDAY,—Tho Chinese Embassy has received a despatch "ally confirming the news that the French were defeated in a battle which was fought at Taman' on the 15th. The Chinese forces greatly exceeded the French. The French operations were in a great measure frustrated by torpedoes.

THE CHOLERA. Rom?, WEDNESDAY.—According to this morning's offi- cial bulletin 23 cases of cholera occurred at Naples yester- day and four deaths. At Genoa up to 10 p.m. there had been no farther cases. Two persons previously attacked had, however, succumbed. In the provinces there were 76 cases and 25 deaths, including 22 cases and 12 deaths in the province of Cuneo, two cues and one death in the province of Genoa, and 14 cases and three deaths in the province of Naples. One death and 16 fresh cases are reported from Salerno. Roam, THIIRSDAY.—The official bulletin to-day states that sixteen fresh cases of cholera occurred yesterday at Naples, and one death. Paws, THIIRSDAY.—The reported outbreak of cholera at Yport, near Rouen, is confirmed. Eleven cases and six deaths have occurred daring the last week. The disease is understood to have been hnported by a sailor from Cette. Precautions have been adopted against the spread of the epidemic.

BELGIUM—LIBERAL VICTORY. BRUSSELS, SUNDAY —The Liberals have carried the day here by a majority of about 3,800 votes, and at Antwerp by a majority of 1,110 votes, in the communal elections. In all the large towns, with the exception of Matinee, the Liberals maintain their former positions with considerable increased majorities. The result of the elections is considered as a condemnation of the Education Act. Disturbances occurred at Malines. The windows of several convents and other Roman Catholic establishments were broken by the mob. Seventeen of the rioters were arrested. RENEWED RIOTING. BRUSSELS, WEDNESDAY.—There has again been some riot- ing between the Clerical and Liberal partisans in different towns, notably at Courtrai and Hasselt. In a village near walines a shot was fired upon a group of persons, causing the death of one individual and wounding four others. BnusseLs, WEDNESDAY, 12-50 P.M.—The King gave audience this marning to M. Melon. A Cabinet Council was summoned at 11 o'clock, immediately after the Pre- mier's interview with His Majesty. It is still sit- ting. The visit to the Palace paid yesterday by M. Bara, Minister of State and Minister of Justice in the last Liberal Cabinet, is much commented upon. It is surmised that the King summoned M. Sara in order to request him to counsel his political friends to maintain a prudent attitude at the present juncture. BRUSSEL, THURSDAY.—The King having demanded the withdrawal of MM. Woeste and Jacobs from the cabinet, M. Melon has sent in his resignation as a protest. M. Ma- lon said to his Majesty :—" Sire, for forty years have I strug- gled to defend the country and Royalty against the schemes of Liberalism and Radicalism. I now retire; I have had enough of it." The report that the Chambers will be dis- solved appears to be unfounded. MM. Malon and Bernaert will be again received by the King this evening. MINE DISCOVERED IN ST. PETERSBURG.—EXECU- TION OF NIHILISTS.—GREAT FIRE. ST. PETERSBURG, SATURDAY.—Tne other night a mine was discovered in a cellar in a street named Kronoverski Prospect It was directed against one of the ravelins of the the fortress of St. Peter and St. Paul. Seven persons, four Russians and three foreigners, have been arrested. BERLIN, SATURDAY.—Six condemned Nihilists, together with the celebrated revolutionist, Mary Fignera, priest's daughter, and another woman, named Wolkenstein, were executed this week in the citadel of St. Petersburg. The prisoners were condemned to death about ten days ago. MOSCOW, SUNDAY:A fire broke out this evening in a building situated in the centre of the city used for ware- housing. The flames spread to larger warehouses on the Petrowka, Kusnetzky, and Mosty streets. The neighbour- ing German theatre also caught fire, and the houses are in great danger. MOSCOW, MONDAY.—Tbe fire was put out at an early hour this morning. Altogether sixty-seven shops in the Sete- downikoff passage, the German Theatre nine other shops, and two offices have been burnt. The damage is estimated at 3.000,000 roubles. DISCOVERY OF ANOTHER PLOT AGAINST THE CZAR. BERLIN, WEDNESDAY.—lntelligence from St. Petersburg states that on Sunday night a secret printing press was seized by the police and several persons arrested. The 1 police also discovered documents concerning a projected attempt on the life of the Czar. Several arrests continue to be made. THE CONGO CONFERENCE. BERLIN. MONDAY.—The news that England has accepted in principle the invitation to the Congo Conference is con- finned. It is stated that the British Government, before giving its final adhesion, desires to discuss several points. The United States have now also accepted the invitation. Prince Bismarck will probably preside. SOUTH AMERICA. NEW YORE, SUNDAY. Intelligence from Lima esti- mates that there were four hundred killed and wounded on both sides during therrecent three days' fighting at Tux- illo, preceding the capture of that place by the Govern- ment force. GREAT FIRE IN AMERICA.

NEW Yo, TIJESDAY.—A. great fire has occurred at Carthage, New York State, in which 160 buildings have been burned down, including several factories and churches, and many private houses. The dwellings which have es- caped the conflagration are insufficient to shelter the inhabitants. The loss is estimated at nearly one mil- lion dollars.
