17 AtIZETI;I3o FAFTHESS AT ASHTON:— OD Monday even- 'ling a very well attended and influential- meeting of farmers )(residing in and adjoining the Fee of Makerfield) was held lat the Gerard Arms Hotel. The meeting- bad been convened by notice, and its object was to discuss the presentrdepres- ' i3ed'etate of agriculture.. One of the gentlemen present hay- ing been unanimously, called to the chair; the business of th'e meeting proceeded. The chairman, in a lengthy speech, detailed the difficulties-under which they laboured whilst titling and enriching our native soil, high rents, tithes, foreign competition, increase in labourere7"wages, bad sea- sons, and the present depressed condition, of agricultural produce. All these things the farming capitalist had to contend with and against, and whilst it was not for him (the chairman) to suggest what was to be done, hat, on the con- tr.o7, that it was for thent to decide on the matter, yet he thought the time had come when they should' seek redress for the wrongs they suffered, and endeavour to remo-Te those things which had hung so heavily upon their shoulders for many years,- viz., tithes- and high rents. It was the farmers- who made the land valuable by their labour; and yet, was it not a fact that while they tailed and suf.. fered, those who derived the chief benefit of their labours— the landowners—did not know how to spend their money fast enough ? He felt that they were fully justified in ask- lug for a reduction in their rents and the removal of tithes, and, in conclusion, urged those present to persevere in their object, pointing out that they had public opinion on their side, and if they only took upetheir cause as they ought to do as Englishmen they would be sure to succeed. (Ap- plause.) It was then resolved unanimously that a petition be got up and presented to the various landowners in the district—in which their case should be fairly and fully stated—and it was further resolved that a committee con, sisting of two farmers from each township represented by- that meeting should form the same. The townships in- cluded Ashton, Billing°, Has-dock, Golborne, Prewton, Bur- tonwood, Abram, and Lowtor.. It was next resolved that a fund should be established to defray the expenses-incurred in carrying out the objects of the meeting and a secretary and treasurer were afterwards appointed to assist the com- mittee in managing the same. Several other matters were also discussed, and at the close a vote of thanks was unani- mously given to the chairman for presiding; andthe meet- ing terminated shortly after ten o'clock.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

--- A young man named William McKinley, of Tolerotere Airdrie, died on Tuesday of injuries received whilst playing football on Saturday. The laying of the Meckay-Sennett cable, giving dine communication between Europe and New York, was sace easefully completed on Saturday. Orders are gazetttsd for the Courts going into mourning from the 22nd inst. teNoveraber 12th, for the late Duke el, Brunswick, second cousin to ides Majesty. The Dublin pelice are inquiring into the death of a. waiter named ICelly, who, it is alleged, received fatal injur- ies during a fracas in a fashionable hotel in the city. The funeral of the late Hon. Gilbert Leigh, M.P., whose body arrived at Steneleigh Abbey from America on Tues- day, took place on Wednesday morning in the parish church of Stoneleigh. The fund raised in Ireland to defray the costs of Mr. O'Brien, M.P., editor of UnitecTleelaad, in the recent actions for libel in connection with the Dublin scandal, amounts to close upon £5,000. At the Birmingham Quarter Sessions, on Wednesday, George Robert Lee, who was alleged to have committed frauds on the false pletence that he was the "Rev. G. R. Lee, LL.D was accruitted. At the Central Criminal Court, London, on Wednesday, Elizabeth Baker was charged with attempting to poison her mistress, Caroline Browning. at Catford, by placing sulphate of copper in the supper beer. The prisoner was found guilty, but recommended to mercy, and was sentenced to 15, months' hard labour. THE MURDER of A SOLDIER.—An inquest was held on Tuesday on Corporal Ashworth, found dead in Ringabella Bay,Cork. An open verdict was returned. Four men have been arrested, and the evidence slightly incriminates one, named Murphy. A witness heard Murphy say " 'Tis not the blue I want, but the red." STARVING a CHLLD.—A woman named Eleanor Liverno was charged at the Croydon Police Court, on Wednesday, with causing the death of herchild by starvation. The ' child weighed only 31b. at death. The prisoner was remanded to await the decision of the Treasury respecting the prosecution. Her husband believes her to have been insane. Two men have been arrested, in the neighbourhood of Queenstown on suspicion of causing the death of Samuel Ashworth, a corporal in the 2hd battalion of Lancashire Fusiliers stationed at Fort Camden. Ashworth, who was the son of a police-sergeant at Bolton, was murdered when on his way between Fort Camden and Queenstown on Sun- day last. A LITTLE GIRL SHOT BY HER BROTHEL—A little girl, named Ethel May Rhodes, daughter of John Rhodes, farmer, of Northowram, Halifax, on Monday went with her brother, ten years old, into their father's potato warehouse. Finding there a gun, the boy pointed it at his sister. The weapcn, which was loaded, went off, and. the pellets entered the child's head, causing her instantaneous death. THE PREMIER.—Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs., Mr. Henry, and Miss Mary Gladstone, left Chester on Tues- day for London. The Premier was loudly cheered, and as the train was departing a voice cried "No compromise.", Mr. Gladstone arrived in London on Tuesday afternoon. Shortly after be reached Downing-street Earl Spencer and Sir Charles Nike had a lengthy interview with the Prime Minister. WIFE MURDER.—At Willenhall on Monday, Thomas Hughes, locksmith, and landlord of the Crown Inn, was remanded on the charge of causing the death of his wife. The prisoner is a noted pigeon fancier, and, having lost £5 in a match, he returned home bad tempered. His wife, to escape his violence, ran up, the yard, and, falling down, broke her leg and ankle, her foot hanging by a piece of skin. The prisoner then struck her violent blows on the face and head with his boot. The woman died on Saturday last.

THE FIRE or; TME NF.VADA.—The fire aboard the Guion steamship Nevada was not, as was supposed, extinguished at Queenstown. The vessel came safely to Liverpool, but when unloading began it was found that the fire still burned In the main hold. The Liverpool and Bootle fire brigades were fetched, and after some hours of bard work the flames were finally quenched, not, however, until most of the cargo —cotton, hops, bacon, &c.,—had been destroyed by fire or water. The vessel will probably sail again to-day, being little damaged. THE RATING OF CREWE RAILWAY AND LOCOMOTIVE WORKS.—The appeal by the London and North-Western Railway against the assessment of the Crewe Railway and Locomotive Works was resumed at Crewe on Saturday, when Mr. Marshall, valuer. was examined as to the basis upon which he raised the rateable value from £52,945 to £23,ooo—Without callibg upon Mr. Webster to reply, the Court held that the whole of the property in the union ought to have been valued, and quashed the rate, with costs against the union. "SIR RoGme."—The claimant, after ten years and eight months' imprisonment, was set at liberty on Monday morn- ing. Thursday was the proper date, but it had been under- stood for several weeks that tbe liberation would take place earlier to prevent a "demonstration." The Claimant in- tends to try another" lecturing "tour' but its financial suc- cess is doubtful. It is said, too, that he intends to contest Chatham. Roger " Tichborne," the eldest son of the Claimant, who has for some time been employed as a clerk in an office in Manchester, went to London on Tuesday to Join his father. The young man gained his first intimation of the release of his father from the evening papers on Monday. SIR STAFFORD NORTMCGTE ON CRAMMING.—Sir Stafford Northcote, on Monday, attended a banquet at Kingsley. College, Westward Ho, and, addressing the boys, said that the great secret of their successfully carrying their life to such a result that they might feel they had done their duty to their God and their country was, in the highest sense of the term, to respect themselves from the beginning of their career. For that sort of cramming which put into boys' mouths a certain amount of knowledge which never got into their brains or bodies he had the greatest contempt, and thought very mischievous; but that kind of cram which en- abled them to bring out that which was in them, and at the proper time, was very valuable. Speaking of the study of history, they should get up and endeavour to realise the highest ideals, and even amongst themselves admire those companions who were noblest and purest in their senti- ments. FIVE PERSONS BURNED TO Dumf.—A fire occurred at Kirkby Stephen, Westmorland, early on Saturday morning, by which a family of five persons was burnt to death. A fire broke out in a chandler's shop belonging to a Mr. Faw- cett. The family (husband, wife, and three children), who met with their death, was named Varty, and occupied the cottage at the rear of the shop. It is supposed that Mr. Varty, having discovered that his dwelling was on fire, made an effort to escape, but perished in the attempt, as he was found dead with two of his children in his arms, and the mother with the third, their retreat having been cut off by the flames. Another man, who got into the chandler's shop, fell into a vat of grease, and was fearfully, if not fatally, scalded. The low situation of the shop and cottage accounts for the non-discovery of the fire. It was four o'clock in the morning before the discovery was made, and all the members of the family were then dead. At an in- quest held the same day, a verdict of "Accidentally suf- focated" was returned. Gun NAVY.—Sir E. T. Reed occupies four columns of Monday's Times with a review of the condition ef the Navy. Vessels each as the Dreadnought, built sixteen years ago, are, he maintains, still first-class men-of-war ; heavy ar- moured vessels are capable of resisting the fire of nineteen- twentieths cf the guns that may be brought against them, and are therefore indispensable ; there is a good supply of fast unarmoured or lightly armoured vessels ; and behind these a large available supply of ocean-going merchant steamers capable of easy conversion into vast cruisers, but the British Navy is none the less weak. To cope with the two strongest naval Powers in Europe England should have ten more of the largest class of war ships, and to meet a combination of the three strongest naval Powers, eighteen new vessels would be required. Sir Edward is not satisfied with existing war ships, but feels sure that " with less than half-a-dozen 20-knot armour-clads, each with a large coal supply, we might sweep the seas of everything that can at present assail our commerce," and he is " perfectly satis- fied that no other main defence for our mercantile marine would in the end be one-ball as effective or one-half as economical." FUNERAL OF MR. A. M. SuLmvate. The remains of the late Mr. A. M. Sullivan were on Monday interred at Glas- nevic Cemetery, Dublin, near the site of the O'Connell monument, in presence of many thousands of spectators. The procession that took part in the funeral was of very large dimensions. It was headed by a number of public bodies, the hearse was surrounded by the staff of the 2Vation, and after the relatives of the deceased came the Lord Mayor and Corporation of Dublin, and the members of the Irish Parliamentary party, except Mr. Parnell, who was com- pelled to remain in London owing to a severe cold. Many Protestants and Conservatives also took part in the pro- ceedings, and the route through the city was crowded with spectators. The coffin was carried from the hearse to the chapel and grave by Irish members of Parliament, of whom 18 were present. The grave, after the coffin had been pla- ced in it, was almost filled r with wreaths and flow.—

- ups. .0 flowers, in- discriminately thrown in. The crush was very severe. There was no speaking, and the crowd chspersed immedi- ately. The United Kingdom Alliance sent a deputation. A splendid site has been allotted for the grave near the O'Con- nell monument, the cost of it being about £2OO, but which was granted free of expense. Mn. GLADS'rro,^ DISEST/

div.p: PRESCOT.

A NEGL:GEIsTT HUSBAND.—Before Messrs. H. Gaokell and W. L. Evans, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, William McNamara was charged with leaving his wife and three children chargeable to the Prescot Union, on the 3rd September.—Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Guardians, pro- secuted.—The prisoner's wife and family were admitted to the Workhouse on the date named, and had since been main- tained at the cost of the Union. He was found in full work at a chemical works at Irvine, Scotland.—The Bench com- mitted him to prison for two months, PRESCOT Parry SESSIONS.—On Tuesday, before Messrs. H. Gaskell and W. L. Evans, John Atkinson, a lid, wee summoned for throwing stones in High-street, Prescot,.on the 19th inst. He was cautioned and ordered to pay the costs.—Another lad named N'Vln. Pimbley was summoned for breaking a 'window and doing damage to the amount of ls 9d, at the residence of Mrs. Smith, Prescot. The Bench ordered defendant's mother to pay the costs and the damage. —Thomas Mulloy, Philip Brady, Wm. Devaney, and John Gavin were summoned for playing at pitch and toss on Saturday afternoon in an entry off High-street, and, they were ordered to pay the cats. IMPUDENT THEFT OF CLOTHING —Patrick Macalynn, a labourer, was charged at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, with stealing a pair of trousers • and a vest, value 20e, from the dwelling-house of Thomas Oates, of Holmes Buildirgs, Eccleston. On the 6th August the prosecutor and his wife left home, leaving a girl named • McMahon in charge. During their absence the prisoner forcibly entered the house, notwithstanding the protests of the girl Mc- Mahon, went upstairs and deliberately stole the articles, which he pledged. He subsequently abscoaded and eluded the police authorities until a day or two ago.--He was committed to prison for two months with hard labour. OPENING GP, NEW SCHOOLS.—The opening of the New Schools in connection with the Zion Chapel, Kemble-street, Prescot, was commemorated with special services on Sunday and a public tee meeting on Monday evening. The preacher on Sunday afternoon was Mr. J.,F. Drinkwater, of Newshaw Park, Liverpool, and in the evening the preacher was Mr. William Sanderson, of Liverpool. There were large con- gregations, and the collections for the day realised nearly £l5. On Monday evening a tea meeting was held in the lower-room. About 400 persons -partook of the good things provided. A meeting was subsequently held under the presidency of Mr. William Tyrer. Addresses were given by the Chairman, Mr. Sanderson, Rev. J. Jahnson,, of Prescot, Mr. W. Brimelow, of Bolton, Mr, Eaeson, of Liverpool, and Mr. Drinkwater, of Liverpool ; and the ohoir of the chapel under the conductorship of Mr. W. Beesley rendered a selec- tion of music. Miss Quick efficiently presided at the har- monium. The proceedings concluded with the customary vote of thanke

SHOOKECG NEGLECT OF A CHILD •AT PRESCOT.— At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs Hol- brook Gaskell and W. L. Evans, Ann Range and her hus- band Thomas Range, were charged with wilfully neglecting to provide sufficient food and nourishment for their child. whereby its life was endangered. The prosecution was con- ducted by Superintendent Barker, and Mr. McKenzie, of Prescot, defended the male prisoner. From the evidence it appeared that on the 27th September the child was taken to Dr. Hall's surgery, in a very emaciated, dirty, and neglected state- It weighed rather less than silbs, though it was born on the 17th April last. It suffered greatly from *ant of food. The prisoners lived together for sometime after their marriage, but, the female prisoner took. to drinking heavily and sold the furniture in consequence of which her husband left her. She then went to the workhouse where she was confined; but she subsequently left the workhouse and again lived with her husband. The latter, however, again left her in consequence of her drunken habits. She fre- quently left the child alene in thehonee for hours at a time, and greatly neglected it until the 21th September, when a coloured woman named Chesworth, who entered the house in the absence of the mother, conveyed the child to the police station and afterwards to Dr. Hall's surgery. The Bench said it was one of the most painful cases they had ever had before them. It was a case of utter neglect on the part of the mother, and she must go to prison for six months with hard labour. The husband was discharged on enter- ing into his own recognisance to look better after the child in future.

C:LAIM AGAINST A WHISTON, COLLIERY PROPRIETOR,— Before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, Judge, and a special jury, at the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Thomas Pye, a sinker and contractor, residing at Huvton Quarry, brought an action to recover the sum of £24 51 from Messrs. C. N. Higgin and Company, colliery proprietors, Whiston, for breach of contract. The plaintiff was repre- sented by Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor. St. Helens, and Mr. Goldthorpe, barrister, instructed by Messrs. Atkinson, Denby, and Paterson, solicitors,. Manchester, appeared for the defendants.—Mr, Riley explained that the action arose out of the boring of a tunnel in the Halsnead mine, Whis- aon, owned by the defendants. The contract was entered into on the 12th June last, and the plaintiff was to be paid at. the rate of 363 per lineal yard. The tunnel was bored 23 yards, something less than half the distance, when on the 28th June the manager of the company infomned the plaintiff that the work would have to be stopped for a few days owing to the presence of water in a portion of the mine. The plaintiff. repeatedly saw the manager when he was to start again, but he received no definite instructions until the Ist September, when hs was informed that the work must be stopped, altogether.—The defence was that the contract was determined on the 28th June, when the plaintiff received notice to stop the work—the defendants having power to determine the agreement at any time they thought fit, by a. clause in the agreement. Several witnesses were examined on both sides. The jury ultimately returned a verdict in favour of the plaintiff, damages MO) and costs. , PRESCOT Smoot, BoanD.—The monthly meeting of the Prescot School Board was held on Monday evening, when Mr. W. L. Evans presided. There were also Dreamt Messrs. Goldsworth, H, Fogg, and H. Cross (clerk).—Mr. Baylis (school attendance officer) reported that since the last meet- ing 278 irregular scholars had been reported, and 17 parents had been ordered to appear before the Attendance Commit- tee. Twelve summonses had been issued, and a fine of 6d and costs was imposed in each case: He suggested that as the winter season was approaching, and the tiregrates of the schools were in bad condition, stoves should be tried. He thought stoves would be much better than fire grates.—Mr. Goldsworth thought a great saving was to be effected by the use of stoves, and there was an improvement in the heating of the room—After some discussion, Mr. Baylis was in-- grunted to furnish the Board with an estimate of the cost of stoves required, and also the cost of firing.—The Clerk, read a,communication fi.om the Education Department etat- ing that they had re-examined the plans of the Board school, and had decided that the accommodation of the boys' school should be for 196 scholars.—The Chairman re- marked that for the present month the average attendance of boys had been 206, and last month 205. He thought some of the boys would have to be turned away.—The Clerk said according to the Act they could turn boys away who did not live in the district if there was no room.—Mr. Fogg expressed the opinion that the Department were cur- tailing the accommodation now that the School Board was getting out of debt.—Some further discussion took place, it being decided that Mr. Green, the schoolmaster, should be instructed to turn away the worst boys and the most irregu- lar attenders who lived out of the district. The Clerk was also instructed to write to the Education Department com- plaining, of the injustice of their proceeding.

WELSH EDUCATION.—The new university college of North Wales was formally opened at Bangor on Saturday, amidst much popular enthusiasm. The inaugural address was delivered by Earl Pow,is, in the presence of a distin- guished company. A luncheon followed, at which about 500 gentlemen sat down, includir,g Mr. Mundella, M.P., Mr, Osborne Morgan, M.P., and Sir R. Cunliffe, M.P. A letter was read loom Mr. Gladstone, apologising for his inability to be preient,

EARLESTOWN At the Wigirxectuntv Police Cour: on Friday,. James Berry, Billinge,. wan summoned for carrying a gun without a license on the 25th September. The offence was commit- ted at Billinge.—Defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined 5s and costs. THE UNITED MIITNLION Amu-Welt,—A party of forty gentlemen left Eatiestown on Tuesday morning by, the seven o'clock train,. to take part in the gatherings at 'Ain- cheater in connection with the. anniversary of the United Kingdom Alliance. The party enjoyed the out, and arrived borne about I2o'clotk at night. Tuis EanrasTowft, CONSEIMTITE CLlli3.—Anotber interesting discussion took place in- the Barlestown Conser- vative Club, Earle-street, on Thursday evening, when there was a large attendance, and Mr. Sutton pre- sided. The subject of debate- was "The slacknes.l- - trade, and what is the canoe for it." Several members gave excellent 'addresses; and when the time for eloekig the meeting arrived it was urranimouely decided to adjourn the debate for a week. Tata Eantatsrowts 17ocrritemr, CDUL.—OIn Tuesday evening the members of the committee and the players in the first team were entertained to a capital supper at the Sunbeam Inn, Wargrav-J-- Moss, the headquarters of the club. About 30 persons eat down, and at the subsequent proceedings Mr. P. Hastie presided. The proceedings were enlivened with several songs and recitations. and hearty thanks were accorded to the host and hostess (Mr. and Mrs. R. Morris). A similar gathering was held in the same place on Thursday evening. A HAYSTACK ON FIRE' AT WINwIC'E.—On Wednesday at noon a stack of hay, estimuted to contain about a ton,.in the stackyard of Mr. E. C. Cooper, of 'the Swan Inn. Win- wick, was discovered to be on fire. Some men who were passing noticed smoke issuing from the stacks and they hn- mediately gave an alarm. Several buckets were procured, and water subsequently poured on the burning hay, with the result that the fire was soon extinguished. It is not known how the stack caught fire but fortunately the out- break 'was early discovered. -Tile -damage- woo not very serious.

BLun RIBBON Any MEETING. A public meeting nnper the auspices of the Earlestown Gospel Blue Ribbon Army was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Tuesday evening, when there was a good' attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. JoSeph Cordingly. After an ' appropriate address from the chairmana programme of songs, duets, &c., was gone through. Solos were nicely given by Mrs Walker, Miss Rhoda Maven Mr. J. Gee, and others ; and duets by Mrs Walker and 'Miss Jameson, and Miss Rhoda Massey and Miss Whiny; A very pleasant evening was spent.

ANNIVERSARY TEL MnExtrtGru--The anniversary tea meeting in connection with the Hope of Barlestown Lodge of Good Template was held in the lodge room, Bridge-street, On Saturday evening, when about sfl persons sat down to a capital tea. Brother George Clarke, D.M.,. presided over the subsequent proceedings, which were of an enjoyable character. Songs were rendered by Brother John McDonald, Sister M. Whiny, Brother W. Walker Mrs. K. Smith, Brother H. Warburton; a duet by Sisters El and J. Clarke; recitations by Brother R. Walton. liter Barnard, Brother George Warburton, Brother John. Clarke, Brother Charles Walton, Brother R. Walton, and*Brdtket John • Warburton ; and readings by Brothers John Warburton, a Barnard, and B. Newman. Brother Joseph Cordingley gave an excellent address, in which he pointed out. there'll effectoof the drink traffic,which he contrasted with the benefits of total absti- nence. On Monday evening the weekly session of the mem- bers was held under the presidency et Brother Allan Taylor, W.C.T. Three new members were-initiated: The programme "A night with the Poets," and an interesting selection of _poems was read.

lAN .EARL ESTONIAN'S F/SEETITO ANTRIMOISI NARROW EseAFl3.—On Sunday an Earlestown man had a narrow es- cape from being drowned at Chester. It seems that on the morning of the previous day, he and three )r four more "jolly anglers" left Earlestown to . spend the week end in their favourite avocation in the ri•rer Dee, at Chester. Well stocked with both grubs and "grub," the party duly arri- ved at their destination, and like fishers ef old, cast their " tines" throughout the night, but- when morning broke they were minus the fish they were so ansioue t) possess. One of the company then took up a new position at the water's edge, and was in the act of again throwing out his line when the ground upon which he was standing gave way. The result was that the individual inquestion fell headfore- most into the river, at a spot where the water was some 12 or 14 feet deep. His companions. seeing the dangerous pre- dicament in which he was floundering, immediately ran to his assistance, and being unable to "draw" out anything more pleasant or agreeable, they quickly "fished" out the unlucky member of their party. It is needless to add that there was not much " sport " after this unlooked•for inci- dent, and at least one " fisher " retuned home a wetter, if not a wiser man.

_ HARVEST FESTIVAL AT ST. .7CtITN'S auun,Cll —Special thanksgiving services for the ingathering of the harvest were held on Sunday in the church of St. John the Baptist, Earlestown. The church for a considerable time past has had an unenviable notoriety for the scenes that have occurred therein, but Sunday's services had a tendency to dispel easy thoughts of a dispute which any of the congre- gation might have had. There seemed to be unanimity of feeline among those present, but, there was lacking that heartiness and that warm enthusiasm in the services which have been manifested by the congregation en previous occa- sions. The interior of the churok.h.t irow wry trsatorf bedecked with plants, flowers, fruit, and corn, with a sprinkling of evergreens; and its attractive appearance re- flected credit upon the parties- who had had the task in hand. Ths communion table was relievei with plates of fruit and vases of flowers; while- the pulpit and reading desk were adorned with wheat,, flowers, and floial devices; the fo3t being decorated with ferns, flowers, &c. The windows were arched over with -evergreens, and the window ledges were filled with piles of vegetables and fruit. In the morning and evening the services were of an ordinary char- acter, the preacher being %honey. F. S. Barber,who also con- ducted a children's service in the afternoon. There were fairly large congregations, pepeoially at night, when about 25P persons were present. The collections for the day amounted to between £4 and 15.

Lamm cier " QUEER. Pisonz."—On Tuesday even- , ing Mr. A. Pitt, of Liverpool, lectured on " Queer People I I met with," at the Baptist Chapel, Earlestown, before a large audience. The lecture Wal largely composed of humorous anecdotes, lay which Mr. Pitt adroitly pointed his morals. Speaking of indiscriminahe -alms-giving and the imposition of beggars, he said that all. could find someone to whom, pr respecting whom, help might be given and thankfully, re- ceived, but indiscriminate charity was unnecessary and in- jurious, interfering with else exercise of proper beneficence. Passing on to speak more directly of religious matters, the lecturer offered sound advice to Sunday school teachers. He urged such to qualify themselves by education to fill their position properly,, and not to rely solely upon the spirit of God without themselves helping to conduce to their improvement and fitneae. He did not dispute .the power of the spirit of God,J3at that spirit would-work bettor, through an enlightened intelligence than an ignorant one. He condemned the systensof announcing special sermons and meetings on " clap-trap" subjects, instancing a case where .- a minister ins town, affected by a local strike, annorsuced that he would lecture on "Strikes." By this announce-. ment a large audience was. secured, but the lecturer never named the local strike aboat which they haddno doubt coma to hear, but exhorted them to strike working in the devil's- service. That audience was secured by false pretences,- a system calculated to do more harm than good in the long run. One clergyman announced that he would preach on. Peace, the marelerer,"and took as his text the words " Christ, our peace," which the lecturer ccnsidered horrible. Incongruous texts were also dealt with, and instanced in a humorous manner. In conclusion he urged his hearers to avoid hypocrisymnd double dealing, for, he said, one would rather have an honest devil than a dishonest, dissembling saint. The Rev. W. C. Taylor presided. The lecturer was frequently appl auded‘ ES.III.I3enOWN W73.37-11i1N MISCELLS.IIIIOCs CONCERT.—The assarably-room of the Viadact Institate, Earlestown, was nicely filled on Monday evening, he a miscellaneous concert was held under the auspices of the choir connected with the Brunswick Wesleyan Chapel, Cross-lane, Earlestown. The proceeds were in aid, of the fund for the purchase of an organ for the place of worship mentioned, and it was a succees in every respect. The pro- gramme-was a varied one, consisting of songs, duets, violin solos, and part songs by the che:e. The :atter was under the efficient, eonductorship of Mr. H. Grtun4e e and Miss E. L. Greenall accompanied at the pianoforte with, marked ability. The-programme opened with "The Belfry Tower" (J. L.,. Hatters), which received, a good interpretation from the choir. Mr. S. L. Swann next appeared, and was ap- plauded for hisrendering of "The Skipper." A. dnet, "The Sailor Sighs," ley Miss Swann-,and MA T. J. Gilmour, was well given. One of the attractions of the everilag was the appearance of Herr I. 0. Praeger, of Warrington, who has attained a high reputation hy his ability as an, instrument- alist andmorapeser ; and be was very warmly received. His violin solo " Grand Duo Concertante " (Setiot), was 1, executed in a brilliant manner ; and the audience, de. mending his recall, Herr Praeger bowed his acknowledge- ments. The next item was "The Xepnean's Wedding ,Song," hy Mr. P. Hartle. The style in which he rendered the selection brought forth enthusiastidapplause. An encore being demanded Mr. Hardie gave "-The Irish Emigrant." Miss Sydes nicely gave "Tell her I love her so," and Mr. T. J. Gilmour rendered "The Romany Lass," the efforts of both being duly appreciated. Here Praeger next gave another exhibition da his remarkable abilities. His render- ing of "Air Vane da Benot " was a masterly effort, and the piece was encored. The part song "All is Still" (Macfare ran), by the choir brought the first part of the programme to a close. After a short interval the choir effectively gave "The Bells of St Michael's Tower," and were succeeded by Miss C. Roberts, who sang Lowthian's " Gates of the West." It wasrendered with great effect, and on being re- called she gave "Once Again." In his interpretation of "Out on the Deep" Mr. S. L. Swans appeared to better ad- vantage than in his previous selection. The style in which he sung merited the recall he received; and as an acknowledg- ment he repeated the last verse. Miss Swann sang "Let. me Dream Again" to the satisfaction of the audiences and she too was rewarded with an encore. After Herr -Praeger had given another selection and bean recalled, Mr. P. Nov PAT Tim.—An honest John was asked by a friend," Has your sister got a son or a daughter ? " The answer was, "Upon my word I don't know whether I am an uncle or an aunt .' A young physician once asked Dr. Oliver Wendell Holmes for a suitable motto. "Small fevers gratefully received," was the witty response. Yo Ho !—An admiral of the Turkish fleet, sea-sick in a storm, was disturbed by a grating noise. He inquired whence it proceeded, and, on being told it was the rudder of the ship, he desired it might be immediately taken off! GISTrING HOME Lays.—" Why, titer I went in last night the house was so still you could base heard a pin drop." "Oh, yes, to be sure. I did hear it." "Hear what?" The pin drop. A rolling-pin, wasnt it?" A talented lady who advocates "woman's rights" was recently speaking upon the subject, and "brought down the house" with the following argument—" I have no vote; but my groom has, whose rent I pay. I have a great respect for that man in the stables; but I an sure, if I were to go to him and say, 'John, will you exercise the franchise ? he would reply, Please, mum, avbich'orse be that?'" A prisoner tried before a certain eminent judge for larceny had admitted his guilt when appreheaded, but at the trial was defended with great pertinacits by an able counsel. "Gentlemen," said the judge to the jay, • the prisoner says he is guilty. His counsel says he is nat. You must decide between them." Then, after a pause he added, "There is just one thing to remember, gentlemen The prisoner was there, and his counsel wasn't." WHY HE Din was a case d breach of promise. The evidence being "all in," the deferdant was allowed to say a word in his own behalf. "Yes,' he said, "I kissed her almost continually every evening leaned at her house." Counsel for the plaintiff, with satisfact on : "Then you con- fess it?" Defendant : "Yes, I confess it; but I had to do it." Lawyer, fiercely: "had to do it? What do you mean?" Defendant: "That was the oily way I could keep her from singing." Some funny things happened on the Yew York telephone lines occasionally. Several evenings ago a young fellow repaired to the store where he is emplcyed, after working- hours, and rang up the residence of his sweetheart. The connectioa was made, and the young bbod inquired, "Is that you, Miranda ?" "Yes, George, dew," came the reply. "Are you alone?" "Yes, darling." "I wish I was down there." "I wish so too." "If I were tiere, do you know what I would do with my darling ?" "No, George." "Well, I'd unbuckle the crupper and put some dirt in her mouth." "Oh, you brute !" cried Miranda; and now they never speak as they pass by. And the mar who was talking to a farrier about the best plan for etalaiug a. balky mare says that anybody who will advise a man to put his arm around the neck of an obstreperous horse, and hug and kiss it, and hold it on his lap, and whisper words of love in its ear, ought to be hung to the nearest lamp-post; while the telephone-girl, who mixed the conversation on purpose, smiles blandly on all the parties concerned. DIAIitOND CIIT DIAMOND.—A rustic-looking man sat in the smoking-car of the Omaha train, when another rural looking person came in. "Is this seat taken ?" asked the new-corner. "No; sir; sit right down, sit down," said the other, making room next to him. Soon the two old farmers were in conversation. "Where do yon hail from ?" "I live near Buda. Where are yon from ?" "I'm a pretty near neighbour of yours; I live near Kewanee." "Farming." "Yes. Are you?"" Yes—farming and stock." "Been to town with stock ?" " Yes ; I brought up a hundred head of steers." "I brought hogs." And so the conversation ran on until just before the train reached Mendota, and the two old farmers were well acquainted. Presently another man, who looked like a merchant, came in, and was surprised to see one of the old farmers. " Well, well, well," said the new man, "I'm glad to see you; may be you can help me out of a little embarrassing trouble. I want to pay a man a little bill on the train before I get off at Mendota, and I haven't money enough. If you will let me have one hundred dollars on my cheque, I'll be very much obliged." "Certainly—l'm glad to do it ;" and out came the farmer's pocket-book. But, alas, he had only forty dollars in small bills and a beautiful crisp five- hundred-dollar bill! "You're perfectly welcome to the forty dollars. if that'll help you out, or to the five-hundred- dollar bill, if you can get it broken." "Perhaps your friend can help us out; the forty dollars would hardly answer," said the merchant; and then he apologised for giving so much trouble. "Well," said the other farmer, softly, who, until now had been silently locking on, "I can't change a five-hendred-dollar bill; but Ican give you another one for it, and I think it came out of the same batch, and was printed on the same press." And then, turning to the other old farmer, he added, "If your partner hadn't come just as he did, mine would have beer here in a minute. I've been getting ready to work you on the same game ever since we left Chicago." At Mendota four very much disgusted con- fidence men stepped off the train and stood around in the cold, waiting for a train returning to Chicago.

A great meeting was held in the Free Trade Hall., Man- chester, on Thursday night, to celebrate the 50th anniver- sary of the abolition of slavery. Mr. H. M. Stanley was the chief speaker. Mrs. Smitherman, whose husband, a journeyman painter, was killed on the South-Eastern Railway in 1878, has been publicly presented with £750 at Maidstone, the amount hav- ing been subscribed for her. SHOCKING ASSAULT ON A LADY.—Mts. Coates, a Cheshire lady, has been brutally garrotted at Northenden, in that county. She was returning home, when some ruffian sud- denly seized her from behind, placed his band over her mouth to prevent her screaming, forced her on her back in the mud, and stole her satchel, which she states contained two purses, one with £l7 in gold, and the ether with LI in gold and t3s in silver. The Rev. W. T. Dale discovered Mrs. ' Coates after the occurrence lying in a most serious condition, suffering from shock to the system. DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT WELSHPOOL.—EXCITING SCENE. —Early on Saturday morning the Bradford Assam Tea Stores, Church-street, Welshpool, were discovered to be on fire. The manager, Mr. W. Blackband. was in the house, and an assistant, named William Samuels, courageously entered a window above the shop and managed to awaken Mr. Blackband, who was in an upper room. He remained there as long as the intense heat would allow him, and then got on to the window sill, from which perilous position he was rescued. He was completely surrounded by the flames which burst from a lower window. The poor fellow, who was seriously burnt, was conveyed to a chemist's, where be was attended to. The premises were completely gutted, and some £3OO or £5OO worth of stock was destroyed. The ad- joining premises met with a like fate. The cause of the fire is unknown.
