div.head: SLANDER OF MR. JOSEPH ARCH.
div.p: THE SLANDER OF MR. JOSEPH ARCH.

Sir,—Enclosed is a copy of a letter which I have received from Mr. Joseph Arch in reply to one which I addressed to him about ten days ago, which serves to illustrate the reckless manner in which men, such as he, who have striven for the elevation and amelioration of the condition of those amongst whom he laboured and dwelt, have had libels and calumnies covertly flung at them, which have absolutely no foundation in fact. Your readers will doubtless remember a letter published by you on October 11th from your occa- sional correspondent ("Clifford Dix "), in which he hu- mourously described the Tory demonstration (?) at Tatton Park, and a discussion which afterwards took place in a neighbouring" pub," wherein his opponent asserted " that the strikes of the agricultural labourers had enabled Joseph Arch to ride about the country with a pony and carriage." The assertion would be childish were it not for the Dase mo- tives which it insinuates, namely, that he has been actua- ted by a desire for his own personal aggrandisement rather than the benefit of his fellows. Having some personal know- ledge of the character and circumstances of Mr. Arch, I knew this to be a malicious falsehood, and determined to give him an opportunity of publicly refuting it. Accord- ingly, I wrote to him calling his attention to the statement, and he has availed himself of this opportunity in a manner which I think will satisfy your readers as to its veracity. Thanking you for its insertion, I remain,. vonrs,
RATHBONE. 7, Arpley-street, Warrington, Oct. 23, 1884. (Enclosure.) _ Bartord, Warwick, . 0ct...19,1884.

, Dear Sir —A r s a matter of courtesy to you, I eply to yours of the 14th inst. I may say the unmitigated lie that appeared in the paper you sent me has been refuted over and over again. The only conveyance I ever owned in my life is a wheelbarrow; and I never was the proprietor of a pony, nor even a donkey.—Faithfully yours._ __
'JOSEPH ARCH.
THE "STRIKE" AT THE PARISH CHURCH.

Sir,—As a member of the congregation of the above church, I must congratulate you for having placed before the people of Warrington such a true account of the above strike. I found last Sunday that our new organist had been unable to find any of our townsmen contemptible enough to take the places of the late choristers, although one or two simple-minded individuals had allowed them- selves to be "walked in" so as to "fill up a bit," and they no doubt were much pleased at being able to walk in church clad in " tattered," although white, surplices. Any way, they looked about as comfortable, and seemed about as much use, as the two who deserted their comrades and "went in" the Sunday previous. Now, Sir, I think it is a scandalous state of things when we are bound to have such a man as the Rector amongst us, under the guise of religion, who before he will treat his choir with common courtesy, after serving him well for such a number of years, is mean enough to throw them over and hate certain members of them as he does. "flow dwells the love of God in him?" we may well &alt. I think that the congregation should tell the Rector, and in no unmistakeable language, that they have had enough of his despotic acts; and the sooner his resignation becomes an accomplished fact, the better it will be for the parish and all in it.—Yours,
AN OLD CHURCHMAN.

Sir,—Tha poor Rector has got a bad name, and everyone seems desirous to make it worse. Really I don't know what we are coming to. If the rector of a parish cannot do as he likes with the parishioners who can ? Are we not de- livered over into his keeping ? Is he not held responsible for our soul's welfare? Then why should he sot be the beat judge as to the conduct of the Parish Church ? Time was when the choir would as soon have thought of flying as to have interfered with any arrangements the Rector might have made. It makes one sigh for those good old days when squire and rector, between them, took all responsi- bility off poor ignorant folks' shoulders. But things are altered ; you Radicals have come forward, and now one can see no advantage in being either rector or squire. Let them take things into their own hands in ever so small a degree, and down upon them comes swooping first "One of our staff," and then a whole host of minor lights in the shape of newspaper correspondents. The best thing that could happen to this country would be the passing of some measure prohibiting the circulation of newspapers of a Liberal tendency. Wuat we want is papers with gentlemen at the head, who will deal out to us such pabulum as will neither upset our stomachs nor Tat turn our heads, and then rectors will be able to do as they like with their own. Can anyone look around thin town of ours withoat feeling an inward satisfaction that all things are as well as they possibly could be ? It is well known that the Rector and his highly respected lady work almost beyond the power of human endurance. Their familiarity with the homes of the poor is beyond all praise. When the Rector left the east end of London to come amongst us poor be- nighted provincials, it was with a firm determination to carry out the good work he had there begun amongst the poor. And lam happy to say that the district immediately surrounding the Rectory is like East London, a very para- dise upon earth. The rich and the poor live in such happy fellowship with each other that squalor and misery have no abiding place amongst them. Allow me, in conclusion, to advise the choir to do as the Rector wishes them; a man of his superior judgment cannot err.—Yours, Src., ......

div.head: MA.WWOR!>I. THE MANAGEMENT_OF_THE NEW CONSERVA.
div.p: MA.WWOR!>I. THE MANAGEMENT_OF_THE NEW CONSERVA.
TIVE CLUB.

. Sir,—lt is now over three weeks since the Conservatives of this town advertised extensively for a man and wife to take the management of our new Temple of Conservatism in Sankey-street. In answer to those advertisements there were about 100 applications sent in for the office. Out of that number there were 20 which were sent from amongst our own party in Warrington. The committee (self-elected) who had this affair in hand either through extra exertion or excitement caused by the propects of having a sight of some of the leaders of our party in town, allowed the matter to remain in abeyance for three weeks, thus keeping in sus- pense the whole of the applicants. At last, awakening from their stupor, they decided to have a Cabinet Council in Imitation of our Imperial Parliament, having sent to various parts of the globe invitations to five couples to pat in an appearance. In answer to those invitations 41 "couples" accepted them, to parade before this enlightened committee. Having been shown into the saddling paddock, they were then put through their preliminary canter, much to the amusement of the spectators. When fairly in the race, four couples failed to clear the first fence. The last one to jump carrying a light weight, being thorough-bred, not being handicapped, and belonging to the Liverpool course, did better than the others, and was about being declared the winner of the political plate, when it was found out that be was a bachelo., and not entitled to the prize. Then com- menced the final scene in which " Billingsgate " was the predominating feature, language being hurled against two of our local magistrates which would disgrace any assembly and therefore not fit for repetition. Had it not been for the body frame of one of our local town councillors which was called into requisition, the scene would have ended much worse than it did.

Now, sir, what I protest against is tho have a per- fect stranger palmed upon us when we have men able and willing to undertake the duties, who are better qualified in every respect, and who are well known to us. It reflects very much upon the Conservative party here if it has sunk in- to such a strait as not to be able to find in a town of 40,000 Inhabitants one couple of good and honest people amongst them who can be trusted for honesty, cleanliness, and good cooking. If this is so, it is time for us to change our po- licy, and to ally ourselves to that party which we have hitherto opposed. They have set us a good eximple to elect one of their number to any office that may fall vacant in their club, and thus bestow the " loaves and fishes" to those who are entitled to them till confidence has been for- feited. The Conservative electors of Warrington protest against this injustice which is going to be inflicted upon us by the committee who have this in hand, and if we can- not have redress before the mischief is done let us record our protest when we enter the polling booth by putting our mark opposite the name of the Liberal candidate, and de- monstrate the fact that Conservatism in Warrington is no- thing more than a sham, snare, and a delusion. I would also ask the guardians of our rising generation if they think it wise to spend £6,000 on this modern gaming saloon, when that is enacted within its walls whice, if it were committed in the middle of Arpley fields, and the par- ties detected in the act, they would be brought before our local tribunal and sent to durance vile, and there treated as rogues and vagabonds. I feel sure that any parents would object to the payment of 21s per annum to educate their children in the pernicious habit of billiard and card playing, which has wrought so much mischief in days gone by, and which is the only education that can be acquired, except that of learning to have empty pockets. A CONSERVATIVE ELECTOR. Warrington, October 24, 1834.

Admiral Chaloner, C. 8., died on Monday, at the age of 70, at Longhill, Guisborough, Yorkshire. The gallant ad- miral, who retired from the navy 20 years ago, had since devoted himself to agriculture. Mr. Benjamin Riley was on Wednesday evening elected Mayor of Altrincham. This is an old unreformed Corpora- tion, the Mayor having the disposal of a fund of £3OO chiefly devoted to hospitalities incident to the position. At the London Central Criminal Court, en Thursday, Edward Smith, otherwise Rendell, was convicted of assault- ing a number of little girls. Mr. Justice Hay said he would make an example of the prisoner, whom he sentenced to penal servitude for life. The Judge complimented the police upon their conduct in the case. ALLEGED SHOCKING NEGLECT OF CHILDREN.—On Thurs- day, at the Old Bailey, Anne Wright (33) was indicted for the manslaughter of her child,ten months old, by starving it. It was alleged that she neglected all her five children, and that the result in one case was fatal. The prisoner was found guilty and sentenced to 18 months' hard labour. COMMERCE ON ma CONGO—Mr. H. M. Stanley was entertained at luncheon on Tuesday by the Manchester Chamber of Commerce, and afterwards delivered a lecture on the extension of civilisation and commerce on the Congo. Mr. Stanley saw no reason why the Congo trade with Manchester in cotton cloths should not amount to £20,000,000 annually. He urged that England's best policy would be to support the International African Association, and send a cruiser 0 the mouth of the Congo,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1884
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1884
Wetter,' to the editor.
THE CORPORATION AND THE SHIP CANAL.

Scr--f, I ;;;;;ts-help-Vondering sometimes whether those persons who are so eager that a twopenny rate should be levied in support of the Ship Canal, ever consider the startlingly serious nature of the new departure they are wishful to make. Hitherto the use of corporate funds has been strictly limited to the promoting of the health and con- venience of the community, each individual being left to conduct hi 3 private affairs and business as he thought beat. It is now proposed to over-step this limit, and it would be well to look forward a little to see where the new path may possibly lead. These gentlemen who are so eager that the rate should be laid for the intended purpose, would no doubt feel shocked if they were described as having social- istic tendencies. Yet can it be denied that what they pro- pose is a distinct step in the direction of that state of socialism or communism in which every business, both pub- lic and private, is to be done by the community for the corn- inanity—which, by the way, is one of the most unnatural and mischievous of the multitude of schemes of "reform " propounded by soi-disant reformers. In the present in- stance, it is true the community is to take part in a private enterprise, not directly but by deputy, the deputy being the Ship Canal Company. Bat the distinction is without a difference ; or, at all events, not more than there is between the Corporation doing its scavenging by contract and by its own workmen. So that if this rate is levied we shall have irrevocably adopted the socialistic principle of the community conduct- ing the private affairs of its members. It is not difficult to see to what lengths this principle might lead. The argu- ments which are used for promoting the Ship Canal by pecuniary assistance, because it will be of benefit to War- rington, will apply with equal cogency to the promotion or fostering of some local industry, or even to the Corporation erecting and maintaining workshops of its own. That it will be carried to this length is, of course, another thing ; but the thin end of the wedge once inserted we all know how apt it is to be driven further and further.—l am, sir,

Sir,—l cannot exactly understand why the ratepayers were called together to approve of the Mayor's resolution at the meeting last night, as our Council has not yet agreed to levy the rate of 2d in the L—and I should have thought the Mayor should have been first authorised by the action of the Council before asking the ratepayers to approve of the rate. It seems a queer proceeding, and rather one to interfere with the jud4ment of independent members of our Corporation. It makes it appear impossible that the Cor- poration can now refuse—but as a large ratepayer I sincere- ly hope that there are men in the Council who will ignore the proceedings of the meeting of last night, and will not allow us to be forced into paying a rate to push on an un- dertaking which is of a purely speculative character. I think if actual ratepayers were called together, the majority would not sanction such a'n imposed tax—they are heavily burdened enough already with local taxes—and it seems naonstrotts to take the vote of tenants who will only be affected if their rents are raised, which is not likely to be done, looking to the fact that many of them find it hard work enough to pay their present rent. No doubt it would be a good thing for this town if large moneys were to be expended in our neighbourhood, and for this reason I hope that the canal may be made—better pleased though should I have been if the canal had run thro,:gh ourlborough instead of just cutting outside it; but is it net surprising that this grand undertaking, which is to benefit Manchester so much cannot be done by Manchester man? Where are the wealthy men of Manchester? If the scheme is to be such a grand benefit as it is painted by the promoters, surely one hundred gentlemen interested in the welfare of Manchester could be found to subscribe say £5OO each, and so avoid sending round the bat in this miserable begging fashion. The promoters should send "The Doctor" out to Tenessee to make a collection. lam in want of funds for a grand undertaking, within the town, which would give immediate employment to workpeople, and may turn out a grand thing or may be an utter failure. Will the Corporation grant me a sum of money to mate a start ?—Yours, HEAVY-TAXED COTTAGE OWNER.

Sir,—The gentlemen who from the platform of the Pub- lic Uall last night advocated the levying of a rate in aid of the Ship Canal scheme, are such large and influential rate- payers as compared with the firms who memorialized the Mayor against that proposal, that it may interest your readers to know what the assessments of the respective par- ties are.

Taking the net annual value I find the total asqessment for the borough to be (Warrington and Latchford) £141,832. Ten of the firms opposed to the proposed rate are together assessed on £14,083, or ten per cent of the whole borough assessment, and four of them on £10,941. On the other hand the four gentlemen who spoke in favour of the propo- sal last night, are together assessed on £397, and the amount they would together contribute, should the rate be enforced, would represent £3 632 d. The following are the details : Assessment. Net annual value. Bate at 2d in 2. The Mayor lB3 10 0 ... 1 10 7 Alderman Burgess— 100 10 0 ... 0 18 9 Alexander Markle...-. 94 0 0 ... 0 15 8 George Woods

Total 897 0 0 ... 3 a 2 from these figures it will be seen that while the four chief advocates of the rate will have only together £3 6s 2d to provide, four of the opponents of the rate will have no less than £9l 3s 6d to contribute. Dr. Mackie says he has paid over £l,OOO in promotion of the scheme; also, that it cannot go on unless Warrington provides by a rate £1,200. If it will provide £1,200 he will only have 15s. Bd. of it to pay ; and there Is a possibility that his £l,OOO may be pulled out of the fire by keeping the scheme afloat long enough for the profits on the Ship Canal advertisements to cover this sum. M. George Woods's 3s. 2d. is not much to lose even if the scheme fails. If it should be carried out, why he may , be able to find a credit to cover this heavy debit of 3s. 2d.

Sir. the proposed rate is opposed on principle, and when principles are at stake there can be no compromise. The opponents to the rate, I hope, mean war to the knife, and the knife to the hilt.—Yours, October 23.
LIBRA.

Sir,—There are one or two points in connection with last 'Thursday night's meeting which in my opinion are worthy of further consideration. First of all it was a "Town's meeting," at which any and every ratepayer had an equal right to express his view. The meeting was called for the purpose of sanctioning or refusing the laying of a rate of 2d in the £, for the purpose of promoting the Ship Canal Scheme. Two of the speakers, at any rate, Mr. George Woods and Dr. Mackie, entirely slipped over the main ques- tion, and simply, in a rambling and somewhat incoherent way, repeated the old stale arguments in favour of the seller:A.. Nobody for a moment now doubts the desirability of the scheme, and very few indeed doubt its feasibility ; but that the rates of a borough shall be applied for the purp.)se of furthering a "private speculation" is a very different question. As the Mayor rose for the purpose of announcing that be was about to " put " the resolution in favour of the "rate," Mr. Thomas Morris rose from the front row of seats is the body of the hall, evidently for the purpose of opposing the resolution, but His Worship, who either didn't or wouldn't see him, at onee (and, in my opinion, hastily) took the vote, which, of course, as was expected, was largely in favour of the resolution. Mr. Morris then gave notice of his intention to demand a poll, and was about to give his reasons for so doing, hut was practically refused a " hearing " by His Wor- ship: and this is what I protest against. Well now, sir, although the reselntion was passed,and may be confirmed by the Town Council, I am strongly of opinion that it will be an illegal as well as an unwise act to apply the borough funds for the purpose indicated Looked at it in its legal aspect. the Ship Canal scheme is I neither more nor less than a" private undertaking." Under no circumstances can it be held to be one of those measures to assist in the promotion of which the " Borough Funds Act " was passed. It is quite true that Warrington, as well as the whole of the district through which it will pass, will materially benefit in consequence, but in the same manner, although boa less degree, do we benefit by the erection of every works which is built within our area, but who would for one moment suggest that the rates of the town should be expended, even to the most paltry extent, in assisting private firms to build new works, or to extend their present ones? Yet this is precisely what the reselution of last Thursday night proposes. Again, although the rate may be laid,! do not think that payment of it can be enforced, and it remains to be seen whether those upon whom the inflic- tion will fall most heavily will allow themselves to be coerced into a payment the legality of which is so question- able. Further, the promoters of any undertaking (not being a Limited Company) are morally, if not legally, responsible for the carrying out of their proposals, and Ills a very de- bateable point as to whether by subscribing to the funds for the procuring of the Ship Canal Bill the Cerporation of Warrington may not become responsible for a proportionate am^,unt of the capital required for the completion of the scheme afterwards. If this should turn out to be the case, and it is by no means improbalsle, I think the most enthu- siastic admirer of the scheme would pause before commit- ting us to so stupendous a liability. At any rate we should make ourselves as safe as possible b-, following the ex- ample of the Manchester Corporation, and before we part with our money we should obtain from the Provisional Committee of the Ship Canal a guarantee which will in- demnify us against any liability whatever beyond the pay. men' of the levy referred to. In conclusion let me advise th 3 ratepayers of Warrington to LOOK BEFORE YOU LEAP.

CUURCH ATTENDANCE AT RUNCORN. Sir,—l see by our worthy vicar (Canon Barclay's) pas- toral letter that he csmplains of the falling off in the con- gregation of this church. I venture to predict had he been able to attend the church during the last few months he would very easily have discovered the cause. I attend the church fairly regular, and must really confess that I have not heard a sermon worth listening to for several months, but my object in calling attention to the sermons at this church is to induce our vicar to impress upon his curates the necessity of preaching better sermons and more extem- pore. I am sure on Sunday morning last we had a sermon from the Rev. J. S. Madden which I consider was anything but agreeable for one to be obliged to sit and listen to, as he not only read every word, but did that very imperfectly. I sincerely trust that our good vicar will not attempt to put ' such a preacher in the pulpit again (at the Parish Church
at least) far a very long time to come, as I am convinced this is the real cause of the falling off in the congregation of which he complains.—l remain, sir, faithfully yours, A CHURCHMAN.

WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.—PUBLIC MEETING. On Thursday evening a largely-attended public meeting was held at the Public Hall, Warrington, having been called by the Mayor in response to a requisition. Before the meet, ing commenced Mr. William Diggle, who is strongly °nosed to the scheme, took a front seat on the platform, and a run- ning fire of chaff ensued. Mr. Diggle's power of repartee being considerable, the audience was well entertained until the arrival of the speakers. The Mayor (Alderman Harri- son) who presided, was cheered on taking his seat. He was supported by Mr. Leader Williams (engineer for the pro- moters of the scheme), Alderman Burgess, Councillors Dixon, Caldwell, Mackie, and Pierpoint, Dr. Gornall, and Messrs. J. Lawrence, Woods, T. Robinson, S. Barlow, Hall, Guest, liepherd, H. Whitham, Jeans, S. Davies, Adams, W. Roberts, S. Kenyon, N. B. Percival, E. Bolton, J. W. Harvey, and F. E. Connell. The Catamaran' said that he thought he hardly need go through the preliminary of informing them why they were met together that night. He thought they knew that pretty well, for he should think that perhaps there was nothing that had created more excitement amongst them since the Tichborne case—he thought that the Manchester Ship Canal scheme had been discussed as much and had created as much controversy. Therefore he thought he might fairly assume that they knew as much of the scheme as he himself did, and he scarcely needed to introduce the subject or in- form them what was the question that had called them to- gather that night. Having read the notice convening the meeting, the Mayor proceeded to say that in plain lan- guage it meant that they were asked to sanction the Cor- poration contributing 2d in the pound on the rateable value to go ie aid of the promotion of the canal scheme, for the period of one year. Having read the result of the requisi- tion that had been got up, it was hie duty in common fair- ness to read a requisition of a very contrary character which he that morning received. It was signed by some of the most influential firms and manufacturers In Warrington. They were entitled to be heard, and it was his duty to read the requisition and She names attached to it. It was as follows : We, the undersigned, being large ratepayers, respectfully urge upon the Mayor and Corporation the impolicy of at- tempting to levy a rate for the purpose of paying the Par- liamentary expenses of the Ship Canal. We consider such a precedent would be a most objectionable one, and that the borough has no funds to spare from its own proper work. The rates at present are high, trade in every department is bad, and the ratepayers are not in a position to take upon tnemselves any burden which by law they are not compel- led to bear.—ltylands Brothers, Limited, The Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited, Joseph Croe- field and Sons, The Whitecross Wire and Iron Company, Limited, Peter Stubs. Peter Walker and Sons, Robinson, Son, and Skinner, James Fairclough and Sons, Winner and Com- pany. F. Monks, John and James Tinsley Thewlis and Grif- fith, Thomas Jolley, W. Pierpoint, Samuel Horton!' There were the Chairman continued, evidently two sides to the question; some took one and some another. He did not thinkthat it was his province that night to say much upon the matter ; his duties were purely of a ministerial character. The question had not yet come before the Council, and con- sequently it might be objectionable to say very much about It. It was laid down in the Borough Funds Acts that the Council should deal with an appropriation of money and then appeal to the ratepayers for confirmation or otherwise, but at the same time there was no impropriety or illegality , in coming to the ratepayers first. He thought the ratepayers I would put a proper interpretation upon it—that it was more respectful to them that they should be first consulted I with reference to this propoul expenditure. (Cheers.) If the meeting chose to sanction the expenditure the Council I would feel more confidence in what they themselves after- I wards did after hearing such an expressioe of opinion. (Ap- plause.) When the cue came before the Council some time ago, it collapsed and carne to a deadlock. On that occasion they were asked to contribute towards the promotion of the bill, and they considered it would be right to do so, but the l Town Clerk had some doubts about it. In consequence, ' counsel's opinion was taken, which was to the effect that public funds could not be contributed for the purpose of I promoting the bill, but they had a right if they chose to pro. ' mote a bill themselves or to help to promote it. Therefore they came now before the public as promoters of the bill. (Mr. Diggle : Oh !) Having introduced the matter, it was his duty to propose the resolution. (Applause.) It was a I curious thing that the law obliged him to do it whether he agreed with it or not; but it did so happen, if they would allow him to express an opinion, that he thought that if the Ship Canal was made it would be an immense boon to Warrington. (Loud and continued cheering.) He was not wishful of prejudicing the case one way or the other; he desired to stand there in a sense neutral, but he could not help expressing the belief that the canal would be a boon, because in the first place the construction it would take, and other works in and about Warrington, would involve the expenditure of something like 2,000,000 of money. (Applause.) In additien, it would give another waterway and would enable manufacturers to send their goods for a small tonnage of 4d per ton. He then proposed : "That this meeting consents to the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burges- ses of the borough of Warrington promoting in conjunc- tion with others a local and personal bill in Parliament for the purpose of incorporating a company, and empowering such company to construct a canal from the river Mersey to the city of Manchester, navigable for large steamers and ships of large burthen, and the contribution upon the borough rate te the cost of such promotion of a eons not exceeding 21 in the £ upon the annual rateable value of the borough, for one year." (Cheers.) He would call upon Alderman Burgess to second the resolution, although a seconder was not absolutely required. Alderman Burgess rose to address the meeting, and Mr. Diggle rising at the same time uproar ensued. There were cries from the audience of "Turn him out," "Sit down, Diggle," "Give him a drink of water," and "Ay, diddle, diddle."

The CHAIRMAN : For fear anybody should suppose that any injustice is being done to Mr. Diggle, or that the least restraint will be put upon him from speaking legitimately and properly, I wish to tell you that before we can go fur- ther, or before we can hear him at all, we must hear Mr. Burgess, and then it is quite competent for Mr. Diggle, if he chooses, to take his own course. (Applause.) Alderman BURGESS, after a few prefaratory remarks, said that was the third time that the Ship Canal scheme had been brought prominently before the country, twice in Par- liament, and now a third time befom the constituencies out- side Parliament, previous to its going there again. In his judgment, no great scheme for the well-being of the country at large ever received such scurvy treatment as the Ship Canal had done. He thought there was something degrad- ing in the fact that in the committee rooms of two houses of Parliament opportunities should exist of preventing such a great measure being settled with the speed that it was entitled to. He trusted, however, that when the bill again came forward it might be found that the time had not been wasted, and that the further opportunities afforded Mr. Williams. the engineer, would have enabled him to prepare a scheme that would not only satisfy the opponents, but be more satisfactory to the promoters themselves. He had seen the outline of the scheme now advocated, and so far as Warrington was concerned it possessed all the advantages that the former scheme possessed, and the privileges that were conceded to Warrington were being again conceded. There had been nothing, in his opinion, In the history of Warrington, that had at all approached this question in its consequence to the borough. If the bill were lost it would indeed be a blow to the pro- gress of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) When they had a dockage of over 20 acres, giving access to the canal at all parts by day and night, at a tonnage of 4d a ton, he thotaght it would be a concession and a boon to Warrington to which they had no right, but having had it offered they must make sure of it. (Cheers.) He was sorry a counter memorial had been prepared, and thought those gentlemen who had signed It should have attended the meeting to advocate their views, for, he asked, if they believed that they were in the right, would they not have been there in support of their own cause ? No one better knew the advantages that would accrue to Warrington by the scheme than did those gentlemen them- selves. But there were such things as interests in this world. There were sometimes railway interests. Might not the larger manufacturers have made arrangements by which their larger freights might be removed out of War- rington, and the lesser men have to pay for them? It was in railway phraseology called special rates and terms, and,if these gentlemen had secured special terms with the railway companies they were not to be blamed, but be thought they might have been quiet with the advantages they bad got. He appealed to them to act for their own interests and pass the resolution unanimously. (Applause.) Mr. DIGGLE rose to oppose the resolution, and was greeted with groans and cat-calla. The Mayor was, he said, in error in stating that they should have another waterway to Liverpool. One great objection to the scheme was that the present waterway from Latchford to Runcorn would be destroyed,and that dairng the making of a canal the source would be dried up. (0 No," and laughter.) (Cries of " Will you have a humbug, William," and " Sit down.") The MAYOR : Gentlemen, I ask you to be so good, in order to save time, as to allow Mr. Diggle to proceed. (Cheers.) Mr. DIGGLE : It is a most important matter. What are we to do during the construction of the canal ? The cheapest and most convenient waterway to Liverpool (inter- ruption and cries of " Nonsense," "How do you know.") I'll go on when the Mayor gets order. (A Voice : "Spell o x ox, Diggle," and laughter.) Here is our friend Alderman Burgess—(laughter)—l have beard his twaddle before on this subject. (Renewed laughter.) Alderman Burgess says we have great works in Warrrington which have made arrangements with the railway companies to carry cheaper for them than before. How do you know? (Laughter). / think he knows nowt about it. I conslier Mr. Burgess un- justified in making these statements unless he can verify them to be true. I want to give you some information fallout the canal. (Interruption.) I'll have my say. Get- ting on depends on you, not me. (A Voice: "Now, William, you are only banging on the bridge.") I want to give you information. (Voices : " Go and have some supper, Wil- liam, and come to-morrow night," " Let him have a drink.") The CHAIRMAN : Is it your desire to hear Mr. Diggle. (Groans and cries of" No.") Mr. DiGGLE : I have had to do with ragamuffins before. I'm a ratepayer, and I'll have my i say. (" Pat him out.") Who dare put me out, Pm a ratepayer. The sooner you hold your noise the sooner I shall have done. Ihe CHAIRMAX then called upon Mr. Woods, and Mr.
Diggle, amidst cries of "Fetch a bobbi," and Chuck him out," protested against being denied a hearing*. Quietness having been obtained,

Mr. %Stoup, apported the resolution in an atiq speech, giving numerous instances of how manufactured cods and provisions were brought to England at much cheaper cost of transit than the same could be carried from Londcn into Lancashire, or vice versa.

Councillor MacalE, called upon by the MAyor, rme to speak. Mr. Diggle also rose, protesting against the Mayor calling upon anybody. They bad, he said, bad plenty of twaddle before. Be refused to take a seat until he was pulled on to his chalr.

Councillor MACKIE said that Mr. Diggle had had minutes in which to speak, and if all claimed an equal time they would not be done until Christmas. He appealed to Mr. Diggle's good sense—(a voice: "Be has uone")—and , hoped that his friend Dixon would preside if Mr. niggle called a special meeting. (Laughter.) Mr. Mackie then proceeded to speak of a placard against the scheme issued by Mr. Bleakly, who, be said, was once in favour of it, and subscribed the sum of .f.. 50 and then "backed out" of it by paying £l2 104. Following that gentleman's example, be had himself paid £l,ooon hard cash, so that he was in interested person, but at the same time a man who had given hostages to that extent to his town and the district in which he lived was not likely to turn tail at the first appearance of defeat or opposition. (Cheers.) If the gentleman wbo wrote that placard (which complained that the promoters bad not pub- lished a debtor and creditor account of the money received by them) would go to the office of the Ship Canal Com- pany and pay the remainder of his subscription—(applause) —he (the speaker) could pledge his word that he could take a clerk and copy every penny that had been entered on the books. In the promoters of the canal they were dealing with honest gentlemen, who were able and willing to give an account of how the money was spent. (Applause.) He urged them to pass the resolution, and in conclusion said , he thought that Mr. Diggle was looking for a sort of local immortality. (Mr. Diggle: "That's all twaddle.") The Cmainaus, referring to tbe counter memorial, said that one gentleman whose name was attached to it—Mr. Peter Stubs—a gentleman who was above suspicion would have been present, had not a family affliction called him out of town. He than put the resolution, which was carried almost unanimously, and with great applause. Mr. Thomas MORRIS demanded a poll, and the Mayor asked him to withdraw the demand in view of the expense it would incur, and the almost unanimous expression of the opinion of the meeting.—Mr. Morris, in reply said that all would like to have a ship canal, but asked was it right for the corporation to levy a rate upon the pockets of those who could not afford. If they decided that the principle was right, he had no more to say. (Interruption.) Mr. Dixon proposed, Mr. T. Hall seconded, and Messrs. Woods. N. B. Percival, and J. Dodds supported a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding, the latter remarking that the Mayor's conduct in the chair had been a credit to him, but unfortunately he did not see that be- fore he put the resolution Mr. Morris was on his feet to ad- dress the meeting. If Mr. Morris had been allowed to speak he was sure there were hundreds i& the room who would I have voted against the resolution. (Cries of " No" and hisses). Mr. W. STIRRUP also supported the resolution. He re- lated how last year he was at a dinner at Glasgow when the conversation turned upon the canal, ht which the City of Rome was right up to Glasgow, and it was narrated how one of the severest opponents to that scheme was a lady of the name of Betty Wiggles. (Laughter.). He was also told that she and the family had left the district, and there was only one member left, who had, it was believed, changed his name te Diggle. (Renewed laughter.) He was proud of strangers who came to Warrington, but thought that people should send their beet men. He was really ashamed that Warring- ton should be annoyed by that family that had been driven from the Clyde and he hoped that was the last they should hear of him. (Roars of laughter). Alderman Bananas, in putting the resolution, which was unanimously passed, said he thought it was a mistake on the part of one who had spoken to assert that hundreds would have voted against the resolution, when at the time it was Out that gentleman was sitting with his back to the chair- man.—The Mayor having briefly responded to the vote of thanks, the meeting terminated, and Mr. Diggle was after- wards escorted to his home under the protection of the police.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT- OPENING or THE AUTUMN SESSION. THE QUEEN'S MECH. The Autumn Session of Parliament was opened by com- mission on Thursday afternoon. Tin Queen's Speech, of which the following is the text, was read in the House of Lords,.by the Lord Chance.lor

MT LORDS AND GENTLEMEN, I have brought you together after a recess, unusually short, in order that you may be enablei at once to give your further consideration to the great subject of the Representa- tion of the People in Parliament. I conVinue to maintain relations esl amity with all Yoreign Powera

The information received from the Soudan Includes pain-, ful uncertainties, but the energy,courege, and resource con- spicuously displayed by General Gor.lon in the successful defence of Khartoum deserve my warm recognition. The advance of my troops to Dongola has for its object the rescue and security of that gallant officer, and of those who have so faithfully co-operated with him. In Egypt itself I am using my best endeavours t) promote further improve- ment, and I have given my support to the Egyptian Govern- merit in the-difficult financial position in wbich it has been left through the failure of the recent Conference. I have to regret that circumstances have occurred on the South-West frontier of the Transvaal which demand, my vigilant attention. In conjunction with the Government of the Cape Colosy, I have been engaged in considering the means which may be required to secure the faithful observance of the Conven- tion of the present year. Papers on this sab:ect will be presented to you atkatt early date. GENTLEMEN OF- THE HOUSE OF COMMONS, The operations in the Soudan will render it nesessary to ask from you a further pecuniary provision. MY LORDS ANYPGIMITLEMIEN, The Bill for the exteosion of the Parliamentary Pranchise will at once be introduced.
In conclusion, I humbly and most anxiously trust that the blessing of Almighty God may attend upon your labours.

In the Lords the Address, in reply to the Queen's Speech was moved by Lord Belper, seconded by Lord Lawrence, and was agreed to after a debate, in which the Marquis of Salisbury, Earl Granvillerand the Earl of Derby were the principal speakers. Their lordships then adjourneti till the 3rd of November.

, HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TRIIRSDAY. New writs were ordered to issue for Radnor and Stirling. —On the motion of Mr. Courtenay for the adoption of the usual sessional order to prevent the obstruction to the pas- sage of members to the House, Mr. Chaplin renewed h'dis attack on the Home Secretary in reference to the great Liberal procession which passed Parliament during the last session. The Home Secretary replied, and Sir Stafford Northcote having made a brief speech on the subject, the motion was agreed to. Between 70 anal 80 notices of motion, or notices of the introduction of bills) were given.—The Ad- dress in reply to the Speech from the Throne was moved by Mr. E. S. HOWARD, seconded by Mr. W. StrENERS.—A pro- longed debate followed, in which the Premier and Sir Staf- ford Northcote took part.—The debate was eventually adjourned.—ln the early part of the sitting Mr. GLAD- STONE gave notice that on Monday he will introduce the Franchise Bill. HOUSE OF 'COMMONS:—.S,--- The House met at four o'clock,

div.head: MANCHESTER CITY COUNCIL AND THE SEIIP CANAL,
div.p: MANCHESTER CITY COUNCIL AND THE SEIIP CANAL,

A meeting of the General Purposes Committee of the Manchester City Council was held on Thursday morning in the Town Hall, the Mayor (Mr. P. Goldschrnidt) presiding. The proceedings of the Parliamentary Sub-committee with reference to the Ship Canal were proposed by the Mayor for confirmation.—Mr. Alderman Grandy said he should feel it his duty at the proper time to oppose the resolution with reference to the rate proposed to be levied as a contribution from the Corporation towards the cist of obtaining parlia- mentary powers to construe the ship canal. The resolution would formally come before the Council on Wednesday next, and lest there should be any misunderstanding, he gave notice of his intention to oppose it.—Mr. Alderman King and Alderman Keywood safl they would do the same.— Several councillors having expressed opinion in favour of the proposal, the Mayor said he was as auxieue as any man in the Council, or as any man in Manchester, that a poll should be taken, and he did everything possible to get one, but they were advised by their legal adviser and fortified by Counsel's opinion, that it would be illegal to hold a poll. He could not, therefore, in justice Order one to be Liken. There was another thing which bethought had been hardly considered as it should have been, he meant the 21 rate. It could not be denied that the great majority 0 the Council and the great majority of the people of Manchester were in favour of the canal. (Hear, hear.) When the promoters of the canal came before the sub-committee they declared positively that unless the Council assisted them not only morally but with an amount equal to 211 in the pound on the rating they would abandon the project and not go for the bill at all. Knowing that he felt that he had no alternative but to support the bill in every possible way.—The resolu- tion was carried.

div.head: NEW TITEADIE ROYAL,
div.p: NEW TITEADIE ROYAL,
WARRINGTON.

The new theatre for Warrington, which, as we have pre- vious stated in these columns, is being erected by Mr. Bring- ley Sheridan, of the old time honoured Prince of Wales Theatre, is now rapidly approaching completion, and will, we believe, be ready for °prang at an early date in Novem- ber. Originally Mr. Sheridan intended to build a less pre- tentious structure on the old site, but having once put his hand to the plough he was loth to turn back, and he has gone on extending and improving on the original model until in the end we shall have a most commodious,. and what pron:iiees to prove a very handsome theatre.

The following is an architectural description of the building :—lt is built in a free Italian style. The ground storey,. including the piers, cornices, strings, and. other or- namental features, is wrought in a composition of cement, the contrast with the upper portion of the- building, which is in the best red pressed brick facing, being very pleasing. The entrance doors, of which there are three (boxes, pit, and stags), all open to the front with the spacious corridor and stone staircase to each. The chief entrance in the centre of tke building is intended to be covered with.light orna- mental iron and glass roof about the width of the footpath. The doors are hung so as to elide into cavities in the walls, and are easily opened. The means of exit have been well considered, extra doors, etc., having been provided in case of fire. There is a well-arranged refreshment bar, and abun- dance of lavatory accommodation. The auditorium, when further extended and completed, will be of the regular horse- shoe pattern, with a good view of the stage from any part of the house. The balcony (or upper homes) is supported by ornamental iron columns. The ceiling is formed in panels, with heavy mouldings, which admit of decorative treatment.

The stage is a fairly large one with a gentle slope towards the orcbestva, and is planned with good entrances, suitable dressing rooms, stock and property rooms, and other accom- modation. The stage and its appliances, upholstering, and seating, are being executed by Mr. Thomas Cavanagh, of Manchester, the well-known theatrical upholsterer and de- corator, the seats being similar to those in 11843 at the Lyceum, London, and other theatres,, and, hoown as his " registved chairs." The total cost of the structure will be about £3,000, and has beer . carried out from plans and under the superinten- dence of Messrs. Pierpoint and Adams, architects, Warring- ton. to whom great praise is due for the skilful planning and construction which have resulted in the erection of a convenient house on a difficult and irregular site. . . .

Mr. Sheridan, in building this theatre, is supplying along, felt want, for since the closing of the old theatre there has.' been little or no dramatic entertainment provided in the town, if we except a fugitive performance in the Public. HalL The theatre will also be an ornament to Warrington from an architectural point of view, as is proved by the numbers of interested spectators which it attracts daily. It is to be opened early in, November with precisely the same programme as that provided on the closing of the Priam of Wales Theatre, " Miriam's Crime," in. which Mr. /bins. ley Sheridan has a out precisely suited to his ability. The proeeeds of the first performance, it is gratifying to. state, are to be handed over to the local Infirmary. We trust this may be the beginnisg of a long,, prosperous career fur the Warrington New Theatre Royal.

THREATENING 11 POLICSALAN.—Ox Tuesday, at the War- rington Borough Police Court, three young men named Michael Henneesey, Cropper's-brow, Thomas. Fleming, Fennell-street, and dohs Garretty. Ship-yard, labourers, were charged with drunkenness. When spoken to by P.C. Hennessey, on Monday afternoon, prisoner Hennessey, amongst other threats, said he would use a knife if there was a row. The other two showed their clogs and said what they would do. Prisoners were taken into custody with the assistance of P.S. Bowen and P.C. Bruen, and were very violent when at the police station.—Chief Con- stable lint remarked that an Irish polioeman appeared to be a target for the Irish population in Warrington. Such men as the prisoners thought they should not be interfered witk by an Irish policeman,but if they meddled with Con- stable Hennessey they would get the worst of it —Prisoner Hennessey : I am not dull of apprehension nor ignorant of the law. I never carry a knife, and I will reform if you let me off. I hope you will temper !Entice this morning with a bit of mercy,—They were each fined 10a and costa, or 14 days,

• MISCELLANEOUS:A new writ•was-issued for Scarborough In the room of Mr. Dodson resigned.—Mr. RITCHIE gave notice, on an early day, to call attention to the system of foreign bounties, and to move a resolution stating that it be the duty of the Government to take step/ to prevent the ruin of British trade by a syetem.of bounties.—Lord Han- TrbraTow. replying to Mr. Chaplin, said Egyptian papers promised would give full information,as to General (dor- don.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Mr. Broadhurst, said if he introduced the Franchise Bill to-night he would put down the second reading for Monday; Met he would not move the second reading that night unless he could do so at an early hour.—Mr. FAWCETT, replying to Mr. Ruston, I said sixpenny telegrams would come into operation on the let of August, next year.

, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN AND HIS- CRITICS, Sir F. MILNER asked Mr. Chamberlain if a certain report of his speech at Birmingham was correct. The right loon. gentleman re- plied that the report was accurate, and the distnrbance that took place was occasioned by roughs en- gaged by the Tories as " chuckers out." He did not reply to Mr. Chaplin' speech because he thought he was acting as jackal to Lord Churchill.— An angry discussion ensued, Lord R. Churchill and Sir Stafford Northcote condemning the observations of Mr. Chamberlain.—The Speaker did not think" jackal," unpar- liamentary•—Mr. Catemnicatanr said he only used the term In a figurative masa. He was willing to withdraw the obser- vation if it was hurtful to the feelings of: the noble lord. DERATB-ON• THE ADDRESS.—On the adjourned debate re- sumed on Mr. Harrington'- amendment to the Address for inquiry intoiithe circumstances attending the Maans• trasna murder, Mr. A. O'Connor supported the amendment. —The SOLICATOR•GENERAL for InaLatanopposed the amend- ment, and repudiated the charge made against the Crown officials in Ireland.—Mr. HEALY supported the amendment, and severely censured the Government for the manner this matter bad been treated by. Crown officials.— Colonel Nosaw.urged that there should be a further inquiry. —Lord R. CHURCHILL regretted that independent members had not taken part in tha discussion. Rea admitted there was difficulty in the case because concession meant diminu- tion of the Government majorityon the Franchise Bill, and would involve the resignation of Lord Spencer.— Mr. TuEvEratAta.denied that party or political considerations would influence the Government in arriving at the decision of the present amendment. He belie7ed there had been perfectly adequate inquiry under-the circumstances Further inquiry would be to strike at the foundation of justice in Ireland. The declarations made by the three men on the scaffold would not be produced; and such statements ought to have no weight against the overwhelming testimony brought forward at the trial.—On the motion of Mr. PAR- NELL, the debate was adjourned. THE RBTRESENTATION ON THE- Pncput.—Mr. GLAD. sroax,amid loud cheers, asked for leave to introduce a hill to amend the law relating to the representation of the people of the United Kingdom. He proposed that the second reading should be fixed for Thursday.—Lord' R. CHURCHILL said that on that occasion he should move-as an amendment that no bill would be satisfactory which did not provide a pro- per provisionfor the arrangement of electoral areas.—Leave was given, and the bill was brought in and read a first time. The House adjourned at ten minutes to one.

div.head: MISS HALLWOOD'S CONCERT.
div.p: MISS HALLWOOD'S CONCERT.

Miss Annie Hal(wood may be said to have opened the Warrington musical season on Wednesday evening by a con- cert in the Public Hall, which was successful alike in point of attendance and in tbe satisfaction given by the artistes The ball was well filled in every part with the exception perhaps of the reserved seats,though these were by no means anything like empty. In the rendering of the varied and excellent programme which she had, arranged, Miss Hall- wood was supported by an adequate company of vocalists: and instrumentalists which comprised.the well-known name& of Madame Laura Smart, Mr. Ludwig (of the Carl Rosa Opera Company), and Mr. Josef Cantor, who acted as con doctor. The instrumentalists, who contributed in no small degree to the success of the concert, were Mr. T. Shaw, (violin), Mr. J. Bell (corset) e Mr, V. L. Needham (fiute); and Mr. A. E. Workman (harmonium); the pianoforte being under the skilful management of Mr- Cantor. The concert was opened by an overture by the band, after which the lively chorue of fishers from "The Maniac " "Merry Boys Away "" was rendered by the whole company, the brief solo parts being taken by Mesdames. Laura Stuart, E. Eborall, Miss Hallwood, and Mr. S. Kirkham. A quartette "Lo the early beam of morning"' (Siege of Rochelle) by Madame E. Eborall, Mies Hallwood, and Messrs. Broadley and Burt followed, and was efficiently rendered. Mr. E. Edwards was successful in giving the solo from the defendant's' song "-When first my old, old love "fmom the "Trial by... 1 cry,' and was rewarded by coniiderable applause; and ,Mr. H. Broadley, who took the .solo in the Bohemian rang with chorus "To the Greenwood." achieved a like surmises. Madame Smart's first solo was that of the " Swal:ew song" " Cofickle swallow "-from " Esmaralda," which was-given with chorus. Madame Smart's peculiar qualities .of voice ' are excellently adapted for the efficient rendering of such a., song as this, which is. full of rapid, transitions and needs a flexible treatment, and it May be said te have been her meet successful effort. At its close there was a round of applause, which was continued for scam-time. The only other piece in which .Madame Smart appeared as a 'aoloist was in the servants'chortee "The hiring,fair,," from 1" Les Cloches de Corneyille," in which she was again well ireceived. The song" Tnou'll passing hencal"Ware the first which fell to the lot of Mr. Ludwig, and the_ exceedingly • capable manner in which ha dealt with it at, once installed him as the most successful vocalist of the evening. At its conclusion Le was recalled by the persistent applause, and repeated. The pieces which Mr. Ludwig mthseemently sang were " There is a green bill " (Gotueod) and "Molly Bawn," for-both of which he was recalled by; the nnanimona, plaudits onthe audience. In coming forward to sing he. first song, wkich was a canzone, " Fierce flames were raging," from "II Troseatore," Miss Hulivreod was very cordiall7, greeted, and was afterwards called upon for an encore song. In addition to officiating as conductor Mr Josef Cantor gave two songs, one 'Travellers all," from "The Siege ol Rochelle," and the other "The Judge's career," from "Trial by jury," both of which were greatly enjoyed, .a prtion of the latter baying to be repeated; in re- pones to the loud applause. Mies Kate Nono, who took the song in the song and chorus "The torpedo and the whale," scored a enema, and part of the piece was repeated. Amongst the numerous other items oath° programme a grand duo,' " Qui eat Homo," by Madame Laura Smart and Mies Hall- ooed, is specially deserving of notice owing to the eery efficient manner in which it was rendered by these two 1 artistes. The concert vas suitably brought taa close by a very effective treatment of the lively chorus. if Let's give three cheers," from " H.M.S. Pinafore," by the full com- pany.

BOARD.--The final meeting of the members of this,Board, as at present consti- tuted, was held at the Board School on Tuesday. evening. Present—Bev. T. P. Kirkman (chairman and clerk), and Messrs. James.Hatton, LeW4Birehall, Richard Turner, and Alfred Dixon iiattendance officer)..--The Attendance Officer submitted his monthly report, which stated, that he had visited the various schools in. the Board's district during the past month, when he found that the attendance had im- proved except in a few eases. He reported that 14 children had been away from school sick; and that, the average at- tendance at the Board School for the past month had been 118. lie stated that that being the end of his three years' term of office as attendance officer to the Board, he desired to tender his resignation, as he did not wish to be re- appointed again. The report having been adopted, and the reaigeation accepted, it was unanimously resolved "That tXe best thanks of the Board be tendered to Mr. A. Dix,on forth, very obliging and efficient way in which he has with even mere pains and detail than what were deraanged of him, discharged the duties of his office as attendance officer of the Board, and that the same be recorded in the minutes to his credit, with the highest praise." Severed accounts having been passed, the proceedings terminated,

THE ELECTORS OF vvgsT SUTTON WARD.— LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, —The term of three years, for which you did me the honour of electing me as one of your representatives in the Council for the West Button Ward, will expire on the let November, and I therefore beg again to offer you my services. Should you again honour me with this mark of your confidence, my best efforts shall be exerted in the in- terest of your ward, and of the borough generally.-1 remain. Ladies and Gentlemen, your obedient servant, ED WARD JOHNSON. Elephant-lane, Button, October 17th 1884. TO THE BURGESSES OF PARR WARD.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—My present term as one of your representatives at the Town Council will shortly expire, and I beg again to offer myself as a candidate for a renewal of the honour. During the 12 years for which I have represented you many very important matters have been dealt with ; in these I have tzlken an earnest and active part, and I trust that my actions have met with your approval. Whilst a great number of important questions concerning the health, the sanitary con- ditions, and the general interests of the town have been dealt with, many still remain for disposal, and my wish and hope is that, as your representative' I may assist in their considera- tion by the Town Council. My sole desire has been to secure the true interests of the town, and if I should again be returned by you my best energies shall be given with the same object in View. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obliged and faithful servant, RICHARD PILEINGTON. Glass Works, St. Helene, 15th October.,lBB4. ELIZABETH MATHER Deceased:Pursuant to Statute 22 and 23 Victoria, chapter 35. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that all Creditors and other Persons having claims affecting the estate of Elizabeth Mather. late of Wellington place, in Latchford, in the County of Chester, widow. who died on the 12th day of November 1881, and whose Will was proved in the District Registry at Chester of the Probate Divi- sion of the High Court of Justice on the 4th day of March, 1882, by James Marsh, of Warrington, in the County of Lan- caster, Flour Dealer, and John Hickson, of Weaver-view, Barnton, Northwich, in the County of Chester, Waterman, two of the executors therein named, are hereby required to SEND THE PARTICULARS OF SUCH CLAIMS in writing to me the under- signed, the Solicitor to the said Executors, at No. 6. FROG- HALL-LANE, in WARRINGTON aforesaid, on Or before the 15th DAY OF DECEMBER, 1881, after which day the said Executors will distribute the assets of the said Testatrix among the par- ties entitled thereto, having regard to the claims only of which they shall then have had notice; and the said Executors will not be liable for the assets so distributed to any person or persons of whose claim or claims they shall not have had notice at the time of such distribution. Dated this 15th day of October, 1884. THOMAS RICHARD SHEPHERD.
